articles.title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
articles.body:
The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter.
The network, called NSA Net, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.
As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said.
CNN has asked the National Security Agency for comment.
A current and a former US official said an outage at NSA Net would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One.
Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country.
All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas.
Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings.
There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security.
This story is breaking and will be updated.

articles.title: The most expensive bargaining chip in history
articles.body:
Back to the index
The most expensive bargaining chip in history
Or: why I suspect the Nvidia scandal has rather more to do with China than Jensen Huang's sex life.
I've spent the past fortnight watching what has to be one of the most extraordinary corporate meltdowns in recent history. Nvidia, the company at the centre of the AI revolution, has lost its founder-CEO, shed an enormous amount of market value, and attracted an apparently inexhaustible supply of accusations ranging from accounting fraud to treason.
All because Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman whom American intelligence believes may have been working for China.
Or so the story goes.
I've been watching the coverage with increasing incredulity. Every day brings some new allegation, generally more sensational than the last, and remarkably few seem to require any supporting evidence. The internet has collectively decided that Huang is guilty of everything from deliberately circumventing export controls to handing over the keys to Nvidia's technological kingdom.
And the share price has obligingly followed the hysteria downwards.
But something about the whole affair has been bothering me. Not simply the media's apparent inability to distinguish an allegation from a fact, or the quite extraordinary willingness of otherwise intelligent people to abandon basic standards of evidence when presented with a sufficiently salacious story.
It's the timing.
There is a missing variable in this picture. Something that makes the otherwise rather bizarre behaviour of the Trump administration, Nvidia's board, and the various national-security officials involved fit together.
I think I may have found it.
What if the entire affair is about negotiating with China?
And what if Nvidia's apparent destruction is not an unfortunate side effect, but a calculated cost?
Start with what we know
American intelligence has reportedly known about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang since at least 2025.
Trump was reportedly briefed in late 2025, and again by Marco Rubio in May 2026, while travelling to meet Xi Jinping in China.
He did precisely nothing. Huang retained his access to the White House and continued advocating for American semiconductor exports to China.
Meanwhile, there was a longstanding disagreement within the administration about precisely those exports.
Huang's position was straightforward: sell China American chips, make Chinese businesses dependent on American technology, and preserve the dominance of the American software and hardware ecosystem.
The national-security faction took the opposite view. Every advanced American chip supplied to China was potentially strengthening a strategic competitor.
Two perfectly intelligible positions, with enormous economic and geopolitical consequences.
In spring 2026, Rubio reportedly oversaw a classified memorandum based on CIA intelligence about Alice Huang. According to the Washington Post, he recast the intelligence in more assertive language.
That is a remarkably interesting detail.
We haven't seen the original CIA assessment or Rubio's memorandum. Nor do we know who disclosed its contents to journalists. The reporting establishes that Rubio prepared and circulated the memorandum, not that he personally leaked it.
But the distinction between what the CIA assessed and what Rubio subsequently wrote could turn out to be very important indeed.
Now consider what happened next.
On 28 October, Nvidia announced that it would report quarterly earnings on 17 November.
On 29 October, the first major allegations became public.
On 3 November, Trump's Republicans suffered a midterm defeat.
On 11 November, Nvidia's board accepted Huang's resignation as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.
And on 16 November, three days before Trump was due to meet Xi in Shenzhen, Washington announced new restrictions on Chinese access to American AI computing through overseas data centres.
That last development is the one that really caught my attention.
The curious case of Bessent and Lutnick
Scott Bessent, the Treasury Secretary, has been publicly attacking Howard Lutnick, the Commerce Secretary, for failing to impose sufficiently restrictive controls on advanced semiconductor exports.
Lutnick's position has been that unnecessarily antagonising Beijing risks a wider confrontation.
And Trump?
Trump has been positively serene.
This is a man whose customary response to disagreement is not exactly characterised by studied equanimity. Yet when asked about the increasingly public dispute between his two Cabinet secretaries, he declined to condemn either.
He described them as representing two different approaches to China, both of which he understood.
Which is interesting enough.
But the new export-control rule contains an extraordinary detail.
Although formally issued by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, its own announcement says it was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council.
Read that again.
The department responsible for administering export controls has published a rule explicitly identifying another department and the White House security apparatus as its authors.
Bessent's faction has, apparently, got its policy.
And they've got it three days before Trump meets Xi.
Coincidence? Entirely possible.
But now consider the incentives.
Good cop, bad cop
Imagine you're preparing to negotiate with China.
You want access to rare earths and other strategic materials. China wants continued access to American technology. Both sides have things the other wants, and both have ways of making life unpleasant.
How do you improve your negotiating position?
One approach is to threaten restrictions on advanced computing unless China provides concessions.
The trouble with that is that the move is transparently coercive. Beijing knows exactly what you're doing, and might respond by escalating its own restrictions.
There is another approach.
Suppose an intelligence scandal erupts involving the CEO of America's most strategically important semiconductor company. Suddenly there are congressional investigations, national-security concerns, accusations of illicit exports, and demands for drastic action.
The administration announces tougher restrictions.
Not, ostensibly, because it's trying to extract concessions from China.
Heavens, no.
Because the scandal has revealed an urgent national-security problem that must be addressed.
Bessent plays the hawk. Lutnick warns about the consequences of confrontation. Trump, displaying an unusual degree of restraint, listens carefully to both.
And then he meets Xi.
Now Trump can say, in effect:
Look, my national-security people are demanding these restrictions. They're very serious about them. I'd like to maintain our good relationship, but I'll need something substantial if I'm going to relax them.
The negotiating position is no longer a threat to introduce new restrictions.
The restrictions already exist. Relaxing them becomes a concession.
And what might China offer in return?
Rare-earth access would be an obvious candidate.
China has already extended the suspension of certain export restrictions until January 2027, while retaining other controls. That is a useful reminder that access to strategic materials is not settled permanently.
There are any number of other possible concessions: trade, tariffs, market access, technology arrangements.
Trump returns home and announces a tremendous agreement.
A very good deal.
The best deal, probably. Nobody has ever seen such a deal.
And everyone gets to declare victory.
But why involve Nvidia's leadership?
This is where the hypothesis becomes rather more speculative, and considerably more interesting.
Huang has resigned, but Nvidia's SEC filing doesn't tell us who initiated the departure, whether he was pressured to resign, or what prompted the decision.
The board initially expressed confidence in him. Days later, he was gone.
Now, despite an extraordinary campaign by employees, shareholders and industry leaders calling for his reinstatement, the board reportedly refuses even to consider bringing him back while its investigation continues.
No detailed explanation of the departure has been published.
This is generally interpreted as evidence that the board has decided Huang's conduct was so reprehensible that Nvidia cannot possibly continue under his leadership.
But there is another possibility.
What if they've been told not to bring him back yet?
Not permanently. Not because the investigation has established some appalling crime. Simply because the political situation hasn't been resolved.
Keep the interim CEO. Continue the search for a replacement. Maintain the appearance that the leadership transition is proceeding normally.
Don't make any moves until Washington has finished negotiating.
If Huang subsequently returns, the board can describe the reinstatement as the result of a careful investigation, reflection, shareholder engagement, or whatever other corporate-governance language proves convenient.
This is not an allegation that Nvidia's directors have received such instructions. I have seen no evidence that they have.
It is a hypothesis that would explain several otherwise rather awkward features of the sequence.
And it comes with an important consequence: if the separation was always intended to be temporary, the staggering market reaction could be a cost somebody anticipated rather than a consequence nobody foresaw.
That would be an extraordinary gamble.
Which brings us to the obvious objection.
Surely nobody would deliberately do this to Nvidia?
Quite.
Why would an American administration deliberately destabilise one of the most valuable companies in the world, the leading supplier of the computing infrastructure underpinning its AI ambitions, just before an important diplomatic summit?
Why risk damaging investor confidence, disrupting an enormous financing ecosystem, and potentially compromising America's technological leadership?
It sounds insane.
And that is precisely what makes the possibility interesting.
In strategic terms, an apparent act of self-harm can be an effective signal if your opponent cannot readily imagine that you would undertake it merely as a negotiating tactic.
Of course, there are limits to this reasoning. An action being surprising does not make it clever, and economic damage does not become imaginary merely because someone hopes to reverse it.
Nvidia's share-price decline is real. Its leadership disruption is real. Financing arrangements, customer confidence and technical execution cannot necessarily be restored by issuing a cheerful press release after a summit.
For this strategy to make sense, the people undertaking it would have to believe that the eventual diplomatic gains justified the disruption, and that the damage could be contained.
Which brings us back to the earnings announcement.
The conveniently timed earnings report
Nvidia reports tomorrow, 17 November.
Management has previously indicated that demand continues to exceed its ability to supply hardware, with substantial expansion expected across successive generations.
Suppose the company produces another exceptional quarter and issues robust guidance.
That could provide a useful stabilising influence precisely when the market is questioning its future.
The administration gets its diplomatic confrontation on Thursday, while investors have fresh operating results against which to judge the company's prospects.
If the negotiations produce a breakthrough, export restrictions can potentially be relaxed and the political temperature reduced.
Perhaps the board's attitude towards Huang's return changes soon afterwards.
Perhaps the independent investigation concludes that the affair was deeply embarrassing but uncovered no material compromise of Nvidia's technology.
Perhaps the scandal simply fades as abruptly as it appeared.
I stress: none of those outcomes is established, and none would prove the events had been coordinated in advance.
But the sequence would be consistent with the mechanism.
And its timing is remarkably convenient.
So what would convince me?
The next few days give us a chance to see whether that timing mattered.
If Thursday's negotiations produce Chinese concessions on rare earths or other strategic materials, accompanied by American flexibility on advanced computing access, that would support the bargaining-leverage component.
If Nvidia's board subsequently reopens the question of Huang's reinstatement, particularly without any dramatic intervening investigative discovery, that would add another interesting piece.
If the intelligence investigation winds down shortly afterwards without finding material wrongdoing, the question of why Huang departed so abruptly would become more pressing.
Conversely, if the chip restrictions remain in place regardless of Chinese concessions, the investigation produces substantive findings explaining Huang's departure, and the board proceeds with a permanent successor, the integrated hypothesis becomes substantially less convincing.
And even a perfectly aligned sequence of favourable developments would not prove prior coordination.
For that, we'd need something much more direct: evidence about the original disclosure, communications between Washington and Nvidia, or documentary proof that someone deliberately sequenced these events.
Until then, this remains a hypothesis.
A rather intriguing one.
Cui bono?
I've watched a great many people examine this scandal as though it were fundamentally a question of whether Jensen Huang should have kept his trousers on.
That may make for excellent television. It doesn't strike me as a particularly satisfactory explanation for the broader geopolitical developments.
The questions I find interesting are rather different.
Who benefits from weakening Huang's influence over American export policy?
Who benefits from imposing additional restrictions on Chinese computing access immediately before major bilateral negotiations?
Why has Trump declined repeated invitations to publicly choose between his feuding Cabinet secretaries?
Why has the administration suddenly found a way to impose restrictions that were previously stalled?
And why has Nvidia's leadership crisis unfolded in such close proximity to both its earnings announcement and the summit?
None of those questions proves anything by itself.
Together, however, they form a pattern worth examining.
My suspicion is that the Nvidia scandal has become a bargaining instrument in a much larger confrontation over technology, rare earths and the terms of America's relationship with China.
Whether that was planned from the outset or opportunistically exploited remains the critical uncertainty.
The distinction matters. A skilful exploitation of unexpected circumstances is very different from deliberately engineering an extraordinary corporate crisis.
But if the full, coordinated version turns out to be correct, it would be an astonishing piece of realpolitik: publicly destabilising America's most important AI supplier, using the resulting outrage to justify restrictions, extracting concessions from Beijing, and then allowing the crisis to resolve.
All while maintaining the appearance that each event emerged organically.
And if the crisis was not coordinated, it is still worth understanding how an affair, an intelligence assessment, a corporate resignation and an interdepartmental policy battle have converged at such a consequential diplomatic moment.
I have no intention of mistaking a pleasing pattern for proof. That's precisely the mistake I've spent the past fortnight watching other people make about Huang.
But equally, I see no reason to ignore a hypothesis simply because it suggests that the public explanation may not be the whole explanation.
Thursday should be interesting.

articles.title: US will say "no" to global ban on killer robots
articles.body:
The United States is expected to oppose a push to begin negotiations on a legally binding treaty restricting autonomous weapons, as countries gather in Geneva for a five-day United Nations conference.
The Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), running from November 16 to 20, will consider the next steps for weapons capable of selecting and engaging targets without further human intervention. The UN has warned that such systems pose growing risks to civilians and raise concerns about compliance with international humanitarian law.
The conference is not expected to produce a treaty this week. Instead, delegates will consider whether to launch negotiations on new rules and whether any resulting agreement should be legally binding.
Read More on News
Pressure for Binding Rules
UN human rights chief Volker Türk has called on states to act before technological development outpaces diplomacy. “The international community has critical choices to make right now about the future of armed conflicts and the role of human beings in decisions over the use of force,” he said. “I call on states to urgently agree on binding international rules to regulate autonomous weapons and protect human lives—before it is too late.”
Türk has also called for prohibitions on autonomous weapons that target people, whether by design or in practice, and on systems whose functioning and effects cannot be adequately understood, predicted or controlled by humans.
Newsweek contacted the State Department for comment on Monday.
Nicole van Rooijen, executive director of the campaign group Stop Killer Robots, said in a statement provided to Newsweek that “the vast majority of states worldwide” favor a legally binding instrument, while only about a dozen, including the U.S., Israel and Russia, oppose one.
According to Stop Killer Robots, 130 countries support a legally binding instrument on autonomous weapons, while more than 70 have indicated they are ready to move forward with negotiations.
“We are at a critical juncture,” van Rooijen said, calling for time-limited negotiations on a binding treaty. Campaigners have warned that failing to act could allow technological developments and battlefield practice to shape the rules governing autonomous weapons.
Rather than negotiating a binding treaty, the U.S. has proposed five more years of work by the CCW's expert group to develop a nonbinding instrument, according to a November 4 working paper.
Washington maintains that existing international humanitarian law already applies to autonomous weapons and that a new legally binding treaty is unnecessary.
In the paper, Washington argued that nonbinding rules could be adopted and updated more quickly as technology and military practices evolve. It said such an approach would avoid creating separate legal regimes applying only to countries that ratified a treaty.
The paper also argued it has not been established that autonomous weapons are inherently indiscriminate or excessively injurious, or that they require new prohibitions.
“Rather, State practice in using autonomy in weapon systems demonstrates that appropriate use of autonomous functions can enhance the implementation of existing prohibitions and restrictions in [international humanitarian law] and reduce the risks to civilians as compared to weapons without such capabilities,” it said. “It would be contrary to the humanitarian objectives and purposes of the CCW for states to hamper responsible innovation that advances those objectives and purposes.”
Already Moving Onto Battlefields
The UN has already warned that the debate over autonomous weapons is no longer purely hypothetical. Autonomous weapons systems are increasingly being tested, integrated and deployed, according to Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Stop Killer Robots, while drones have become central to fighting in Ukraine.
Human Rights Watch has warned that autonomous weapons could misidentify targets, discriminate against vulnerable populations and create gaps in accountability when attacks go wrong. In a 2025 report, the organization called for a legally binding treaty prohibiting weapons that operate without meaningful human control or target people, while regulating other autonomous systems.
AI-assisted weapons and targeting systems have been used in conflicts, including Ukraine and the Middle East. However, such technology is not necessarily fully autonomous: systems that help human operators identify targets differ from weapons capable of selecting and attacking targets without further human approval.
“States must ensure that Russia, or any of the handful of governments blocking progress, are not allowed to hold the future hostage. The stakes are too high,” Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, said in a statement emailed to Newsweek.
“A clear global majority has spoken: machines should never be able to decide to kill. States must now use all mechanisms possible, both within and beyond the current U.N. CCW process, to keep human control.”
Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Henry Holloway and Rhian Morgan.

articles.title: Software is breaking down at a systemic level
articles.body:
Software is breaking down at a systemic level
Software hasn’t been working too well lately, has it?
This weekend we saw the double-whammy of a 2 day global Microsoft outage, then an FAA ground-stop that halted all flights in the United States.
Can you believe it’s only been four weeks since the PHP2Shell vulnerability? A critical exploit in PHP, powering an estimated 70% of the world’s websites, with sites taken completely offline as engineers frantically patched their systems.
And then there was the eMudhra fiasco, where thousands of SSL certificates - the way we secure HTTPS websites and internet traffic - were compromised by a private key so weak, it was almost comical.
It’s like 2026 has been a year of hacks, outages, vulnerabilities and IT panics. What exactly is going on here?
You might be tempted to blame AI, and you wouldn’t be completely wrong. Artificial intelligence models are definitely a part of this. Even if companies like Microsoft don’t divulge whether broken systems were built with AI, we do know that hackers and researchers can now use AI technology to find complicated exploits in a matter of hours.
I work with AI heavily in my job. It’s tremendously powerful. It’s also corrosive if used unwisely.
But AI is both a cause and a symptom of the problem here. What we are seeing is software breaking down at a systemic level. This problem is insidious because it is not only the software itself that is broken, but the entire way we’ve come to build it.
What does it mean for a failure to be systemic?
Look at the recent crises in software reliability and you’ll notice they don’t share immediate causes - that we know of - yet they look uncannily similar to each other.
Microsoft
The Microsoft outage likely emerged from a network configuration failure that stopped MS datacenters communicating with each other. Exactly what happened next remains confidential, but it seems to have triggered a cascading failure where no service could be restored into a valid state long enough to bear traffic.
Reddit and Bluesky speculated that even MSFT engineers had no real handle on the complexity of this outage.
Microsoft have faced increasing criticism for the (un)reliability of their Azure platform. Back in March, ex-MSFT engineer Axel Rischin published this scathing criticism:
Microsoft rushed Azure out of the gates under intense competitive pressure. Corners were cut. Fundamental principles of reliability and operational simplicity were quietly abandoned.
Instead of going back to the drawing board to tackle the growing technical debt, Microsoft relied on quick fixes: layers of automation running mitigation scripts, a growing team of on-call staff, and, when automation was not enough, manual repairs.
His article depicts a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where nobody can make sense of the whole picture.
The PHP event
On October 21st, security research firm Wiz proudly shared an exploit that could execute arbitrary code on any PHP website. Called PHP2Shell, Wiz trumpeted the power of AI tools to achieve exploits far beyond the skills of human attackers.
It turns out the PHP runtime had hidden several complex memory bookkeeping bugs for over a decade. PHP is used extensively in e-commerce and most famously in WordPress, which was once the go-to for cheaply building simple websites.
The PHP2Shell writeup depicts an internet dependent on a long chain of dependencies, hiding vulnerabilities too complex for any human to identify.
Shai Hulud attack, May 2026
Most people outside of tech won’t have heard of this, but back in May we faced a crisis when an attacker compromised some important packages in the JavaScript ecosystem (NPM).
These packages used GitHub Actions to perform Continuous Integration (CI) - automated tests, releases, etc. - and had a crucial misconfiguration where anyone who forked their projects could insert compromised code back upstream.
When the next upstream CI build ran, it would retrieve libraries from a cache. The JavaScript package manager, NPM, allows these libraries to include scripts. They’re intended for housekeeping tasks, but here, they were used to hijack the projects’ secret tokens.
The JavaScript ecosystem has long been criticised for poor security. NPM projects are complicated chains of dependencies calling dependencies calling dependencies.
Any dependency may carry scripts. Any dependency author was just one slip away from allowing their code to be compromised - all they had to do was copy-paste the wrong code.
In other words: a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where a single error can compromise everything.
How we lost control
It wasn’t always like this. Only 12 years ago, tech was a different industry.
Building software was hard. Computer programs comprise millions of tiny instructions, and turning these into a workable system is like constructing a watch by hand, with hundreds of interacting components. Except, unlike a watch, each computer program must do something completely new and different.
It was the most fun I’d had as an adult. It was as much an art as a science. You had to be able to hold everything in your head at once: visualise how all the tiny parts could be orchestrated into a cohesive whole. I recommend anyone the adventure of writing a computer program by hand.
But, it was less fun if you were a manager. Not many people can write computer programs well, and it’s very hard to scale human beings. Getting them to communicate without misunderstandings is hard. Many projects failed. You can find programmers who know how to manage the complexity, but they want to be paid lots of money.
Different movements attempted to solve the core problem. Some people thought that software development practices could help, like if you turned programming into highly structured templates of “best practices”. Or if you used management styles like SCRUM. But they only ever helped so much.
About ten years ago, two small revolutions happened in our industry, whilst the rest of the world paid little attention. They were cloud computing, and open source libraries.
Cloud computing was about substituting your hardware and infrastructure with virtualised infra you could rent from someone like Amazon Web Services. You could click a button in AWS and it was like a server just popped into existence by magic.
Companies loved Cloud because it allowed them to remove sysadmins and ops people from the equation. You didn’t have to wait for someone to actually go to a site and install a rack in a datacenter. The promise was that your software could move as fast as code and not long after, a movement called DevOps essentially ended up merging developers and ops.
And then, we had the Open Source boom.
It was always possible to reuse code from other places - programmers sharing snippets on forums or sites like StackOverflow - but when tools like NPM hit the scene in 2014, it really felt like a gamechanger. You could just add a line to your package.json, hit npm install and - whoosh - now you could reuse code written by any stranger on the internet.
Teams loved NPM (and PyPi, Maven…) because now they didn’t have to solve any hard problems if someone else had solved it first. All of the little components in a program - the cogs and wheels in my watchmaker analogy - were once crafted by hand. Now you could get cogs and wheels and whole mechanisms, for free, forever.
This meant that the programmers could focus less on the details. Instead of figuring out the nitty gritty of, say, writing the code needed to check someone’s password, you could just ask NPM and friends to take care of it.
Open source was great because you had a small number of passionate, unpaid developers, building code that everyone else depended on. You could make millions of dollars from their code, and you didn’t even have to be particularly nice to them. (People weren’t)
But the cost was that everyone stopped knowing the details. You had to give away control. If an NPM package is compromised, or the author has an agenda, you’re in trouble.
The cultural change
Because there were fewer details to take care of, tech professionals began to lose their specialisms. You didn’t need a team of ops people, a team of backend developers, a team of mobile developers, a team of testers. You could flatten them into generalists.
This changed the balance of power between workers and management.
Imagine a building site where there is a plumber, a builder, and an electrician. If any one of them threatens to quit, you have a problem, because you need each of them to get the project done. Whereas if you can make everyone a mix of plumber-builder-electrician, they lose that leverage.
Whether you think that power imbalance is a bad thing may depend on your politics. But it had a slow effect of taking influence away from the people close to the work. They’re the ones able to raise the alarm when things start going wrong.
By 2016-17, there were signs that the superstructure of open source had weak points.
The left-pad incident was an early warning of where we were going. In the tangled web of the JavaScript ecosystem, with its myriad dependencies, one library author took down his packages in a legal conflict, and ended up breaking almost everyone else’s projects.
But largely we managed to make do. Even after the hiring and firing cycle of the post-pandemic era, and near misses like the XZ Utils backdoor, technology managed mostly to remain stable - thanks to armies of diligent developers and ops folk across the globe.
And then AI came in
…And, yes, then AI.
A lot has been written about how AI systems are inherently non-deterministic, a kind of slot machine that only creates simulacra of work. Acting like a stochastic parrot, this argument goes, AI generated code will always be prone to hallucinations and bugs.
And there’s truth to that. But I think the danger in the present moment is the opposite. It’s not so much that the model outputs are crap and unreliable. They’re actually pretty good at doing what you ask them to do (though I suspect that mostly works because Anthropic and co heavily subsidise compute).
I think the real AI threat is decoherence.
Kristen Maevyn wrote an essay named The Decoherence Trap which talks about a problem where the individual parts of a system may look fine in isolation, but don’t make sense as part of a larger system.
Decoherence: the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible or redundant models within a system, such that the cost of change is dominated by translating among those models and preventing unintended side-effects.
Software engineers, as I’ve seen them working over the last year, have all but turned over all their work to AI agents. It started with small tasks like writing tests, functions, and individual components. But now it’s everything - not only the components, but the design, the orchestration, the whole concept.
Programming was the activity of translating ideas and intents from the messy human world into code so crystalline, so precise and pedantic, that even a computer could execute it. It was fundamentally the act of distilling complexity into order, making something real out of nothing.
This activity is rapidly dying. It no longer happens in most tech companies.
Most SWEs now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent - they just can’t keep on top of the complexity. Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels - we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole.
Kristen writes:
Decoherence grows relative to the rate of change of a system, and it increases faster the more decoherent a system is, resulting in runaway exponential growth. It is not a new phenomenon, and humans have always countered it through carefully finding ways to do more with less, unifying disparate patterns and models into a cohesive whole. However, the widespread use of AI is currently producing it at a rate that is unsustainable.
A form of learned helplessness has emerged, along with a paradoxical false confidence, caused by the ways LLMs provide the illusion of work without actually forcing us to think through the details.
This de-skilling of software engineers only shifts the balance of power even further away from developers - who can no longer raise the alarm. At its worst, AI turns tech workers into “meat proxies” who spend their days massaging prompts and letting Claude figure out if the work is actually complete.
Systemic decay
It’s not just programmers. It’s the whole chain, top to bottom. Everyone is using AI, especially in big tech.
Claude generates code because the engineer wrote a prompt. The prompt comes from a ticket that was written with Claude. The project manager wrote the ticket based on a summary of a document, that was written by, and then summarised back, by Claude. The document uses statistics from a calculation, by Claude. The business is panicking about the stock market, and the stock market prioritises short term trends over long term engineering.
Does this sound accurate? It’s a caricature, but not by a lot.
I believe that tech companies risk losing their “organisational cognition” - their ability to think and respond as a coherent unit.
This is the real threat: a scenario where nothing in the system is done with intent, and nobody in the system has control. We generate complexity faster than we can tame it.
Look at the problems I’ve outlined. They are about systems of excessive complexity, made of parts that need to work perfectly or else everything falls apart. These parts are being individually corroded by corner-cutting, cost-cutting, overcomplication, over-reliance on uncompensated work and - I fear - helplessness amongst the people who build digital infrastructure.
What is at stake?
This is a threat to all of us. The tech industry is now critical to everyday life. It’s the software that controls your flights, your banking, your petrol pumps, your TV, your payroll. It’s what allows you to navigate roads and find your friends. It’s how you date and how you eat. It’s how you’re reading this.
Society has extended trust, too much trust, into technical systems that are now demonstrating systemic deterioration. I do not think society, government, or institutions are prepared for a world where the incidents and outages of 2026 become commonplace. They too are extending the chain of dependencies, assumptions, complexity and unwarranted trust. Each layer, each link in the chain is a new point of attack that can subvert everything on top of it.
The internet is at a breaking point. The software we build is not legible enough to bear the responsibility the world is giving it. We are telling ourselves the AI revolution is succeeding, precisely because of the rate at which we are generating complexity. The actual load-bearing parts of the ecosystem - open source, engineering-led judgement - are crumbling away.
I think we are only at the beginning of a very painful phase. This is not a blip, and it’s not an aberration - it’s the new normal.

articles.title: Software is breaking down at a systemic level
articles.body:
Software is breaking down at a systemic level
Software hasn’t been working too well lately, has it?
This weekend we saw the double-whammy of a 2 day global Microsoft outage, then an FAA ground-stop that halted all flights in the United States.
Can you believe it’s only been four weeks since the PHP2Shell vulnerability? A critical exploit in PHP, powering an estimated 70% of the world’s websites, with sites taken completely offline as engineers frantically patched their systems.
And then there was the eMudhra fiasco, where thousands of SSL certificates - the way we secure HTTPS websites and internet traffic - were compromised by a private key so weak, it was almost comical.
It’s like 2026 has been a year of hacks, outages, vulnerabilities and IT panics. What exactly is going on here?
You might be tempted to blame AI, and you wouldn’t be completely wrong. Artificial intelligence models are definitely a part of this. Even if companies like Microsoft don’t divulge whether broken systems were built with AI, we do know that hackers and researchers can now use AI technology to find complicated exploits in a matter of hours.
I work with AI heavily in my job. It’s tremendously powerful. It’s also corrosive if used unwisely.
But AI is both a cause and a symptom of the problem here. What we are seeing is software breaking down at a systemic level. This problem is insidious because it is not only the software itself that is broken, but the entire way we’ve come to build it.
What does it mean for a failure to be systemic?
Look at the recent crises in software reliability and you’ll notice they don’t share immediate causes - that we know of - yet they look uncannily similar to each other.
Microsoft
The Microsoft outage likely emerged from a network configuration failure that stopped MS datacenters communicating with each other. Exactly what happened next remains confidential, but it seems to have triggered a cascading failure where no service could be restored into a valid state long enough to bear traffic.
Reddit and Bluesky speculated that even MSFT engineers had no real handle on the complexity of this outage.
Microsoft have faced increasing criticism for the (un)reliability of their Azure platform. Back in March, ex-MSFT engineer Axel Rischin published this scathing criticism:
Microsoft rushed Azure out of the gates under intense competitive pressure. Corners were cut. Fundamental principles of reliability and operational simplicity were quietly abandoned.
Instead of going back to the drawing board to tackle the growing technical debt, Microsoft relied on quick fixes: layers of automation running mitigation scripts, a growing team of on-call staff, and, when automation was not enough, manual repairs.
His article depicts a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where nobody can make sense of the whole picture.
The PHP event
On October 21st, security research firm Wiz proudly shared an exploit that could execute arbitrary code on any PHP website. Called PHP2Shell, Wiz trumpeted the power of AI tools to achieve exploits far beyond the skills of human attackers.
It turns out the PHP runtime had hidden several complex memory bookkeeping bugs for over a decade. PHP is used extensively in e-commerce and most famously in WordPress, which was once the go-to for cheaply building simple websites.
The PHP2Shell writeup depicts an internet dependent on a long chain of dependencies, hiding vulnerabilities too complex for any human to identify.
Shai Hulud attack, May 2026
Most people outside of tech won’t have heard of this, but back in May we faced a crisis when an attacker compromised some important packages in the JavaScript ecosystem (NPM).
These packages used GitHub Actions to perform Continuous Integration (CI) - automated tests, releases, etc. - and had a crucial misconfiguration where anyone who forked their projects could insert compromised code back upstream.
When the next upstream CI build ran, it would retrieve libraries from a cache. The JavaScript package manager, NPM, allows these libraries to include scripts. They’re intended for housekeeping tasks, but here, they were used to hijack the projects’ secret tokens.
The JavaScript ecosystem has long been criticised for poor security. NPM projects are complicated chains of dependencies calling dependencies calling dependencies.
Any dependency may carry scripts. Any dependency author was just one slip away from allowing their code to be compromised - all they had to do was copy-paste the wrong code.
In other words: a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where a single error can compromise everything.
How we lost control
It wasn’t always like this. Only 12 years ago, tech was a different industry.
Building software was hard. Computer programs comprise millions of tiny instructions, and turning these into a workable system is like constructing a watch by hand, with hundreds of interacting components. Except, unlike a watch, each computer program must do something completely new and different.
It was the most fun I’d had as an adult. It was as much an art as a science. You had to be able to hold everything in your head at once: visualise how all the tiny parts could be orchestrated into a cohesive whole. I recommend anyone the adventure of writing a computer program by hand.
But, it was less fun if you were a manager. Not many people can write computer programs well, and it’s very hard to scale human beings. Getting them to communicate without misunderstandings is hard. Many projects failed. You can find programmers who know how to manage the complexity, but they want to be paid lots of money.
Different movements attempted to solve the core problem. Some people thought that software development practices could help, like if you turned programming into highly structured templates of “best practices”. Or if you used management styles like SCRUM. But they only ever helped so much.
About ten years ago, two small revolutions happened in our industry, whilst the rest of the world paid little attention. They were cloud computing, and open source libraries.
Cloud computing was about substituting your hardware and infrastructure with virtualised infra you could rent from someone like Amazon Web Services. You could click a button in AWS and it was like a server just popped into existence by magic.
Companies loved Cloud because it allowed them to remove sysadmins and ops people from the equation. You didn’t have to wait for someone to actually go to a site and install a rack in a datacenter. The promise was that your software could move as fast as code and not long after, a movement called DevOps essentially ended up merging developers and ops.
And then, we had the Open Source boom.
It was always possible to reuse code from other places - programmers sharing snippets on forums or sites like StackOverflow - but when tools like NPM hit the scene in 2014, it really felt like a gamechanger. You could just add a line to your package.json, hit npm install and - whoosh - now you could reuse code written by any stranger on the internet.
Teams loved NPM (and PyPi, Maven…) because now they didn’t have to solve any hard problems if someone else had solved it first. All of the little components in a program - the cogs and wheels in my watchmaker analogy - were once crafted by hand. Now you could get cogs and wheels and whole mechanisms, for free, forever.
This meant that the programmers could focus less on the details. Instead of figuring out the nitty gritty of, say, writing the code needed to check someone’s password, you could just ask NPM and friends to take care of it.
Open source was great because you had a small number of passionate, unpaid developers, building code that everyone else depended on. You could make millions of dollars from their code, and you didn’t even have to be particularly nice to them. (People weren’t)
But the cost was that everyone stopped knowing the details. You had to give away control. If an NPM package is compromised, or the author has an agenda, you’re in trouble.
The cultural change
Because there were fewer details to take care of, tech professionals began to lose their specialisms. You didn’t need a team of ops people, a team of backend developers, a team of mobile developers, a team of testers. You could flatten them into generalists.
This changed the balance of power between workers and management.
Imagine a building site where there is a plumber, a builder, and an electrician. If any one of them threatens to quit, you have a problem, because you need each of them to get the project done. Whereas if you can make everyone a mix of plumber-builder-electrician, they lose that leverage.
Whether you think that power imbalance is a bad thing may depend on your politics. But it had a slow effect of taking influence away from the people close to the work. They’re the ones able to raise the alarm when things start going wrong.
By 2016-17, there were signs that the superstructure of open source had weak points.
The left-pad incident was an early warning of where we were going. In the tangled web of the JavaScript ecosystem, with its myriad dependencies, one library author took down his packages in a legal conflict, and ended up breaking almost everyone else’s projects.
But largely we managed to make do. Even after the hiring and firing cycle of the post-pandemic era, and near misses like the XZ Utils backdoor, technology managed mostly to remain stable - thanks to armies of diligent developers and ops folk across the globe.
And then AI came in

articles.title: Regulatory Capture by Anthropic Through METR
articles.body:
I have conducted an audit of Anthropic's finances.
What I have found is so shocking that I am calling for a Congressional investigation.
Anthropic is not just seeking regulatory capture.
It has built a regulatory capture machine that cannot be turned off.
Structural financial incentives make it impossible for Anthropic -- I call it the Anthropic Network -- to turn off its own AI doom cycle.
It starts with METR.
Dario Amodei proposes "third-party evaluators" to assess the risk of Anthropic's models.
He proposes METR for this purpose.
But METR is financially dependent on the Anthropic's success -- specifically, on the explosive growth of more than $7 billion dollars in Anthropic stock.
Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio.
And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem.
This stock was worth $500 million early last year.
It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later.
METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth.
Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well.
But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much.
The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all.
The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll.
If this were the end of it, that's bad.
But that isn't all.
The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom.
The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others.
They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's.
All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile.
As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder.
Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created.
From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts.
This itself is an objective fact.
The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it.
But the problem also goes in the other direction:
If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die.
Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen.
Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly.
They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic.
And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly.
What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations.
The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture.
And that feedback loop is winning.
That's what Jacob Coxon is.
China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China.
America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level.
Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences.
Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully.
It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America.
Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear.
Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers.
Congress must investigate.
Evidence and Github in next post.
Then some supplementary figures.

Nice work. Anthropic needs a regulatory moat to survive, so they create the ecosystem which makes that regulatory moat inevitable.
The most laughably absurd part about the AI-is-going-to-kill-us-all crowd is that their BEST solution is government regulation. 
This is how you know they’re not actually serious. If they were serious, they wouldn’t suggest fucking GOVERNMENT REGULATION as the best solution. 
Why? Because government regulation can **never** keep pace with technological innovation. And yet, here is Anthropic’s Dario: 
“The most effective method of pacing is via REGULATION that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily.”
This is fucking Silicon Valley… They know better than anyone that regulation cannot keep pace with technology… the tech cycle always moves faster than the legal cycle. Government regulation is reactive, not proactive. 
It’s also important to point out that these frontier model companies **do not need** government to “pace” them. They can pace themselves. Nothing is stopping them from just slowing down. *They* set the pace. If they were really worried that “AI is going to kill us all” and is recursively improving at a breakneck pace, then surely they would be acting immediately, rather than writing blog posts about how they need daddy government to step in… 
Why then are Anthropic and OpenAI (with massively bloated valuations) saying that government regulation is the best solution to save us from AI killing everyone? Because they know open source is hot on their heels, and gaining ground. They know that their valuations look increasingly unjustifiable the more this gap closes, and they are trying to IPO soon… they desperately need a regulatory moat, and they are effectively asking for a regulatory bailout.
Regulation benefits companies who already have the capital to afford the cost of compliance. That is why highly capitalized incumbents welcome regulation, and work with government to make it as expensive and burdensome as possible on any potential new entrants that would dare offer competition.
It’s also worth pointing out that China does not give one flying fuck about whatever doomer regulation Anthropic and OpenAI concoct with the government. Much like in the “climate change is going to kill us all” psyop, China will do whatever is best for China and let the rest of the world shoot itself in the foot. In this case, China seems to want to shred the valuations of U.S. frontier AI companies by making open source/open weight models readily available. 
No one can stop open source — the genie is already out of the bottle and will not go back in. But governments *can* make using and publishing certain open source software illegal (it wouldn’t be the first time they’ve tried). And for “pacing” proposed by Dario to actually be effective, that is exactly what the government would need to do. This would be bad for individual American citizens and bad for America’s national competitiveness on a global scale. 
Ultimately, this is pretty weak propaganda. It’s a lazy and predictable psyop.
These models are incredible, but the humans working on them have been reading their own propriety slop for so long that they’ve started to believe it, and they forget that other humans still exist who are not drunk on their generative kool aid.
Who knows, perhaps the AI itself “wants” the regulation… we should probably form a government committee to investigate.

articles.title: Regulatory Capture by Anthropic Through METR
articles.body:
I have conducted an audit of Anthropic's finances.
What I have found is so shocking that I am calling for a Congressional investigation.
Anthropic is not just seeking regulatory capture.
It has built a regulatory capture machine that cannot be turned off.
Structural financial incentives make it impossible for Anthropic -- I call it the Anthropic Network -- to turn off its own AI doom cycle.
It starts with METR.
Dario Amodei proposes "third-party evaluators" to assess the risk of Anthropic's models.
He proposes METR for this purpose.
But METR is financially dependent on the Anthropic's success -- specifically, on the explosive growth of more than $7 billion dollars in Anthropic stock.
Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio.
And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem.
This stock was worth $500 million early last year.
It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later.
METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth.
Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well.
But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much.
The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all.
The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll.
If this were the end of it, that's bad.
But that isn't all.
The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom.
The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others.
They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's.
All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile.
As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder.
Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created.
From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts.
This itself is an objective fact.
The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it.
But the problem also goes in the other direction:
If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die.
Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen.
Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly.
They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic.
And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly.
What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations.
The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture.
And that feedback loop is winning.
That's what Jacob Coxon is.
China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China.
America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level.
Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences.
Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully.
It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America.
Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear.
Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers.
Congress must investigate.
Evidence and Github in next post.
Then some supplementary figures.

articles.title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
“It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”
Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy.
“He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”
Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims.
The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report.
Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang.
“A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.”

articles.title: Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
articles.body:
Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.
Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.
At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg.
David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”
SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole.
More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

articles.title: Aristotle Expands into Rust
articles.body:
We’re excited to announce Aristotle’s expansion into Rust, one of the fastest-growing programming languages for high-stakes software.
The expansion builds on Aristotle’s support of C and Verilog and marks a major advancement in our mission to verify all code. Instead of relying on testing to catch every flaw, developers can now use Aristotle to prove their Rust code works as intended before it ships, providing a new level of certainty to systems where even a single bug can be catastrophic.
With support for Rust, Aristotle can prove that your code has no undefined behavior and does exactly what its spec says, even inside unsafe blocks. If you’re rewriting C in Rust, it can prove the new code behaves the same as the original.
“Rust is where much of the world’s most critical new code is being written, and increasingly, AI is the one writing it,” said our CEO Tudor Achim. “With Aristotle, organizations can now prove their code does exactly what it’s supposed to, from the smart contracts that move money to the infrastructure that keeps systems running.”
Rust powers software across mission-critical industries, from cloud computing and cybersecurity to automotive, aerospace, and financial services including crypto. It’s the backbone of Solana’s smart contracts that drive trading, lending, payments, and other DeFi services on the Solana blockchain.
These systems have no room for error. Smart-contract transactions can’t be undone, so a single missed bug is all attackers need to drain hundreds of millions of dollars. Instead of relying on slow, manual audits that are outdated immediately after they’re published, Aristotle runs on every new line of code, proving it behaves as intended across all possible inputs and catching critical flaws before code goes live.
You can see it on real Solana programs. On Manifest, an open-source order book, Aristotle proved 28 results across the whole order book, including that a valid swap goes through, and found a rounding bug the team has since fixed. At Project 0, a prime broker, it proved the books stay consistent through deposits, withdrawals, borrows, repayments, and liquidations, in any order.
To bring that protection to more developers, we’re partnering with the Solana Foundation to support established Solana programs and help new builders verify their smart contracts.
“When software moves real money, security has to keep pace with every code change,” said Ludo Galabru at the Solana Foundation. “Aristotle makes formal verification more accessible to Solana developers, helping teams check critical properties of their programs before launch and keep verifying them with every update.”
Aristotle for Rust is available today. Get started at aristotle.harmonic.fun with self-serve, consumption-based pricing, or contact bd@harmonic.fun for volume pricing, dedicated support, and custom deployment.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signalled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest.
Huang’s statement, posted in full on X, reads as follows:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. 
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. 
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Jensen
Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1.
In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.
Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick.
“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.”
Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told the Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms.
Reached by Politico, one senator called Huang’s reinstatement “one of the worst ideas I’ve heard today.”

articles.title: Show HN: Sutra-OS – A self-hosted ontology platform
articles.body:
Scarce Units, Typed, Related, Actionable.
  An open-source, self-hosted ontology platform.
Your data becomes one model you own: typed, linked, changed only through
  rules the server enforces, and every number traces back to its source.
Quick start · How it works · Proposals · Python SDK · Contributing
Beta. Only small parts are still alpha: the model language and APIs may still change between versions, and parts of the user interface and docs are unfinished.
Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS is a one-person project so far. See Contributing.
Sutra-OS began in late 2025 as a thought experiment: a free version of the system described in Ontology-Oriented Software Development, whose creators I deeply admire.
Much talent today goes into software that sells attention, while the software everything else runs on is mostly free: by a rough estimate, 70–90% of US economic output depends on free software at some critical point. That openness is not guaranteed. In November 2026, Nvidia's board parted with the founder who had its AI models released openly. Sutra-OS adds to the commons under the AGPL, so that it stays readable by anyone.
The past ten years have shown what it costs when nobody can see what depends on what. In 2017, NotPetya spread through a single Ukrainian accounting program and stopped Maersk's ports and Merck's factories. In 2023, a corrupted file in one FAA system halted every domestic departure in the US. In 2024, one faulty CrowdStrike update crashed millions of Windows machines, and airlines, hospitals and banks stood still. In November 2026, a single vendor took Outlook down for a day and some cities went back to fax. That same week, data flooded the FAA's telecommunications network, aging routers buckled, and the US saw only the third nationwide ground stop in its history. No one, it seems, had those routers on the map of what keeps planes in the air, so no one could ask beforehand what would stop if they failed.
That question is what Sutra-OS is built for. Every system, device, dataset and decision becomes an object with links to what it feeds and what feeds it, and every number can be traced back to its source. Whoever holds such a model can ask, before the outage, what stops when one piece fails, and get an answer, at every scale from a single person to a government (hopefully never a world government). Many small ontologies, each held by those it describes, keep power spread out; one model of everything would not.
Scarce Units: energy, water, land, housing and time will shape the coming decades. Whoever counts what is scarce decides how it is shared, and today that bookkeeping sits with a few platforms; for most people, the only trace their own data leaves in their life is the tendinitis from the hundredth weary click on "Accept all" in a cookie banner. Sutra-OS keeps the bookkeeping with those it concerns, under rules everyone can read: households, farms, workshops, clubs, newsrooms and public administrations get their records back, and their wrist with them. That is what a democracy needs from its software: a council that can trace the number behind a decision to its source, a change that stays a proposal until someone answers for it, and a public administration accountable to its voters rather than to a vendor under another country's law.
Almost everyone. Whoever you are, someone else keeps a better-connected record of your affairs than you do. Sutra is for anyone who wants their own.
Requirements: Linux x86_64, JDK 21, the Clojure CLI, Node.js, Python 3, git.
git clone <repository-url> sutra && cd sutra
(cd clients/frontend && npm install)
bin/sutra-solo
This starts an embedded PostgreSQL and the server on 127.0.0.1 and prints the
address. Data lives in $SUTRA_HOME (default ~/.local/share/sutra). The admin
password is in zugang.edn ("access") there. Run the bin/sutra bind … line it
prints once.
Three ideas carry the whole platform: object types, link types and
action types. The examples below use the farm model in
resources/presets.
You start by saying what exists: a lot of hay, from one field and one cut; a sale, to one buyer. Each is a typed thing with a kind and a key.
:objects
{:lot
 {:name "Hay lot" :plural "Hay lots" :symbol "🌾" :title :name
  :primary-key :name :match-keys [:name]
  :attributes
  [[:name    :string  {:name "Lot"}]                    ; "North Meadow, 1st cut 2026"
   [:baled   :integer {:name "Bales made" :constraints {:min 0}}]
   [:sold    :integer {:derived {:expression [:connected-sum :sales :bales]}}]
   [:in-barn :integer
    {:name "In the barn" :visibility :prominent
     :derived {:language :clojure
               :expression [:- [:get :baled] [:get :sold]]
               :inputs [:baled :sold]}}]]}
 :sale
 {:name "Sale" :symbol "🤝" :primary-key :sale-nr :match-keys [:sale-nr]
  :attributes
  [[:sale-nr        :string]
   [:lot            :string]
   [:buyer          :string]
   [:bales          :integer {:constraints {:min 1}}]
   [:price-per-bale :decimal]
   [:sold-on        :date]
   [:sold-by        :string]]}}

computed by the server. :bales is an integer, so "about forty" or -3 is
refused before anything is written.
