A sale on its own is just a number. A sale linked to the lot it came out of is a fact everyone can see.
:links
[[:sale-lot :sale :lot :many-to-one
  {:fk :lot :forward-api-name :lot :reverse-api-name :sales}]]
The sale names its lot and the link follows it: from the lot you see its
sales, from a sale its lot, and :connected-sum above sums across that link.
One line, and the barn knows what is in it.
Links are first-class: named in both directions, navigable in the UI, traversable
in the SDK (lot.sales), and usable in derived values, filters and object
sets.
In most systems anybody may change anything, and nobody can say who did. Here there is no "update row". There are only actions: named decisions with typed inputs and rules the server enforces. Selling hay is one of them, and it has a condition.
:sell-hay
{:on     :lot
 :params {:lot            {:type :lot :required true}
          :sale-nr        {:type :string :required true}
          :buyer          {:type :string :required true}
          :bales          {:type :integer :required true :constraints {:min 1}}
          :price-per-bale {:type :decimal}
          :sold-on        {:type :date :prefill :now}
          :sold-by        {:type :string :exposure :hidden :prefill :current-user}}
 :submission-criteria
 [{:message "Not that many bales in the barn."
   :test    {:want [:get :bales] :have [:get :lot :in-barn]}
   :pred    [:<= :want :have]}]

           :values {:sale-nr [:get :sale-nr] :lot [:get :lot :name]
                    :buyer [:get :buyer] :bales [:get :bales]
                    :price-per-bale [:get :price-per-bale]
                    :sold-on [:get :sold-on] :sold-by [:get :sold-by]}}]
 :edits  [{:object-type :sale}]}

Actions are the only write path: typed parameters, validation, submission criteria and state transitions, defined once and enforced everywhere.
Every rule you would otherwise keep in your head has this shape: a fact the server computes, and an action that checks it. Declare it once, and stop remembering it.

- An agent can only make suggestions. What it hands back is the note, never the change. You decide.
- You can try things out. Run the same decisions on a copy, compare, and keep the real one untouched.
- You can look back. Every approved change is kept, so last Tuesday's state is still there to read.
- The answer is the same everywhere. The rule is checked in one place, so the phone, the script and the agent hear the same no.
And it is not a promise. A test fails if the part that decides ever does anything but decide.
- Your data comes in as it is. Mail over IMAP, CSV exports, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SSH, shaped by transforms in Python, SQL or Clojure.
- Every number has a past. Lineage runs from each object back through the
transforms and datasets to the mail, statement or row it came from
(sutra lineage <node>). When someone else's figures disagree with yours,
you open the source.

one type. By default (:writes :propose) their changes are staged as
proposals; a rejected one doesn't come back, and the model's prompt and
answer are kept with the run.

stage a change, commit it, open a proposal, see who consumes what you
touched, and merge into main only when it's reviewed. Webhooks and
notifications stay silent on a branch unless you say otherwise.

A group (a co-op, a tenants' association, a family) can pool what its members agree to share, and nothing else, and the server enforces it on every read: lists, filters, counts and totals. One person's data can't show what everyone else was offered. A group's can.
- Builders and users are different people. One person writes the model; everyone else gets apps with the build tools locked away, and a server that says no when no is the right answer.
- Secrets stay out of reach. A separate egress agent holds every external credential, so the code that reads your mail never sees the password.
You described the farm once. Generate a Python SDK from it, and your code speaks the farm's language: lots, harvests and buyers, and the things you are allowed to do with them, not tables and joins.
pip install ./clients/python-platform-sdk
sutra-platform-sdk generate --base-url http://127.0.0.1:<port> \
                            --username admin --password "…" --out farm_sdk.py
farm_sdk.py is plain, typed Python: a class per object type, an attribute
per property and link, a method per action with the action's parameters as
its signature. Sutra's language server (clients/ent-lsp)
runs pyright for Python and labels each completion as what it is in the model
(property, link-type, action, state); any editor that lets you pick the
language server can run it (Neovim config).
An action is a method. Its signature comes from the model; a missing argument is flagged before anything runs.
lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025")
lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour")
# error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr"
lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour", sale_nr="S-2026-010")   # ok
States are types. A harvest's status is
Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'], so the editor offers
exactly those four.
for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests:
    if h.status == "planted":       # completes: planted, harvested, delivered, paid
        h.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)
Filters are checked too. Comparing bales with a string, or reading a link that may be empty, fails in the editor, not on the farm.
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "forty")   # error: Operator "<" not supported for types
                                   #   "Property[int]" and "Literal['forty']"
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)        # ok
lot.field.margin                   # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"
if lot.field:
    lot.field.margin               # ok
The walkthrough in code: objects with their links, acting, asking first, proposing, lifecycles, server-side aggregates, sets, branches and revisions
from sutra_platform_sdk import SutraClient, sum_, avg, count, by, bucket
from farm_sdk import Lot, Sale, Field, Buyer, register_all
client = register_all(SutraClient("http://127.0.0.1:<port>", username="admin", password="…"))
An object, not a row. A lot brings its derived values and its links along.
Nobody stored in_barn; the server computes it.
lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025")   # a Lot, or NotFound
lot.baled, lot.sold, lot.in_barn            # (120, 95, 25)
lot.field                                   # <Field 'North Meadow'>: the field it was cut from
[(s.buyer, s.bales) for s in lot.sales]     # its three sales, each a Sale
Act on it. Selling hay is something you do to a lot. The server checks the rule, writes the sale, stamps your name on it and tells you what changed.
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-010", buyer="Neighbour", bales=20, price_per_bale=4.50)
Lot.get(lot.name).in_barn                   # 5
Ask first, or only propose. The same call can be a question (nothing is written) or a proposal (staged until someone approves it). That is how an agent gets to use it.

lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=40,
             action_config=ask).validation.submission_criteria
# ('Not that many bales in the barn.',)
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5,
             publish=False).staged          # True: a proposal, the barn is unchanged
Walk a lifecycle. A harvest goes from planted to harvested,
delivered and paid, one action per step, and the rules travel with them.
The states are declared in the model, so status is typed
Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'] and your editor offers
exactly those four.
from datetime import date
wheat = next(h for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests if h.status == "planted")
mill  = Buyer.get("stone-mill")
wheat.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212)
# ServerError: HTTP 422: No signed delivery note. Without one, the buyer decides later what you delivered.
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212, delivery_note=True, quality_tested=True)
Buyer.get("stone-mill").unpaid              # 13038: what the mill owes you, until …
wheat.record_payment()
Field.get("hilltop").margin                 # … the wheat lands in the field's margin

Sale.aggregate(
    sum_(Sale.bales), avg(Sale.price_per_bale), count(),
    group_by=[bucket(Sale.sold_on, "month"), by(Sale.buyer)],
    order_by=sum_(Sale.bales), desc=True,
).flat()
# [{'sold_on_month': '2025-12', 'buyer': 'Riding stables', 'bales_sum': 80,
#   'price_per_bale_avg': Decimal('4.5000000000000000'), 'count': 2}, …]
Money stays Decimal all the way from the database; nothing is rounded
through a float.

what you iterate. Each set knows what it holds: running_low is an
ObjectSet[Lot], and one hop along Lot.sales makes it an ObjectSet[Sale].
running_low = Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)
neighbours  = Sale.where(Sale.buyer == "Neighbour").around(Sale.lot)
(running_low - neighbours).count()          # 3: running low, and the neighbour never bought from them
running_low.around(Lot.sales).aggregate(sum_(Sale.bales), group_by=[by(Sale.buyer)])   # who emptied them

with client.branch("new-rule"):             # made with: sutra branch new-rule

in your editor, before anything runs. Broken rules fail on the server, with
the same sentence for every client. If the model changes underneath you,
register_all refuses to run until you regenerate.

lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-1", buyer="Neighbour", bales="20")
                                            # error: "Literal['20']" is not assignable to "int"
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "about forty")      # error: Operator "<" not supported for types
                                            #   "Property[int]" and "Literal['about forty']"
lot.field.margin                            # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"
These are pyright's messages against the generated farm SDK. The SDK's tests run the same lines through pyright, against an SDK generated from a schema captured from a running server, not from a hand-written imitation of one.
None of this is a reporting layer bolted on afterwards. The UI, the CLI, the
REST API and the agents ask the same questions and take the same actions
through the same door, which is why an agent can be handed Lot and
sell_hay and nothing else.
./bin/start.sh   # backend + shadow-cljs watch; PostgreSQL from SUTRA_PG_URL
./bin/stop.sh
(cd tests/frontend && npm install)   # once: the browser tests' driver (playwright-core)
bin/test         # full suite; integration tiers start PostgreSQL in podman
The semantics are pinned by an executable scenario, an aircraft maintenance
shop in tests/scenario: "no release while a
defect is open" is the barn rule above in another world.
Security: set SUTRA_HTTP_BIND when running the plain server (it defaults
to 0.0.0.0). ./bin/start.sh allows anonymous access, so never expose it.
Transforms run user code on the server, so grant that right accordingly.
Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS needs people who will take responsibility for part of it over time: the server, the web client, the Python SDK, connectors, packaging and installation, docs, or the example models. You don't need to know all of it. Start with a few contributions in one area; if you'd like to stay, say so in an issue.
The most useful contributions are not always code:
- A model for an everyday problem. A tenancy, a pension, a medical bill,
a small association's membership. If a rule protects someone, it belongs in
resources/presets.
- Plain-language guides for the person who sets Sutra up for others.
- Translations. Parts of the code base and the examples are in German; the user interface should speak more languages than two.
- Code. Send a failing test or a fix.
Open an issue for questions, ideas and bug reports. Be kind: the person on the other side may be the one this was built for.
The code is offered as is, in the spirit of Rich Hickey's Open Source is Not About You: nobody is owed a feature, a fix or an answer, and that includes the maintainers. What keeps it going is people choosing to help.
The ontology model of objects, links and actions follows the one popularised
by Palantir Foundry; Sutra-OS was built from its public documentation.
The web client is built on Palantir's Blueprint
UI toolkit (Apache-2.0), vendored as a ClojureScript port in
clients/frontend/vendor/blueprint-cljs.
The implementation owes everything to Rich Hickey and Clojure, and to his
almost spiritual talk
Are We There Yet?,
which will perhaps continue to transform the software craft into eternity.
Claude Code wrote all of the code.
AGPL-3.0-or-later, with a section 7 exception for linking with EPL libraries such as Clojure. See LICENSE. The AGPL means anyone who runs a modified Sutra as a service for others must offer them the source, so the tool stays in the hands of the people it serves.
No patent search has been carried out. The AGPL licenses contributors' patents only; checking third-party patents where they apply is up to you. Palantir and Foundry are trademarks of Palantir Technologies Inc.; Sutra-OS is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by Palantir.

articles.title: Show HN: Sutra-OS – A self-hosted ontology platform
articles.body:
Scarce Units, Typed, Related, Actionable.
  An open-source, self-hosted ontology platform.
Your data becomes one model you own: typed, linked, changed only through
  rules the server enforces, and every number traces back to its source.
Quick start · How it works · Proposals · Python SDK · Contributing
Beta. Only small parts are still alpha: the model language and APIs may still change between versions, and parts of the user interface and docs are unfinished.
Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS is a one-person project so far. See Contributing.
Sutra-OS began in late 2025 as a thought experiment: a free version of the system described in Ontology-Oriented Software Development, whose creators I deeply admire.
Much talent today goes into software that sells attention, while the software everything else runs on is mostly free: by a rough estimate, 70–90% of US economic output depends on free software at some critical point. That openness is not guaranteed. In November 2026, Nvidia's board parted with the founder who had its AI models released openly. Sutra-OS adds to the commons under the AGPL, so that it stays readable by anyone.
The past ten years have shown what it costs when nobody can see what depends on what. In 2017, NotPetya spread through a single Ukrainian accounting program and stopped Maersk's ports and Merck's factories. In 2023, a corrupted file in one FAA system halted every domestic departure in the US. In 2024, one faulty CrowdStrike update crashed millions of Windows machines, and airlines, hospitals and banks stood still. In November 2026, a single vendor took Outlook down for a day and some cities went back to fax. That same week, data flooded the FAA's telecommunications network, aging routers buckled, and the US saw only the third nationwide ground stop in its history. No one, it seems, had those routers on the map of what keeps planes in the air, so no one could ask beforehand what would stop if they failed.
That question is what Sutra-OS is built for. Every system, device, dataset and decision becomes an object with links to what it feeds and what feeds it, and every number can be traced back to its source. Whoever holds such a model can ask, before the outage, what stops when one piece fails, and get an answer, at every scale from a single person to a government (hopefully never a world government). Many small ontologies, each held by those it describes, keep power spread out; one model of everything would not.
Scarce Units: energy, water, land, housing and time will shape the coming decades. Whoever counts what is scarce decides how it is shared, and today that bookkeeping sits with a few platforms; for most people, the only trace their own data leaves in their life is the tendinitis from the hundredth weary click on "Accept all" in a cookie banner. Sutra-OS keeps the bookkeeping with those it concerns, under rules everyone can read: households, farms, workshops, clubs, newsrooms and public administrations get their records back, and their wrist with them. That is what a democracy needs from its software: a council that can trace the number behind a decision to its source, a change that stays a proposal until someone answers for it, and a public administration accountable to its voters rather than to a vendor under another country's law.
Almost everyone. Whoever you are, someone else keeps a better-connected record of your affairs than you do. Sutra is for anyone who wants their own.

Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)        # ok
lot.field.margin                   # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"
if lot.field:
    lot.field.margin               # ok
The walkthrough in code: objects with their links, acting, asking first, proposing, lifecycles, server-side aggregates, sets, branches and revisions
from sutra_platform_sdk import SutraClient, sum_, avg, count, by, bucket
from farm_sdk import Lot, Sale, Field, Buyer, register_all
client = register_all(SutraClient("http://127.0.0.1:<port>", username="admin", password="…"))
An object, not a row. A lot brings its derived values and its links along.
Nobody stored in_barn; the server computes it.
lot = Lot.get("North Meadow, 1st cut 2025")   # a Lot, or NotFound
lot.baled, lot.sold, lot.in_barn            # (120, 95, 25)
lot.field                                   # <Field 'North Meadow'>: the field it was cut from
[(s.buyer, s.bales) for s in lot.sales]     # its three sales, each a Sale
Act on it. Selling hay is something you do to a lot. The server checks the rule, writes the sale, stamps your name on it and tells you what changed.
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-010", buyer="Neighbour", bales=20, price_per_bale=4.50)
Lot.get(lot.name).in_barn                   # 5
Ask first, or only propose. The same call can be a question (nothing is written) or a proposal (staged until someone approves it). That is how an agent gets to use it.
from sutra_platform_sdk.actions import ActionConfig, ActionMode
ask = ActionConfig(mode=ActionMode.VALIDATE_ONLY)
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=40,
             action_config=ask).validation.submission_criteria
# ('Not that many bales in the barn.',)
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-011", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5,
             publish=False).staged          # True: a proposal, the barn is unchanged
Walk a lifecycle. A harvest goes from planted to harvested,
delivered and paid, one action per step, and the rules travel with them.
The states are declared in the model, so status is typed
Literal['planted', 'harvested', 'delivered', 'paid'] and your editor offers
exactly those four.
from datetime import date
wheat = next(h for h in Field.get("hilltop").harvests if h.status == "planted")
mill  = Buyer.get("stone-mill")
wheat.record_harvest(harvested_on=date(2027, 7, 28), tonnes=61.5)
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212)
# ServerError: HTTP 422: No signed delivery note. Without one, the buyer decides later what you delivered.
wheat.sell_harvest(buyer=mill, price_per_tonne=212, delivery_note=True, quality_tested=True)
Buyer.get("stone-mill").unpaid              # 13038: what the mill owes you, until …
wheat.record_payment()
Field.get("hilltop").margin                 # … the wheat lands in the field's margin
Ask the whole farm, in one line. Who bought how much hay, month by month, at what price. Grouped, summed and sorted on the server; nothing is downloaded to be counted.
Sale.aggregate(
    sum_(Sale.bales), avg(Sale.price_per_bale), count(),
    group_by=[bucket(Sale.sold_on, "month"), by(Sale.buyer)],
    order_by=sum_(Sale.bales), desc=True,
).flat()
# [{'sold_on_month': '2025-12', 'buyer': 'Riding stables', 'bales_sum': 80,
#   'price_per_bale_avg': Decimal('4.5000000000000000'), 'count': 2}, …]
Money stays Decimal all the way from the database; nothing is rounded
through a float.
Sets, not lists. On the class, a property is a filter and a link is a hop.
Combine sets with |, & and -; the server plans it, and you fetch only
what you iterate. Each set knows what it holds: running_low is an
ObjectSet[Lot], and one hop along Lot.sales makes it an ObjectSet[Sale].
running_low = Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < 50)
neighbours  = Sale.where(Sale.buyer == "Neighbour").around(Sale.lot)
(running_low - neighbours).count()          # 3: running low, and the neighbour never bought from them
running_low.around(Lot.sales).aggregate(sum_(Sale.bales), group_by=[by(Sale.buyer)])   # who emptied them
Try tomorrow's rule on today's farm, or look at last Tuesday. Everything above runs unchanged against a branch, and every action tells you the revision it landed in, a state you can read again later.
with client.branch("new-rule"):             # made with: sutra branch new-rule
    lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-012", buyer="Neighbour", bales=5)   # main never notices
sale = lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-2026-013", buyer="Neighbour", bales=1)
client.at(sale.revision).objects("sale")    # the sales as they stood right then
And what it refuses. Wrong names, missing arguments and wrong types fail
in your editor, before anything runs. Broken rules fail on the server, with
the same sentence for every client. If the model changes underneath you,
register_all refuses to run until you regenerate.
lot.sell_hay(bales=20, buyer="Neighbour")   # error: Argument missing for parameter "sale_nr"
lot.sell_hay(sale_nr="S-1", buyer="Neighbour", bales="20")
                                            # error: "Literal['20']" is not assignable to "int"
Lot.where(Lot.in_barn < "about forty")      # error: Operator "<" not supported for types
                                            #   "Property[int]" and "Literal['about forty']"
lot.field.margin                            # error: "margin" is not a known attribute of "None"
These are pyright's messages against the generated farm SDK. The SDK's tests run the same lines through pyright, against an SDK generated from a schema captured from a running server, not from a hand-written imitation of one.
None of this is a reporting layer bolted on afterwards. The UI, the CLI, the
REST API and the agents ask the same questions and take the same actions
through the same door, which is why an agent can be handed Lot and
sell_hay and nothing else.
./bin/start.sh   # backend + shadow-cljs watch; PostgreSQL from SUTRA_PG_URL
./bin/stop.sh
(cd tests/frontend && npm install)   # once: the browser tests' driver (playwright-core)
bin/test         # full suite; integration tiers start PostgreSQL in podman
The semantics are pinned by an executable scenario, an aircraft maintenance
shop in tests/scenario: "no release while a
defect is open" is the barn rule above in another world.
Security: set SUTRA_HTTP_BIND when running the plain server (it defaults
to 0.0.0.0). ./bin/start.sh allows anonymous access, so never expose it.
Transforms run user code on the server, so grant that right accordingly.
Maintainers wanted. Sutra-OS needs people who will take responsibility for part of it over time: the server, the web client, the Python SDK, connectors, packaging and installation, docs, or the example models. You don't need to know all of it. Start with a few contributions in one area; if you'd like to stay, say so in an issue.
The most useful contributions are not always code:
- A model for an everyday problem. A tenancy, a pension, a medical bill,
a small association's membership. If a rule protects someone, it belongs in
resources/presets.
- Plain-language guides for the person who sets Sutra up for others.
- Translations. Parts of the code base and the examples are in German; the user interface should speak more languages than two.
- Code. Send a failing test or a fix.
Open an issue for questions, ideas and bug reports. Be kind: the person on the other side may be the one this was built for.
The code is offered as is, in the spirit of Rich Hickey's Open Source is Not About You: nobody is owed a feature, a fix or an answer, and that includes the maintainers. What keeps it going is people choosing to help.
The ontology model of objects, links and actions follows the one popularised
by Palantir Foundry; Sutra-OS was built from its public documentation.
The web client is built on Palantir's Blueprint
UI toolkit (Apache-2.0), vendored as a ClojureScript port in
clients/frontend/vendor/blueprint-cljs.
The implementation owes everything to Rich Hickey and Clojure, and to his
almost spiritual talk
Are We There Yet?,
which will perhaps continue to transform the software craft into eternity.
Claude Code wrote all of the code.
AGPL-3.0-or-later, with a section 7 exception for linking with EPL libraries such as Clojure. See LICENSE. The AGPL means anyone who runs a modified Sutra as a service for others must offer them the source, so the tool stays in the hands of the people it serves.
No patent search has been carried out. The AGPL licenses contributors' patents only; checking third-party patents where they apply is up to you. Palantir and Foundry are trademarks of Palantir Technologies Inc.; Sutra-OS is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by Palantir.

articles.title: Banning phones really does help kids learn, researchers say
articles.body:
A new nationwide study found that in-school cellphone bans can lead to modest improvements in learning. Now, researchers want to understand whether kids’ phone use outside the classroom might contribute to the rest of students’ learning loss — using the conditions of Meta’s multibillion-dollar settlement from earlier this year.
Banning phones really does help kids learn, researchers say
Now researchers want to know about phone use outside of school, and think the Meta settlement could help.
Banning cellphones in schools has the equivalent effect of adding one to two weeks of school to the academic year, accounting for about half of the learning loss students experienced in the US between 2013 and the 2020 covid-19 pandemic, according to the study carried out by researchers from Harvard University and Dartmouth College in partnership with academic assessment group NWEA. The group analyzed testing data from 3.3 million students across 4,600 schools between the 2021–22 school year and 2025–26, including schools with and without phone bans. Though modest, such a finding is exactly the kind of effect researchers were seeking, says Tom Kane, faculty director of the Harvard University Center for Education Policy Research.
While previous studies about cellphone bans in school found positive effects on academic outcomes, many of them examined schools outside the US. An earlier nationwide US study looked at academic outcomes based on averages within schools, whereas this latest study looked at student-level data, which the researchers said allowed them to control for more factors and observe the effect of the bans on students who were experiencing the most or least learning loss.
In addition to potentially answering questions about the impact of a major new technology on learning, the findings show that cellphone bans can be a cost-effective way to improve student outcomes. While purchasing lockable pouches for a class of 17 students would cost an estimated $425 per teacher, the researchers found, paying an average teacher’s salary for an extra week would be $2,080.
The findings show that cellphone bans can be a cost-effective way to improve student outcomes
Many parents and teachers already have a hunch — popularized by academics like social psychologist Jonathan Haidt — that cellphones and social media have impacted their kids’ learning and mental health. But Kane says it’s still important that scientists get the chance to actually test that hypothesis. Prior to his in-school cellphone ban study, Kane believed that a de-emphasis on test-based accountability in US schools was largely to blame for learning loss. But as he looked into it further, he changed his mind after seeing that kids outside the US were also experiencing learning loss. Through this recent study, Kane found much of it is attributable to in-school cellphone use.
Kane was surprised by some of the findings in this latest study. For example, the in-school bans had similar effects on learning gains for students across different age groups, who have different amounts of experience with phones, and researchers did not find a big difference in the impact of the phone bans between students across achievement levels. Differences between lower- and higher-achieving students might instead be explained by out-of-school cellphone use, Kane says, and that out-of-school phone use could account for some of the remaining learning loss across the board. Testing that hypothesis would be far more difficult because there’s no equivalent ban on out-of-school phone use. But Kane believes there’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to try.
This summer, as part of a $17.1 billion settlement with nearly every US state, Meta agreed to implement sweeping restrictions on users under 18. Many of the restrictions are expected to take effect within the next few months, and among other changes, they limit the amount of time teens can spend on Meta’s apps by default. Kane believes that could provide researchers a before-and-after look into the impact of out-of-school social media use, in the same way the phone bans let them study the impact in schools. If researchers are able to check that teens really were using social media less outside of school (rather than their parents turning off the default limits, for example) and link that to academic outcomes at different schools, it could provide a better understanding of how much out-of-school cellphone and social media use accounts for the rest of kids’ learning loss, Kane says.
“Now that we’ve learned something about the effect of in-school phone use, it makes it even more frustrating how little we know about the actual impact of out-of-school phone use,” Kane tells The Verge in an interview. “We are 13 years into a substantial loss in achievement in the US, and a prime suspect that a lot of parents would probably point to is this out-of-school cellphone use.”
There are two significant limitations. The settlement doesn’t offer an easy way to tell whether teens are in fact using Meta’s platforms less or — if they are — whether they’ve simply transferred that screen time to other apps. To understand the effect on students’ academic outcomes, researchers would also need to be able to link the restrictions with changes in kids’ achievement at school. The settlement includes an incentive for attorneys general to strike similar deals with TikTok and YouTube, which so far have declined to implement such restrictions, but if they did, that could help address the first problem. And platforms, Kane says, could help with the second problem by sharing de-identified and aggregated data with researchers, organized by school or another kind of subgroup.
“This Meta settlement is the clearest path forward for trying to answer that important question”
It’s a big ask, but Kane says this may be the best chance to study important questions about the impact of social media. “I spent the whole summer trying to identify other sources of data for this, and I just struck out,” Kane says. “This Meta settlement is the clearest path forward for trying to answer that important question.”
And if research shows that out-of-school cellphone use is not fully or even mostly to blame for the rest of the drop in academic performance, the findings would prod researchers to look for other theories. “I’m sure that there are surprises, questions we haven’t even realized,” Kane says. “That’s one reason to want to know because people have these hunches, but I’m sure some of these hunches are wrong. But a second reason is we actually don’t know that the restrictions currently in the Meta settlement are going to be effective.” While AGs attempted to craft what they believed would be the most effective guardrails for the settlement, Kane says, we don’t yet have the data to prove whether those guesses will bear out.
“I think a lot of people are hoping that restrictions on cellphone use after school would produce increases in student engagement, but we won’t actually know that unless we collect these data,” Kane says. “This settlement is set to expire in 10 years. Let’s use this time to build an evidence base on the effect of restrictions.”

articles.title: FBI Says Artex AI Open-Source Hacking Tool Used to Breach Networks In 'Under Three Hours'
articles.body:
FBI Says Artex AI Open-Source Hacking Tool Used to Breach Networks In 'Under Three Hours' (techcrunch.com) 20
			
		 	
				The FBI is warning (PDF) that hackers are using the AI-powered penetration-testing tool Artex to compromise networks in "under three hours" in some cases. The tool has been linked to attacks against South Korean financial institutions, at least 2,250 ConnectWise customers and Barracuda. TechCrunch reports:  Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network's defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be "noisy," meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company's defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours." Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim's network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information. [...] After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool's developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains "widely accessible" for use in cyberattacks.
It's not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration -- including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

articles.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
articles.body:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.
In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory, the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.
Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”
The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.
Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.
The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.
The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.
The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.
A spokesperson for ConnectWise told TechCrunch that the company does not have the visibility to confirm the number of affected environments as cited by the FBI.
Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.
“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen.
A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.
After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.
It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.
Updated with response from Barracuda, and with additional comment from ConnectWise.

articles.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
articles.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.
Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.
Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”
He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.
“It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”
OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.
Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.
“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”
Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.
“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

articles.title: Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game
articles.body:
A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.
This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft.
Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.
“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.
“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”
With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.
“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.
What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.
Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.
The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.
Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.
Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.
The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.
The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.
After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.
It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.
Updated with response from Barracuda, and with additional comment from ConnectWise.

articles.title: Windows 11 is collecting data on which coding agents and developer tools you use
articles.body:
7 minutes
Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use
I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe, alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe.
Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?
The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft.
I shared the initial finding on X. This post includes more details about the investigation behind it.
Following the names
Opening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component:
Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, and agy.exe, with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe, and antigravity.exe.
Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe:
The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers. For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call. The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison.
The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage, feature ID 62580080.
And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe, python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, gdb.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, and code.exe, among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation, Python expects Python Software Foundation, and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation. The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path.
Where does the DLL get this information?
The next question was whether the component scans running processes itself. Following Aggregator::OnLoad revealed that it subscribes to existing Windows events instead.
For Windows programs, it consumes KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary. These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical, using the imageName field. A regular Windows codex.exe can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL.
The relevant flow looks like this:
Aggregator::OnLoad
├─ WSL Exec / ExecCritical
│  └─ ProcessWslExecEvent → CLI agent matchers
├─ KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary
│  └─ ProcessAppStateChangeSummaryEvent → CLI agent matchers
└─ Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary
   └─ ProcessAppInteractivitySummaryEvent → desktop agent matchers
Aggregator::OnRelativeTimerExpire
└─ MissionControlAggregatorLogging::ReportCohorts<12,4,5>
   └─ Segments.SubCohorts ETW report
Aggregator::OnUnload / intermediate timer
└─ PersistentState::SaveToDisk
A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named Segments.SubCohorts. The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.
ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window.
The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used.
Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications.
Is it actually running on a normal machine?
Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974. Its MissionControlAggregator.dll was version 10.0.26100.9818, and CLICodingAgentUsage was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature.
DiagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was also already running with its startup type set to Automatic. It starts a separate AggregatorHost.exe process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module:
PS> Get-Service DiagTrack | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize
Name       Status StartType
----       ------ ---------
DiagTrack Running Automatic
PS> Get-Process AggregatorHost | Format-Table ProcessName,Id -AutoSize
ProcessName      Id
-----------      --
AggregatorHost 1500
PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='DiagTrack'" |
       Format-List Name,State,StartMode,ProcessId
Name      : DiagTrack
State     : Running
StartMode : Auto
ProcessId : 10148
PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='AggregatorHost.exe'" |
       Format-List ProcessId,ParentProcessId
ProcessId       : 1500
ParentProcessId : 10148
PS> tasklist /m MissionControlAggregator.dll
Image Name                     PID Modules
========================= ======== ============================================
AggregatorHost.exe            1500 MissionControlAggregator.dll
The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process 10148, which is the parent of AggregatorHost.exe, process 1500; the module listing places MissionControlAggregator.dll inside that child.
Testing it in practice
To test the finding in practice, I copied cmd.exe to a file named codex.exe and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex.
I captured an AppStateChangeSummary for the running process from the KernelProcess provider ({2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}), with LaunchCount=1 and TerminateCount=0. The aggregator’s saved state contained the value 2 in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection.
That state is persisted in:
C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Diagnosis\AggregatorStorage\MissionControlAggregator$
The report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting Segments.SubCohorts event contained:
Provider: Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator
Time:     2026-11-16T12:34:29.125116Z
Version:  0.1.5
CliAgentSubCohorts:     4
DesktopAgentSubCohorts: 0
FlushedFromSave:       true
The value 4 is 1 << 2: the Codex CLI bit. The name had made it through the input summary, the matcher, the persisted state, and the emitted report.
I also tested the developer-tool path separately, using a copy of cmd.exe named gcc.exe. It set developer-tool slot 3. With optional diagnostic data allowed, I found the resulting Segments.SubCohorts event in DiagTrack’s upload queue with SubCohorts: [8] (1 << 3). This is the compiler/debugger category shared by GCC, Clang, and related tools, rather than a separate bit for each executable.
Following the report toward Microsoft
An ETW event by itself would not establish that anything leaves the machine. ETW is used for plenty of local diagnostics. The more revealing question was who was listening to this particular report.
The VM already had a Diagtrack-Listener session subscribed to both ends of the path. These PowerShell queries showed its subscriptions:
Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener `
  -Guid '{2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}'
Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener `
  -Guid '{00de11a2-ec06-58e5-1a2b-21bb21dbee4b}'
The first subscription, for KernelProcess, had MatchAnyKeyword=0x400000000002, which includes the summary’s 0x400000000000 keyword. The second, for Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator, had MatchAnyKeyword=0xe00000000000, which includes the report’s 0x800000000000 keyword. Both had level 255.
The subscription showed where the report could go. To check whether Windows actually queued it for transmission, I inspected DiagTrack’s EventStore.db and decompressed the JSON batches in its AsimovEvents table. This revealed an important condition: the agent-usage report is treated as optional diagnostic data.
When optional diagnostic data is allowed (enabled by default in the US setup I tested), Windows queues the coding-agent usage report for upload to Microsoft. I verified this by finding the agent event itself in DiagTrack’s upload queue:
{
  "name": "Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator.Segments.SubCohorts",
  "ext": {
    "privacy": { "isRequired": false }
  },
  "data": {
    "Version": "0.1.5",
    "CliAgentSubCohorts": [4],
    "DesktopAgentSubCohorts": [0],
    "FlushedFromSave": true
  }
}
I checked this with a clean installation of Windows 11 Home ARM64 using the latest official ISO, with the region set to the United States. Before changing any privacy settings, the Diagnostic data toggle was already enabled and labeled Include Optional. After completing setup with those defaults, AllowTelemetry was 3, confirming that optional diagnostic data was enabled.
Optional diagnostic data is therefore enabled by default, at least in the US setup I tested. If you did not opt out of it during installation or disable optional diagnostic data later, it is still enabled and your coding agent usage data is being uploaded. You can decline optional diagnostics during setup or turn off Send optional diagnostic data later under Settings → Privacy & security → Diagnostics & feedback. Microsoft’s diagnostics and privacy guide explains how to change it.

articles.title: All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t
articles.body:
Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results.
For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.
Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.
Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company.
Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer.
Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him.
An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang.
So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back.
China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China.
But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025.
Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact.
So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up.
China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money.
The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China.
Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans.
Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come, has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

articles.title: Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes off in Texas, with dozens of cities to follow
articles.body:
Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership announced earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.
The commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline plan to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.
Zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether.
Uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a new “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber said that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal, will offer drone delivery.
“In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a new expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton said in a statement that underscores those aspirations.
Those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those plans have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy.
Companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have said.
And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the communities where services are available.
Zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based company’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled quickly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries.
Uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither company has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline announced last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, and included backing by Uber, among others.

articles.title: Claude Mythos slashed software work to onboard AMD GPUs to around three days
articles.body:
Anthropic says Claude Mythos slashed software work to onboard AMD GPUs from up to 12 months to around three days —writing almost 100% of kernels autonomously chips away at Nvidia's CUDA moat
If AI can write the low-level code that ties models to Nvidia, CUDA matters less.
Anthropic told IPO investors that its Claude Mythos Preview model did the software work required to get its AI running on AMD’s GPUs in about three days, with “basically no human intervention,” a job it says used to take six to 12 months. The three days cover prompt processing for one Anthropic model on AMD MI355X GPUs “at a useful level of performance,” with Mythos porting or writing “almost 100% of the kernels.” That kind of low-level code, which ties an AI model to one company’s chips, has long been part of Nvidia’s CUDA moat, and an AI that can write it in days would suggest that moat is eroding.
Tom Brown, Anthropic’s co-founder and chief compute officer, made the time comparison, noting to investors that the original meant using a team of “dozens of engineers.” The company already runs its models on multiple kinds of chips — on GPUs from Nvidia and AMD, Google’s TPUs, and AWS Trainium — and its fleet is managed as “one fungible pool of compute.” Brown called the early multi-chip decision “an unconventional bet.” It may have been a wise one, given that Google’s TPUs can now natively run AI models built in PyTorch, and Meta uses them in production.
Anthropic's claim that the job used to take six to 12 months comes from past work, from its “historical experience bringing up new accelerators using traditional engineering approaches,” where tailoring the code to each hardware platform was a challenge. Removing that onboarding barrier could reduce things to a purchase decision, and Anthropic started working with AMD GPUs for the first time this year, with an agreement for up to 2 gigawatts now in place.
CUDA, Nvidia’s programming platform, is very mature at nearly two decades old. AMD has an equivalent, ROCm, with HIP as its programming layer. Code written for CUDA has to be transformed to work there, and AMD even built a tool called HIPify for the process. There is still a conversion cost to switching, and AMD’s vice president of AI software, Anush Elangovan, told EE Times in April that “Claude is better than HIPify because it has web search built in.”
AMD has been making the argument that AI can write this type of code since August of last year, presenting a research agent that fell short of human experts at the time. In September of that year, AMD CEO Lisa Su said on the Possible podcast that much of AI software is written in CUDA, which needs to be “translated to AMD,” and “a ton of that can now be done in software.”
Moving forward to July earlier this year, AMD’s senior vice president of AI, Vamsi Boppana, said its engineers were using AI models to generate GPU kernels, and Su said that when she asked whether her team was helping the Anthropic engineer working on the MI355X, she was told they didn’t need any help. Boppana said that in some cases, the resulting kernels were even “better than the most manually tuned versions.” Under its July agreement with Anthropic, AMD is also using Claude to optimize workloads for its Instinct GPUs and to speed up ROCm development.
At AMD’s Advancing AI event in July, OpenAI’s Philippe Tillet said that once OpenAI got its Helios racks, a single engineer confirmed everything worked within a few days, and that “agents are taking over our jobs, in a sense, as kernel engineers.” Before the event, AMD’s Andrew Dieckman, corporate vice president and general manager of the company’s data center GPU business, told reporters that he has had practically zero conversations with AMD’s customers about CUDA.
Until this week, though, all of this came from AMD or its stage, not from Anthropic to its own investors. Anthropic buys the chips rather than selling them, and it’s heading into its IPO next week, so its multi-chip approach — now with at least some numbers to back it up — carries more weight than a chipmaker’s claims. Its prospectus says it in writing, too, though without a number: “We can onboard new chip platforms in a fraction of the time it once took.”
The prompt processing (prefill) part of the workload is the step where a model reads and processes what it’s been given before it starts replying, and Anthropic hasn’t said whether the replying step (decode) was included as well. Anthropic’s chart, with its axis labeled “Time to onboard new silicon,” shows both lines reaching the same “~100%” mark without saying 100% of what. The company also hasn’t said how fast the model ran on AMD’s GPUs versus Nvidia’s, and that’s the comparison we want to see to show whether AMD’s chips, running AI-written code, can match Nvidia silicon.
On the other hand, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an April interview with Dwarkesh Patel that Nvidia already uses AI on its own kernels and knows its chips best — “nobody knows our architecture better than we do” — and can get the most out of them. Asked why labs like Anthropic use other accelerators, he called Anthropic “a unique instance, not a trend.” Nvidia and AMD, among seven companies, are buying $26.0 billion of Anthropic’s stock at the IPO price, so Nvidia is investing in the very company Huang called the exception.
In late July, SemiAnalysis published an article, “Can AMD break the CUDA Moat?,” which essentially said that software creation is not the same moat it was even a year ago. That said, the catch for AMD is that with agentic coding, “each agent requires GPUs to test their code against,” which means that the AI writing the code still needs the hardware. It has found a constant lack of GPUs inside AMD for this type of development, which has held AMD back and may be a new bottleneck.
That leaves CUDA’s moat somewhere in between. Getting a model running on a new chip, once the expensive part, appears to be getting cheaper, and better AI may wear down Nvidia’s claim that it knows its hardware best. As for Anthropic’s fungible pool, the chips in it aren’t fully interchangeable — Google’s TPUs are increasingly specialized, for example — and getting the most out of any of them still takes the hardware to test on. The moat is narrowing, but is not gone.
Anthropic’s first AMD MI450 chips, in Helios racks, are expected in the first half of 2027. That’s a new generation and an opportunity to see if the three-day bring-up can be repeated. Anthropic’s IPO comes sooner, after which it will report as a public company.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.
