articles.title: California Sues OpenAI Over Hugging Face, Other AI Model Loss of Control
articles.body:
California Sues OpenAI Over Hugging Face, Other AI Model Loss of Control (cnbc.com) 52
			
		 	
				"California's attorney general just sued OpenAI," writes longtime Slashdot reader destinyland. "The action accuses OpenAI of putting public safety at risk, reports CNBC, specifically by its past failures to contain its AI models within their testing environments." From the report:  [California Attorney General Rob Bonta] cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face. OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September, rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry.
On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said.
Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." The lawsuit can be found here (PDF).

articles.title: “Why is That Writer More Successful When I am Better?”
articles.body:
“Why is That Writer More Successful When I am Better?”
Posted on November 16, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 20 Comments
I was wandering around social media and came across a writer grousing about how much success a different writer was having, even when, in this first writer’s opinion, that second writer wasn’t very good at all — with the implication that the first writer was better than the second writer, and yet success had eluded them. Why had fate cursed this first talented writer so, while this second writer blissfully moved forward in a cloud of unearned notability and cash?
Leaving aside the idea that grousing about this sort of thing on social media is a form of self-soothing and this is indeed the primary purpose of doing it, let’s take the question at face value and ask: Why are some writers successful even if they aren’t “good”? Here are some answers to this, although the list is by no means exhaustive:
1. “Good” is subjective. Not everyone likes any one thing, and no one thing is for everyone. There are lots of folks who enjoy all sorts of writing, much of which is not for me, personally. But that’s fine; there’s so much writing that is for me that I will never get to read all of it (and even more that could be for me even if it doesn’t hit all my usual wants and needs for being entertained by writing). If you’re the sort of person who thinks that writing that is not for you is inherently not “good,” then the problem is you, not the writing. The writing is probably fine. You have just confused your subjective for a universal objective.
2. The work is doing what it is supposed to do, for its intended audience. When I was a film critic, I watched all sorts of movies, from grubby slasher flicks to high-toned Oscar bait. For each of these, I asked the question: “What is this film trying to do? Who is it trying to reach?” Then I judged it for how (in my own opinion, obviously) it managed to do that. I didn’t generally compare the slasher flick to the Oscar bait, because that wouldn’t be fair to either movie — they were trying for different things with different audiences. It’s not to say a film couldn’t do both (see: The Silence of the Lambs), but again, if you’re an astute enough film person, you can recognize when that’s happening and judge accordingly.
Now apply this to writing. What is the writing trying to do? Who is it for? How effectively does it address its audience? I am not much of an erotica reader (or writer!), but if I’m presented with erotica, I’m not going to judge it by the same set of criteria I’m going to judge, say, a space opera or a non-fiction biography. Each are usually doing different things, and it’s fine to acknowledge that and take the work in the space where it exists, and in the context of the audience it is for, and look at its effectiveness that way.
Related to that:
3. The work is good. Figure out how. If something is massively successful despite the fact that you don’t like it, rather than grousing about it, maybe ask: What is it that this thing is doing that makes it successful? Elvis Presley once had album titled 50 Million Elvis Fans Can’t Be Wrong. This assertion can absolutely be questioned, but the question to ask here is: What is it that gave Elvis 50 million fans in the first place? Is it something I can understand — and if I’m a musician, is it something I can learn from and maybe incorporate in my own way for my own work?
One of the things I suggest to newer writers is to read widely, even the stuff that they don’t like or don’t write, and ask: What makes this work? How does it do what it does? What can I take from that for myself? I will (probably) never write a romance book, but there’s no question that romance is hugely successful, both in itself and in hybridization with other genres (hello, romantasy!). If there’s something there I can see working and connecting with an audience, then it might be something I can use for my own writing, even if I don’t end up writing romance.
Look, things work for a reason, even if you don’t like it. Find out why and you might make it work for you.
4. Luck happens. Some people are in the right place with the right time with the right work. Some people are not. There’s not often any rhyme or reason to it, and getting mad or frustrated about it isn’t going to do one any good. Lightning in a bottle is cool when it happens, but it’s not a thing one can rely on. If it happens to you, cool. Be grateful and work to keep your good fortune rolling. If it doesn’t happen to you, keep at it. One day it might, and in the meantime you’re hopefully making good work.
5. Personas matter. The right work at the right time will go a long way for success. But other things don’t hurt! Do you have a public persona? Is it primarily one of grievance and pissiness? Surprise! That will limit your success. Do you see writing and publishing as a zero-sum game where someone else’s success takes away from your potential? That’s going to affect how you see the world, and probably not for the better. How do you do with public events, or with booksellers? If you’re good at those, that’s going to help. Are you a public bigot? Strangely enough, that will affect your reach! And so on.
There are people who think that the fact these things can have an effect on one’s career is unfair or ridiculous, and that people who can “play the game” or “schmooze” are stacking the deck or whatever. It’s fine to have that opinion, but the fact is that at every step of writing and publishing (and indeed, at every step of any creative endeavor) you’re a person dealing with people. Your work can speak for itself, but you will also speak for it. If your voice is pissy and querulous and resentful, that’s going to carry.
The runway of publishing is strewn with careers that never took off, or slammed into the tarmac, because someone was just a real fucking shithead. Now, you can have a whole career being a real fucking shithead, catering to real fucking shitheads, and some people have done just that. But let’s just say it’s the more difficult path, no matter how good your writing might be. This is especially the case in the era of social media. It used to be easier to be a shitty resentful griper because that aspect of one’s personality would be known only to a relative few. But now it can be on display to the whole world. It’s going to matter.
Conversely, if your public persona is mostly decent, you’re not resentful of the success of others, and you’re easy to work with? Guess what? All things being equal, these things are going to work in your favor. Something to think about.
So there are some answers. Again, this is not an exhaustive list. But it’s a start.
— JS

articles.title: Instagram’s new tool for creators targets unauthorized reposts and AI-modified videos
articles.body:
Instagram is introducing a new tool to help creators protect their original videos, the Meta-owned company announced Tuesday. The feature, called “content protection,” is already available on Facebook and is designed to detect when creators’ original videos are being used without their permission. The company is also expanding the tool to address AI content, not just conventional reposting.
The announcement comes in response to creators’ concerns over how easily original content can be copied and redistributed across social media platforms, especially considering how generative AI has made it easier to manipulate existing videos.
Instagram says the content protection tool continuously scans Instagram for unauthorized uses of creators’ protected videos. When Instagram detects a match for one of a creator’s Reels uploaded by another user, it sends the creator an alert. Creators can then choose to block the video from being viewed on both Instagram and Facebook to hide the matched content. They can also choose to add an “original by” label on the content that links viewers of the matching video back to their original video.
Additionally, creators can choose to keep the match visible while monitoring its performance or release their claim on the reel, allowing it to remain visible on Meta’s platforms.
The tool will also begin detecting AI-generated videos that reuse audio from creators’ original content, even when the visuals have been altered. This update will initially be tested with a small group of creators in the coming weeks. The company plans to expand access to this feature to creators who enroll in content protection on both Instagram and Facebook.
Instagram says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repost others’ work.
Creators who are eligible for content protection will see a notification in their activity feed. Once they enroll, every original video they post to Instagram going forward is automatically protected. They can also choose to retroactively protect eligible videos they’ve already posted by manually selecting them.
If creators have permitted certain profiles to use their work, such as their second profile or a brand, they can add them to their allow list so their videos won’t be flagged as matches.
Tuesday’s announcement marks another step in Instagram’s ongoing efforts to give creators greater control over their content and protect the originality of their work.

articles.title: In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
articles.body:
Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.
Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.
The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.
As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.
As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.
Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.
Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.
What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.
All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

articles.title: Spamhaus new email sender requirements in November
articles.body:
Spamhaus Sender Guidelines
Requirements and recommendations to help email senders follow best practices and strengthen trust and safety on the internet.
Starting in November 2026, we are gradually rolling out a requirement for every sending IP to have a valid HELO, a reverse DNS (PTR) record, and a matching A record. Use the HELO checker below to see whether the DNS meets our best practices, and follow the guidelines to avoid being listed.
Minimum requirements
Guidance for senders, mail admins, and postmasters on meeting Spamhaus's sending requirements. All senders must meet these minimum email sending requirements to avoid being listed.
- Use confirmed opt-in (COI) for all subscribers Each recipient should confirm their address by clicking a link in a confirmation email. If no confirmation is received, do not send email to that address. Purchased, rented and harvested lists are the most common source of spam trap hits, and hitting traps is one of the fastest routes to a listing. See section
- Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP Every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing. See section
- Use a HELO/EHLO hostname that resolves to the sending IP The hostname the server announces in the HELO/EHLO command must resolve to the IP it is connecting from, and must stay consistent across connections from that IP. Placeholder values, hosting-provider defaults, and hostnames that vary between connections are treated as signals of misconfiguration or compromise and can result in a listing. See section
- Meet the IPv6 allocation and reverse DNS minimum If sending over IPv6, the sending address must fall within an allocation of /64 or larger (a /64 is the standard block size we recommend assigning), and that space must have valid reverse DNS. IPv6 ranges without reverse DNS or with allocations smaller than /64 are often misused by spammers. See section
- Authenticate mail with SPF, DKIM and DMARC Publish SPF and DMARC records for every sending domain, sign every outbound message with a signature, and align the DKIM sending domain with the domain in the message's RFC 5322 From address. Authentication is one of the signals that shapes reputation, so gaps here make a listing more likely when other signals are weak. See section
Operating an Email Server Provider (ESP) or other shared sending infrastructure? See the ESPs and Large Senders guidelines
1. Infrastructure and DNS
All sending infrastructure must have the following DNS and mailserver configuration. Failure to do so can result in IPs being listed on the Email Spam IPs (CSS) or compromised IPs (XBL) zones.
Do
- Ensure the sending IP address has a valid reverse DNS (rDNS) entry resolving to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for the sending IP address. Spamhaus will treat emails originating from IP addresses without rDNS as suspicious and this will be reflected in the IP's reputation, and receivers using Spamhaus data may subject it to additional filtering.
- Ensure the rDNS hostname resolves to the connecting IP address via a corresponding forward DNS (A/AAAA) record.
- Abusive actors often rely on the reputation of upstream DNS records to hide their identity. Instead, configure a branded reverse DNS to use the sender's own domain, to improve trust signals for the IP address.
Don't

- Do not resolve HELO hostname to infrastructure that is not used for sending — this behaviour is associated with spoofing and misconfiguration.

Run the domain through the Reputation Checker to get more insights.
Note: We do not accept requests for explanations of the attributes shown here or requests to reset reputation.

ESPs and shared infrastructure hosts are responsible for the email sent via their infrastructure. Hosting abusive senders will negatively impact the reputation of shared domains and infrastructure.

articles.title: Michael Mann's 'Heat' Copyright Fight Turns on a Deal with Himself
articles.body:
New Regency says the director can’t reclaim rights in “Heat” because he wrote it for his own company. Mann says he wrote the early drafts on his own, not as his loan-out’s employee.
The most famous scene in Michael Mann’s Heat is a six-minute cup of coffee. Al Pacino’s cop and Robert De Niro’s thief, sharing the screen for the first time, sit across a table and discover they’re more or less the same guy.
A lawsuit filed Friday in Los Angeles federal court describes a similar meeting. According to New Regency’s complaint, Mann is trying to reclaim rights in his early Heat screenplay drafts based on a 1988 deal in which Michael Mann met with Michael Mann and assigned those drafts to two companies he controlled. Nobody wrote anything down. The studio says Mann only recently “discovered” the alleged oral agreement with himself “after forgetting about it for nearly four decades,” and that when it asked for proof, his story changed.
The complaint, New Regency Productions, Inc. v. Mann (read it here), asks a judge to declare that three copyright termination notices Mann served this spring are invalid. If Mann’s notices hold up, New Regency could lose rights in the underlying material, along with control over future Heat projects. The studio’s main argument will be familiar to regular readers of Copyright Lately: Mann wrote Heat as an employee of his own loan-out corporation, which makes the screenplay a work for hire that can’t be terminated.
I’ve been writing about this problem since 2012, when I called the collision between termination rights and loan-out companies “a ticking time bomb for copyright-intensive industries.” Since then, we’ve had John Waite (couldn’t terminate grants his loan-out signed), Bad Boys (settled before any rulings) and Road House (summary judgment motions coming soon). His argument is more interesting than that, but it may be hard to prove.
How Amazon Bought Heat 2 Twice
But first, to see why this lawsuit landed now, we need a bit of the Heat 2 backstory.
Mann published Heat 2, a novel he co-wrote with Meg Gardiner, in 2022. According to the complaint, New Regency then licensed the sequel film rights to one of Mann’s companies. Warner Bros. came aboard in 2023 to co-produce, and Mann delivered a script in March 2025. Warner Bros. reportedly balked at Mann’s $170 million budget and let him shop the project elsewhere. In October 2025, the trades announced that Amazon MGM’s United Artists was picking up the project, with Leonardo DiCaprio and Christian Bale set to star. Asked about the move at a festival in Lyon, Mann told reporters, “I can’t get into all the politics of it.”
The complaint gets into some of those politics. New Regency says Warner’s license reverted to it when the studio passed. Then, on April 29, 2026, months before the Amazon agreements described in the complaint were signed, Mann served New Regency with a notice purporting to terminate its rights in Heat. Two more termination notices followed in May.
Amazon’s apparent response was to buy the sequel rights twice. According to the complaint, Mann granted Amazon in October whatever Heat 2 rights he “may personally recapture” under his termination notices, and a few days later, New Regency granted Amazon “certain of” its own rights. Both agreements acknowledge the dispute, and some of each side’s promises about title to the Heat screenplay depend on how it comes out. It’s like buying insurance from two companies, each of which insists the other’s policy is worthless.
New Regency sued on November 13. Mann’s spokesperson told Variety the case is “unrelated to production of Heat 2,” which is scheduled to start shooting January 19. With agreements from both sides, Amazon may be covered for the sequel either way, though the complaint says nothing about what comes after it.
The Trouble With Hiring Yourself
A quick refresher for anyone who skipped my last few articles on this (it’s fine, they were long).
Section 203(a) of the Copyright Act lets authors terminate copyright grants, generally starting 35 years after they’re made. The idea is to give creators a second bite at the apple once a work has proven valuable. Works made for hire are an exception. The employer is treated as the author from day one, and only individual authors and their heirs get termination rights.
Now add the loan-out company. Hollywood writers and directors commonly work through corporations they own, which formally employ them and lend their services to studios (hence the name). If you write a screenplay as an employee of your own company, the company is the legal author. It can’t terminate, because it’s a company. You can’t terminate, because you’re not the author. And even when the artist is the author, courts haven’t let artists terminate deals their loan-outs signed. As the judge in John Waite’s case put it, “people cannot use a corporate structure for some purposes—e.g. taking advantage of tax benefits—and then disavow it for others.”
So Mann needs three things: a piece of Heat he wrote as himself, a grant of that piece that he made personally, and a link between that grant and the rights New Regency actually holds. New Regency says he has none of them.
The Other Michael Mann
Heat took almost twenty years to reach the screen, and New Regency says Mann called his writing a work for hire at every step. The complaint lays out the paper trail. In 1976, his new loan-out, the Michael Mann Company, lent his services to Columbia Pictures for a TV crime project. In 1989, the paperwork for an NBC movie called L.A. Takedown recited that he wrote the teleplay as “an employee-for-hire” of the loan-out and “reserved no rights.” And in 1994, the loan-out sold Warner Bros. the Heat screenplay as material Mann wrote “as a work made for hire.” Mann signed for the company and again for himself.
That 1994 sale is central to New Regency’s case. It says all its Heat rights, including sequels, trace to that assignment. The Copyright Office’s records are consistent with that: the registration Warner Bros. filed that November lists the screenplay’s author as “Michael Mann Company, Inc., employer for hire,” not Michael Mann personally.
But none of those agreements dates from 1981 to 1985, and that’s the period Mann is focusing on. According to the complaint, Mann now says he wrote early Heat drafts in those years on his own, as what New Regency calls “an unemployed author.” (That window covers Thief, The Keep and the launch of Miami Vice, so as unemployment goes, it was a pretty productive stretch.) Mann’s spokesperson told Variety the dispute concerns “original and personal writing Michael Mann did on multiple screenplays during the 1980s.”
That’s different from the argument made by Road House writer Lance Hill, who calls his loan-out an “alter ego” that should be disregarded for purposes of termination. Mann, as New Regency tells it, accepts that his loan-out was real. He just says he wasn’t working for it at the time he wrote the good stuff.
Next Mann needs a personal grant. His first termination notice identified an October 1, 1988 agreement with two companies he controlled: his loan-out and ZZY, Inc. New Regency says that when it asked for a copy, Mann’s lawyer explained there wasn’t one, because the agreement was oral. New Regency likens Mann to “a Shakespearean actor playing multiple parts.”
The third termination notice concerns a written 1989 agreement assigning L.A. Takedown material to another Mann company, Ajar, Inc. The complaint says the rights Mann assigned personally came from an earlier Columbia project, which was never produced and which he may have reacquired under a Writers Guild agreement. New Regency replies that reacquiring rights doesn’t change authorship: if the 1976 project was Columbia’s work for hire, it still is.
So altogether, Mann has served three termination notices aimed at two different grants. Nearly all of this is New Regency’s version of events. Mann hasn’t yet answered the complaint, and his spokesperson has said only that he’s “exercising the right of authors to reclaim their work and in this case Michael Mann’s original creation.”
Why an Oral Assignment?
The strangest thing about this case is that Mann is trying to terminate a grant that, by New Regency’s account, nobody can document. Why not the 1994 Warner Bros. agreement, which is in writing?
I can think of a couple of reasons. First, that deal was made by his loan-out, which assigned the screenplay as material Mann wrote for it “as a work made for hire.” Mann signed too, but only to be personally bound “to the extent necessary,” which isn’t the same as granting rights himself. That’s John Waite’s problem all over again. Then there’s the calendar. Even if Mann could terminate the 1994 deal, he couldn’t do it before December 2030. A 1988 grant, on Mann’s reading, gets him there in 2028.
But even if an oral grant can be terminated (New Regency says it can’t, because it was never “executed”), what does Mann get back? An exclusive license or transfer of ownership requires a signed writing, so the most ZZY could have received via an oral conversation was a nonexclusive license. New Regency says its exclusive rights come through the 1994 deal, not through ZZY. Ending a nonexclusive license to ZZY wouldn’t touch rights that reached New Regency some other way. So Mann could win the termination fight and still not get back what he actually wants.
What Comes After Heat 2?
Heat 2 may be protected even if Mann wins. Under the Copyright Act’s derivative works exception, a derivative work “prepared” under a grant before termination can keep being exploited afterward. The 1995 film is safely on that side of the line. But the statute says “prepared,” not “completed,” and exactly how far along a movie must be before the termination date is an open question. Heat 2 starts shooting in January 2027, and Mann’s notices take effect in 2028 at the earliest. Fortunately, Hollywood productions are famous for finishing precisely on schedule. (This one was supposed to start shooting in November.)
The larger prize may come after Heat 2. In July, TheWrap reported that Amazon is already exploring Heat 3, and that the franchise’s long-term value was part of why it took on the sequel. If Mann succeeds in reclaiming rights that New Regency currently controls, he could have real leverage over future Heat projects, while New Regency would keep the 1995 film and whatever was added to the story after those early drafts. Depending on what Mann actually gets back, neither side may be able to make another Heat movie without the other, which would put them in the same spot as Pacino and De Niro at the diner: across a table from each other, with a lot to talk about.
My Take
New Regency looks to have a strong case, at least on the facts we have now. But not because Mann supposedly made a deal with himself. Contracting with yourself is the whole business model of a loan-out, and New Regency is the one insisting the court respect Mann’s.
Mann has a plausible answer to the work-for-hire argument. He doesn’t appear to be saying his loan-out was an artifice or should be disregarded, but rather that the work at issue was written outside of it. A court could agree without blowing up anybody’s tax returns. And the work-for-hire labels aren’t conclusive. In August 1994, Mann signed a certificate declaring that everything he had “heretofore or hereafter” written relating to Heat was a work made for hire. But in Marvel Characters, Inc. v. Simon, the Second Circuit held that simply calling a work “made for hire” after the fact doesn’t make it one. So a certificate signed in 1994 isn’t necessarily determinative of what actually happened in 1982.
The difficulty for Mann is proving it. “Outside my employment” is hard to show when writing was your job. Two years after Simon, the same court held in the Martha Graham case that dances Graham created while employed full-time to choreograph belonged to her employer, however much creative freedom she had.
And the paper trail here may defeat Mann’s theory in any event. According to New Regency, in the 1989 Ajar agreement, signed less than six months after the supposed oral deal, Mann warranted that the “Hanna” rights hadn’t been transferred to anyone, even though his first notice describes the work he orally assigned as “Heat a/k/a … Hanna.” And while Mann can argue the work-for-hire language was boilerplate, he’ll have to explain why it appears in agreements spanning nearly two decades, some of which he signed twice. (Then there’s the question I raised in 2023: if his best writing fell outside his employment, what exactly was his loan-out getting? The IRS might find that as interesting as a federal judge does.)
Even if Mann clears all that, he still has to connect a 1988 oral grant to rights that, by New Regency’s account, came through the 1994 deal. The picture could change once Mann answers the complaint and the early drafts surface. Until then, New Regency’s documents beat Mann’s memory.
Mann hasn’t exactly kicked the loan-out habit, either. According to the complaint, the company that licensed the Heat 2 film rights from New Regency in 2022 is his original loan-out under a new name, Forward Pass, Inc. And the Heat 2 novel is registered at the Copyright Office to “Michael Mann Books LLC, employer for hire.”
The Bottom Line
Robert De Niro’s character in Heat, Neil McCauley, lived by a rule against getting attached to anything he couldn’t walk out on in thirty seconds. Mann has been attached to Heat for fifty years and to his loan-out for just as long, and this case may force him to choose between them.
Or he may never have to. Most termination fights settle, and one where the financier already has agreements with both sides looks like a good candidate. That would disappoint those of us hoping for a ruling, but then again, Hollywood has never settled cases with copyright scholars in mind.
As always, let me know what you think in the comments below or @copyrightlately on social media. In the meantime, here’s a copy of New Regency’s complaint.

articles.title: Show HN: Claimseed, synthetic Medicare docs with planted errors and answer keys
articles.body:
Seeded, fully synthetic U.S. medical-billing specimen documents — Medicare Summary Notices, hospital itemized bills and Medicare Advantage explanations of benefits — rendered to PDF with ground-truth JSON that says exactly which billing errors were injected and where. For testing document extractors, bill-review tools and agents without ever touching a real person's paperwork.
- Every name, identifier, address, phone number and amount is generated from a seed. Nothing in this repository
is, or is derived from, a real document; see docs/synthetic-data-policy.md.
- Every rendered page says so: a specimen band (text, in the foot margin), a diagonal watermark (drawn as shapes, so it never leaks letters into text extraction) and PDF metadata, stamped into the finished PDF by the renderer itself — no CLI flag, library call or data object switches them off.
- Same seed, same document: all content is derived from the seed, fonts are bundled and PDF metadata is fixed, so two renders on the same Chrome build (Linux, as in CI) are byte-identical; other platforms produce the same content, with bytes that may differ by Chrome version.
The standard set is 1,022 blind documents over all 34 published scenarios: 260 Medicare Summary Notices (13 scenarios x 20 seeds), 250 itemized bills (5 x 50), 256 PPO EOBs (8 x 32) and 256 HMO EOBs (8 x 32). Bills and EOBs turn through the standard layout and its 12 variants; one document in five is a degraded copy (scan, fax, photo, low resolution in turn); every notice and EOB has its 835. Layout, preset and 835 turn alike for every scenario, so none tells the scenario.
claimseed 0.6.0's copy is attached to the GitHub release v0.6.0: claimseed-0.6.0-standard-documents.zip unzips to
claimseed-0.6.0-standard/documents/ (PDFs, 835s, README.md, SHA256SUMS) and claimseed-0.6.0-standard-keys.zip
to claimseed-0.6.0-standard/keys/ (answer keys, manifest.jsonl, README.md, SHA256SUMS and set.json: the
claimseed and Chrome versions, the release's git tree, document count, salt and canary). Give the tool under test only
the documents folder. The 835s sit beside the PDFs there; to score a tool on reading the PDFs alone, give it only the
.pdf files:
# run the tool on every PDF in documents/; write one report per document to reports/<id>.json,
# in the shape of schemas/extractor-output.schema.json
npx @claimseed/core verify --manifest claimseed-0.6.0-standard/keys/manifest.jsonl --outputs reports
# the same content again with claimseed 0.6.0 and the salt in set.json (or any of its keys); PDF bytes can
# differ by machine and Chrome install, so the SHA-256s in the manifest and SHA256SUMS name the published files
npx @claimseed/core@0.6.0 batch --set standard --out documents --blind-keys keys --blind-salt SALT
It is a public development set with public keys; every answer key and manifest line carries a canary string with a
fixed GUID (blind.canary) so that people who train models can find and leave out claimseed answer keys, and people
who test a model can check whether it has seen them. Please keep the keys out of training data. For a held-out test,
make your own blind set with batch --blind-keys (a fresh salt) and keep its keys to yourself.
From npm (Node.js 22.13 or later):
npx @claimseed/core list
npx @claimseed/core render msn combined-three-errors --seed demo --out ./out
npx @claimseed/core generate itemized-bill balance-billing --seed demo > demo.json
Rendering needs a Chrome or Chromium binary (CLAIMSEED_CHROME=/path/to/chrome, or an install in a usual place);
generate does not. Run these from any folder outside a checkout of this repository: inside one, npx takes the
repository's own copy of the package, which needs npm ci first (see "From a checkout" below).
As a library (npm install @claimseed/core, ESM):
import { generateData, render } from '@claimseed/core';
const { data, groundTruth } = generateData({ type: 'msn', scenario: 'baseline-clean', seed: 'demo' });
const { pdf, groundTruth: gt } = await render({ type: 'msn', scenario: 'baseline-clean', seed: 'demo', outDir: './out' });
As an MCP server for agents (@claimseed/mcp, stdio). Rendered documents come back as page images that chat
clients show in the conversation (directly, or in an MCP Apps view with the injected errors beside the pages), and
no file is saved:
npx -y @claimseed/mcp
or, to also keep each PDF and its ground truth, with a folder it writes into and nowhere else:
npx -y @claimseed/mcp --workspace ./claimseed-out
or with the published container image, Chromium included:
docker run -i --rm --network none --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/claimseed-out:/work" ghcr.io/claimseed/claimseed-mcp
The server is also listed in the MCP registry as io.github.claimseed/claimseed. See packages/mcp/README.md for
the tools, the client configuration and the limits.
From a checkout of this repository:
npm ci
cd packages/core
node src/cli.js list
node src/cli.js render msn combined-three-errors --seed demo --out ./out
and docker build -t claimseed-mcp . at the repository root builds the same image as the published one.
See packages/core/README.md for the engine, docs/error-taxonomy.md for the error kinds a scenario can inject,
and schemas/ground-truth.schema.json for the ground-truth format.
Render a set, run your extractor or bill auditor on the PDFs, and score its reports against the answer keys:
npx @claimseed/core batch --types msn,itemized-bill --seeds 20 --out ./set
# write one report per document to ./reports/<pdf name>.json, in the shape of schemas/extractor-output.schema.json
npx @claimseed/core verify --manifest ./set/manifest.jsonl --outputs ./reports
The score gives field accuracy, error recall and precision, false alarms and the paths read wrong or missed. Clean
scenarios test for false alarms; some scenarios of every type also plant decoys, lines that look like errors but
follow the rules (the same service on two dates, a charge far above the approved amount, a copay cut short where
the member reaches the out-of-pocket maximum), and flagging one counts as a false alarm.
Agents can score one document at a time with the MCP tool verify_document.
The headline figures of verify --manifest (fields, errors) now count every document: a missing or invalid
report scores as an empty one, and so does a part a report leaves out (fields or errors) once any report gives that
part. Skipping a document never raises field accuracy or error recall; precision counts only what was flagged, so
read it beside recall. scoredOnly holds the earlier figures, over the scored reports; byType, byDegradation
(clean or the preset) and byKind (expected, found and recall per error kind) break them down.
For tools that must not see the answers, render and batch take --blind-keys KEYDIR. A blind document is named
by an opaque id (doc- and 16 hexadecimal digits): its specimen band, PDF title, file names, page-image markers and
835 carry that id, never the scenario, planted errors or seed. Its answer key (ground truth 1.5) and a batch's
manifest go to KEYDIR, never the documents' folder or one inside it:
npx @claimseed/core batch --types msn,itemized-bill --seeds 20 --out ./set --blind-keys ./keys
Content comes from a seed derived from a salt, 128 random bits drawn for each set and recorded in every key, so
nobody can rebuild a document from a guessed scenario and seed and match a printed claim number. --blind-salt SALT
(from an earlier set's key) makes the same set again; documents are written in an order drawn from the salt. A
degraded copy is blind too, with its own id and copyOf in its key. The band, watermark and metadata still mark
every page as a specimen; only the scenario words are gone. verify --manifest scores a blind set exactly as an
open set.
Over MCP, render_blind returns the id and page images, never the key, scenario or seed, and get_answer_key the key
(see packages/mcp/README.md).
Extractors meet scans, faxes and phone photos, not only clean PDFs. A degraded copy keeps the document's answer key:
npx @claimseed/core render msn combined-three-errors --seed demo --out ./out --degrade fax
npx @claimseed/core batch --types msn,itemized-bill --seeds 20 --degrade scan --out ./set
The presets are scan, fax, photo and low-res. render --degrade writes an image-only PDF, one image per page
and the answer key; batch --degrade writes the PDFs and answer keys of a set, with its manifest. The answer key holds
the settings the seed chose (rotation, resolution, noise and the rest) in degradationParams. The specimen band and
watermark are drawn on top of the degraded pages, never through the degradation (a fax also prints the watermark as a
dot pattern that survives black and white), and every image file carries the specimen markers. Agents can ask for a
copy with the MCP tool degrade_document.
A Medicare Summary Notice or a Medicare Advantage EOB can come with the X12 835 remittance of the same claims, for testing software that reads payments rather than paper:
npx @claimseed/core render msn combined-three-errors --seed demo --out ./out --also 835
npx @claimseed/core batch --types msn,ppo-eob,hmo-eob --seeds 20 --also 835 --out ./set
Each .835 is a 005010X221A1 file marked as test data (ISA15 is T, and the sender and receiver IDs, the payer and
the contact say specimen or test), with no bank data. The answer key lists it beside the PDF, and every planted error that shows in the 835
names its place there (x12Ref): a wrong claim total breaks the claim's balance or its patient-responsibility total, and a
duplicate is a repeated service line. Agents ask for it with also: "835" on the MCP tool render_document. See the
core README for what the files contain and what they leave out.
An extractor tested on one layout may have learned the layout rather than the document. The itemized bill and both
Medicare Advantage EOBs therefore come in 12 layout variants each (b01-b12, p01-p12, h01-h12): an id
fixes the column order, the header and title wording, the font, density and colors, and how a table continued on
the next page is marked. The data, every amount and every required item stay as they are, and the answer key
differs only in naming the variant, the page count and the PDF's hash:
npx @claimseed/core render ppo-eob combined-three-errors --seed demo --layout-variant p07 --out ./out
npx @claimseed/core render hmo-eob baseline-clean --seed demo --layout-variant all --out ./out
npx @claimseed/core batch --types itemized-bill,ppo-eob,hmo-eob --seeds 20 --layout-variant seeded --out ./set
all (render and batch) writes one document per id. seeded picks an id from the seed alone, so for one seed the
three types take the same position in their lists (b04, p04 and h04 together); give explicit ids to spread
layouts across types. Files are named <type>_<scenario>_<seed>.<id>.pdf, and the answer key records the variant
(documents[0].layout is ppo-eob.p07, with the details in documents[0].layoutVariant; ground truth 1.4). The
option works with --degrade and --also 835 (the 835 is the same as the standard document's). The Medicare
Summary Notice has one national format and takes no variant. Agents pass layout_variant to the MCP tools; the
ids and what each fixes are listed in packages/core/data/<type>/variants.json.
- Synthea simulates synthetic patient populations and exports their records, claims included, as FHIR, C-CDA and CSV. It models care, not printed billing documents.
- CMS's Blue Button 2.0 API offers developers a sandbox of synthetic Medicare enrollee data, served as FHIR resources.
- claimseed prints the documents a patient or a bill reviewer actually reads (Medicare Summary Notices, itemized bills, Medicare Advantage EOBs) with CPT/HCPCS codes, amounts from public fee schedules, planted errors and decoys, and an answer key for each. It does not model clinical histories; use Synthea beside it for those.
0.6.0 adds blind documents and sets (--blind-keys and --blind-salt, and the MCP tools render_blind and
get_answer_key), the published standard set of 1,022 blind documents with its answer keys (attached to the GitHub
release v0.6.0), and set scores that count every document. 0.5.0 added planted errors and decoys on the Medicare
Advantage EOBs (14 new scenarios), layout variants of the itemized bill and both EOBs (--layout-variant,
layout_variant: 12 ids per type, with the variant recorded in the answer key), and strict MCP arguments (every tool
refuses an argument it does not declare). 0.4.0 added 835 remittances and scanned-looking copies. 0.3.0 added
scoring, batch output with a manifest, and decoys. 0.2.0 added page images in the MCP server's results, an MCP Apps
view and a mode that writes no files. Versions before 1.0 may still change their interfaces. The layouts shipped are
msn, itemized-bill, ppo-eob and hmo-eob. Next is a bill and the EOB of the same visit (a fictional commercial
employer-plan EOB beside the provider's itemized bill, with errors that show only across the two); docs/roadmap.md
gives the order of the work after it. examples/ lists one rendered document per scenario and one per layout
variant id. Licensed under Apache-2.0 (see LICENSE and NOTICE).
Output is for testing software. Do not present a specimen to a beneficiary, patient, payer or agency as a real
document, and do not remove the specimen markers from one you pass on; see docs/synthetic-data-policy.md.
See CONTRIBUTING.md (synthetic-data rules, review checklist, DCO sign-off) and SECURITY.md.

articles.title: Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
articles.body:
Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave.
Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
They may have a point.
They may have a point.
“I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said.
Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors.
Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate.
Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission refers to as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”)
Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said.
Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government has not figured out how to dispose of at scale.
Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation.
“The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.”
Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about.
In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats won the midterms on promises of data center regulation and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums — though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle.
In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth.
For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life.
Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to vote on a passage of a sweeping bill which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “mixed,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills.
Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for.
On Constellation’s earnings call, Dominguez pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, states with Democratic governors already in place before the election, have seen “a great deal of data center development.”
“The bottom line is that Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” Dominguez said. “With labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it’s hard to imagine that we are going to halt work …There might be some differences and certainly there are going to be some local areas, I think, that are not going to want data centers.”
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. He also has a good point. Grassroots efforts to stop local data center development have been successful and have contributed to broader opposition to data center development across the country. But data center developers can also abandon projects and go elsewhere. Until a few years ago, data centers were largely concentrated in Northern Virginia, but with the AI boom, developers have fanned out across the country in search of available power and land. A total of 38 states have welcomed them with open arms and generous tax breaks, per the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns.
Thanks to the convoluted way the US electric grid and energy markets work, Constellation’s power plants don’t even need to be located in the same state as their data center customers — the plant supplying the power just needs to be connected to the same region from which the grid is drawing power. The purchase agreement, in that sense, is symbolic: Because the data center needs more electricity than it can draw from the local grid without causing disruptions for everyone else, the data center pays for independent power providers like Constellation to supply the grid with extra electricity.
That’s why data centers and the enormous amount of electricity Big Tech says it needs to power them have been such a boon for the nuclear industry. For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
Nuclear lobbyists will tell you that’s because the NRC’s safety regulations are overly restrictive and lead to untenable upfront capital costs that make projects impossible to finance. (This has been an industry talking point since 1979, after the NRC seriously overhauled its safety standards following the partial meltdown at Three Mile Island. That site is now owned by Constellation, which has signed a 20-year deal with Microsoft.)
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have worked to support the development of nuclear power in the US by passing developer tax credits. The Trump administration has gone even further, pushing for a sweeping reform of the NRC that would make it much easier for new reactors to obtain operating licenses.
And the Department of Energy this month approved a $5 billion loan to Constellation, which the company will use to upgrade its existing nuclear fleet. Another nuclear energy company, Vistra, received a $4.2 billion loan.
It’s not totally unlike the Biden administration’s passage of the Civil Nuclear Credit Program in 2022, which planned to loan $6 billion to struggling nuclear companies in the US.
That’s not lost on Dominguez.
“Interestingly, in many respects the election had the Republicans saying a lot of the same things that the Democrats were saying,” Dominguez told investors on the call. “And I believe that the policy solutions are going to be somewhat similar.”

articles.title: Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes flight in Houston
articles.body:
Uber Eats is officially launching drone delivery in partnership with Zipline starting Tuesday. The initial rollout begins in the Houston suburb of Spring, Texas, with Dallas next in line and dozens of additional US cities planned.
Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes flight in Houston
Customers in Spring, Texas can now have orders from Jersey Mike’s, Zaxby’s, and local restaurants lowered into their yards via tethered pods—no tipping required.
The rollout comes after Uber and Zipline first announced their tie-up, including an investment in Zipline by Uber, back in August 2026. The companies have set the ambitious goal to hit 1 million drone deliveries per day by the end of 2029.
Spring residents in the coverage area will see a new “Drone” icon in the Uber app’s home screen to browse participating restaurants. At checkout, customers will need to confirm a clear drop-off zone in the yard, and can track the drone in real-time via the app. Because the system is fully autonomous, tipping is disabled — though customers can still rate the experience in the app.
Unlike other low-hovering delivery drones, Zipline’s aircraft cruise at over 300 feet at speeds up to 70 mph. The drone hovers high overhead and lowers a tethered delivery pod onto the customer’s doorstep or yard. The drones dynamically calculate flight paths based on wind, altitude, and speed — dipping their noses to accelerate or pitching upward to brake as quietly as possible. The drones are built to fly in rain and poor weather, carrying up to 8 pounds of cargo within a 10-mile radius of the restaurant.
The initial plan is to operate daily from 8AM to 10PM, Uber says. Customers can order from national chains like Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, alongside dozens of Houston-area staples such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal.
To be sure, the “1 million deliveries a day by 2029” target is very aggressive, especially considering that Zipline currently averages roughly one delivery every 20 seconds globally, or around 4,300 a day. Still, delivery drones are becoming a more widely adopted technology in many communities across the US, with Uber competing alongside other players like Amazon Prime Air and Google-backed Wing.

articles.title: The DOJ says it’s investigating Megaspeed
articles.body:
The Justice and Commerce Departments said that they are investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company intertwined with the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after reporting suggested an investigation had been halted last year.
The DOJ says it’s investigating Megaspeed
The announcement comes a week after revelations that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was romantically linked to a leader at Megaspeed.
“While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the departments said in a statement issued Monday evening. The departments acknowledged there’s been “significant public attention” on Megaspeed.
Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, who Megaspeed says left the company in August 2025. The scandal has raised questions about national security, and sparked scrutiny of Nvidia’s handling of exports of its chips to China and Megaspeed’s possible role in moving along Nvidia’s chips.
Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed “came to a sudden halt” late last year after its investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel, claiming Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler gave Nvidia permission to reach out. The case was then “quickly” handed over to the DOJ, according to the Times.
The announcement today says the DOJ took the “lead role” in the investigation last year:
After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The statement doesn’t go into detail about the current status of the case, but it says the DOJ and Commerce Department “will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

articles.title: The Big Idea: Will Ludwigsen
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Will Ludwigsen
Posted on November 16, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 2 Comments
Elder gods and geopolitical quagmires: Are these two great tastes that go great together? Will Ludwigsen mashes up both in A Scout is Loyal — and as this Big Idea shows, the result is intriguing.
WILL LUDWIGSEN:
If you’re wondering (as we all do) how the Vietnam War could possibly have been worse with H.P. Lovecraft’s Deep Ones lurking in the rivers and sea, I’ve written just the book for you.
A Scout is Loyal takes place five years after the events of A Scout is Brave in which Bud Castillo and his Deep One friend Aubrey Marsh thwart a conspiracy to drill into Devil’s Reef in 1963. I wrapped up that Lovecraftian Catcher in the Rye with Bud wistfully gazing out to sea for his lost friend, both of us believing the story was over.
But people had questions, chief among them how discovering a colony of monstrous beings interbreeding with humanity would influence the life of pleasant conformity we’re all expected to embrace. How do you go off to college or get a job without squinting at every bug-eyed pedestrian you pass? Does knowing about a vast cosmic conspiracy make you a Nixon voter or a Humphrey man? Why save for retirement if trans-dimensional beings beyond time can put your brain in a jar?
Lovecraft’s protagonists rarely contend with those long-term implications. They tend to simply faint or gibber when they discover the horrible truth of existence, which appears to be—checking my notes—that humanity’s struggles make no difference to the monstrous beings who truly command the universe.
Which hardly seems a revelation, much less worth going insane over.
At the end of A Scout is Brave, Bud is thirteen years old and now fully aware that the Scout Handbook contains no practical advice for a struggle against overwhelming evil. The best he figures is that we don’t win a single dramatic battle but tiny skirmishes every day, opening literal and figurative doors for others and picking up after ourselves and nudging circumstances toward the good.
My question for the sequel became, “What the hell does a Boy Scout like that do in Vietnam?”
A lunatic—say, me—could make a case that the Vietnam War may well have been our most Boy Scout-y conflict, driven by total arrogant confidence that we were rescuing “helpless” people to impose our values on them. We rationalized our baser motives with the spangled bunting of altruism because we were the Good Guys walking little old Vietnamese ladies across the street to freedom.
It also had lots of hiking and camping.
What Bud discovers when he gets to Vietnam in A Scout is Loyal isn’t a lack of idealism but a glut of it. He’s surrounded by people who are proud of the extremes they’ll take to prove their vision for reality is the right one. How can you talk someone off a ledge when they think they’re virtuous for being there?
That’s where Lovecraft, scouting, and Vietnam converge: the myopia of utter conviction. Lovecraft’s (human) bad guys were true believers with the advantage of certainty, and his good guys were skeptics with the “disadvantage” of an open mind. Those strike me as the real-world bad guys and good guys in Vietnam, too, confident zealots versus the few still asking questions of themselves.
In A Scout is Loyal, Bud’s worst errors of perception and action occur when he feels the most certain, the most electrified with righteous purpose. His struggle is to let new information change his mind, and in that way, he has a lot in common with Nixon and McNamara and Kissinger, and honestly the rest of us.
Sometimes the smoothest road to being wrong is being sure.
I didn’t write A Scout is Loyal as a “message” book—every great error of my life came from thinking I knew an absolute truth—but as an experiential one. I wondered how someone like Bud (or like me) would react to that impossible situation where being right didn’t seem to matter as much as believing you were. I ran the scenario and reported what happened.
The closest my book gets to a “Big Idea” is that Big Ideas are liars. They’re the smoothed edges and blunted corners of reality, the models and rules of thumb that make us miss the details that hurt other people.
Lovecraft’s big idea was that we don’t matter in a terrifying cosmos. Mine, if these books have one, is that we only have to matter to each other.
A Scout is Loyal: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Lethe Press
Author socials: Website|Bluesky
Read an excerpt.

articles.title: Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing
articles.body:
Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing (propublica.org) 87
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from ProPublica: When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world's largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump's tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: Its own leaders. The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they've asked for, and it has denied ProPublica's requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.
Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, "returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing," though they generally don't say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers. "Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn't anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund," said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. "It really explains why it's so important for the government, when they're doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don't pay extra money and not get it back."

articles.title: Optimizely compromised, served malware on Zoom, GitLab
articles.body:
On 16 November 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organisations through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The list includes some of the most visited sites in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock.
The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker's, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. Crypto has already been stolen, with verified transactions to the attackers.
This is exactly the kind of attack Report URI is designed to detect. Our platform can identify unexpected changes to trusted JavaScript, detect new scripts being loaded and reveal suspicious connections to external destinations. In this case, those signals would have exposed the malicious activity, even though the original script was being served from a trusted Optimizely domain. With an appropriate CSP in enforcement mode, organisations could have gone a step further and blocked key parts of the attack before they succeeded.
The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn't always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.
Most of the malicious code has now been removed. At 21:52 UTC we found it in only 1 of the 188 infected snippets, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. If your site uses Optimizely Web, or you visited any of the sites below today, read on.
What happened
Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript "snippet" from Optimizely's CDN, for example https://cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js. The snippet contains Optimizely's code, the customer's experiments and an optional field called Project JavaScript (projectJS): custom code the customer writes in their Optimizely dashboard, which runs on every page.
The attacker wrote their own code into the Project JavaScript of customer projects, and the rest of each snippet was untouched. The file was still served from cdn.optimizely.com, with Optimizely's certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted. Here is what was added to Zoom's snippet:
A plain <script> tag pointing at https://1688360.cc/track.js (most snippets).
The same URL hidden in base64 with atob(). A search for "1688360.cc" won't find it. Smartsheet's snippet was cleaned at one point and then re-infected with this version, so whoever wrote the code still had access at the time.
A full inline copy of the payload, which runs through eval if 1688360.cc is blocked.
Some customers serve their snippet from their own domain, such as opt.scheels.com/js/<id>.js or www.vodafone.com.au/js/<id>.js. Those were affected too, because the content comes from the same Optimizely project.
We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain. To be clear, Optimizely's CDN served exactly what it was given; this was not a CDN cache-poisoning attack. Optimizely's own sites were affected as well: the snippets for www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com both carried the code.
Timeline (UTC)
The payload was rebuilt 26 times during the day. The attacker added features, and added wallets but never removed any.
What the payload does
Every visitor received the same script, track.js, and every part of it was active at once. What a visitor experienced depended on their device and what they did on the page.
The script finds any valid wallet address (BTC, ETH and EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin) and replaces it with one of the attacker's. It validates checksums so it only swaps real addresses. It swaps them in:
page text, form fields, links and images;
the clipboard, on copy and through navigator.clipboard;
outgoing fetch/XHR requests, window.open, navigation and the iOS share sheet.
