articles.title: Running coding agents without handing them my credentials
articles.body:
Running coding agents without handing them my credentials
Table of Contents
I built lend to let remote agents use tools on my laptop with my approval. Here's how it fits into my workflow.
Background #
I use agents heavily these days as part of my toolchain. I usually have a few going at once: Claude Code working in one repo, Codex reviewing a branch in another, and something long-running in the background. I often have them review each other's work too. None of them run on my laptop. They run on VMs I can throw away, and my laptop keeps the stuff I care about: my SSH keys, my 1Password vault, and the gh and cloud CLIs that are logged in as me.
I run those agents on picd, our hosting service at pico.sh. It gives me my own VM with a Docker engine and a shell over SSH. I run herdr and the agents there, and my home directory persists across restarts so my dotfiles and tools stay in place.
This works great until an agent needs something on my laptop. In this post I'll go over how I run agents in parallel with herdr and Ovis, and the tool I wrote to deal with credentials, lend.
herdr #
herdr is a terminal multiplexer built for coding agents. You get the usual workspaces, tabs, and panes, and it also knows which agent is running in each pane and what it's doing. The sidebar shows whether each agent is working, waiting on me, or done, so I can tell at a glance which one needs attention.
The CLI talks to the running session, so agents can drive each other. An agent can start Codex in another pane, give it a prompt, wait for it to finish, and read what it said:
1herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane "$PANE"
2herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the diff on am/fix-retries" --wait --until done
3herdr agent read reviewer --source recent
Remote hosts work the same way. herdr machine add agent-vm sets up herdr on the VM and adds its sessions to my local client. Those sessions keep running after I disconnect.
Ovis #
Ovis is a browser and phone client for herdr. It shows each agent's transcript as a chat, with the live terminal a tap away. When an agent asks for approval or has a question, Ovis turns it into a card I can answer and sends me a push notification. It picks up the machines saved in herdr, so my VMs show up without any extra setup. I reach it over Tailscale.
If an agent gets stuck on a question while I'm away from my desk, I answer it from my phone and the other agents keep going.
The credential problem #
Agents on a VM still need to act as me. I use them to monitor CI with gh, call APIs with tokens from 1Password, and SSH into other hosts. There are two usual ways to make that work, and I don't love either of them.
The first is copying credentials onto the VM. A token in ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml can be read by every process on that machine, including the agent and anything it runs, for as long as the token is valid.
The second is forwarding my SSH agent with ssh -A. The private keys stay on my laptop, but the VM can use every key in the agent without asking and without any record of what it signed. It also only covers SSH keys.
What I wanted was for the credentials to stay on the laptop and for the commands that need them to run there too. The agent asks to run something, I approve it with Touch ID, and the agent gets the output back.
lend #
That's where lend comes in. lend is a proxy that sits in front of your existing SSH agent, and you forward its socket in place of the real one. SSH and Git keep working like normal, and lend adds a way to run commands through an SSH agent extension.
When an agent on the VM asks to run gh, the request goes over the socket and gh runs on my laptop with my login. The token never leaves the laptop, so the agent never has it. Every request, whether it's a signature or a command, is checked against a policy on the laptop and needs my approval before anything happens.
1Remote: lend exec -- command args
2                  |
3          forwarded SSH agent socket
4                  |
5Laptop: lend agent -> policy + local approval -> local command
6                                           -> original SSH agent (signing)
The policy lives on the laptop and lists what the VM is allowed to ask for. Everything else is denied. Mine is pretty short:
 1{
 2  "default": "deny",
 3  "commands": [
 4    {"executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh", "approval": "biometric:inline"}
 5  ],
 6  "ssh": {
 7    "default": "deny",
 8    "keys": [
 9      {"fingerprint": "SHA256:...", "approval": "biometric:inline"}
10    ]
11  }
12}
A rule can also take an args_prefix like ["pr", "view"] if you only want to allow some subcommands. biometric:inline puts Touch ID right in the request dialog, so I read the request and touch once to approve it. Plain biometric asks for Touch ID in a second prompt after I click Allow.
To connect, I run lend ssh from the laptop. It starts a proxy for that one connection and stops it when SSH exits:
1lend ssh --config ./policy.json -- agent-vm
I run herdr on the VM. Claude Code talks to lend through lend mcp, an MCP server with a single tool called run_local_command. The tool takes the command to run and a reason, and the reason is required:
1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "laptop": {"command": "lend", "args": ["mcp"]}
4  }
5}
Here I asked Claude Code on the VM for the lend repo's description. It called the tool with gh repo view, my Mac showed the request, and one touch approved it:
The dialog shows the full path to the executable, every argument, the directory it'll run in on the laptop, the reason, and what the remote process said about itself. Once I approve, gh runs on the laptop and stdout, stderr, and the exit code stream back to the agent. The reason and caller details come from the VM, so they're marked as unverified. They're there to help me decide and can't change what the policy allows.
If you'd rather skip MCP, the same request works as a plain CLI call on the VM:
1lend exec --reason "Read the repo description" -- gh repo view antoniomika/lend
Keeping the socket stable across reconnects #
herdr panes survive an SSH disconnect, but the forwarded socket belongs to that connection. When I reconnect, SSH gives me a new socket path. Agents still running in the panes keep the old SSH_AUTH_SOCK.
I use a symlink at a fixed path and update it from ~/.ssh/rc on the VM. SSH runs this before starting the shell, so it sees the socket forwarded by the new connection:
 1#!/bin/sh
 2
 3if [ -n "${SSH_AUTH_SOCK:-}" ] &&
 4    [ "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" != "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] &&
 5    "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
 6  install -d -m 700 "$HOME/.ssh/lend" &&
 7    ln -sfn -- "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock"
 8fi
 9
10if [ -n "${DISPLAY:-}" ] && read -r _ssh_proto _ssh_cookie; then
11  case $DISPLAY in
12    localhost:*) _ssh_display="unix:${DISPLAY#localhost:}" ;;
13    *) _ssh_display=$DISPLAY ;;
14  esac
15  printf 'add %s %s %s\n' "$_ssh_display" "$_ssh_proto" "$_ssh_cookie" | /usr/bin/xauth -q -
16fi
The check confirms the forwarded socket speaks lend before updating the link. The directory is private to my user and keeps this link separate from other agent sockets. I use lend's absolute path because this runs before my shell adds ~/.local/bin to PATH. The X11 block handles cookie setup, which SSH delegates to this file when it exists.
My ~/.bashrc checks the stable path before exporting it:
1if [ -S "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] &&
2    "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
3  export SSH_AUTH_SOCK="$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock"
4fi
New Bash shells in herdr panes pick up the stable path when it works. If the check fails, Bash leaves SSH_AUTH_SOCK alone. MCP, approval hooks, and Git inherit that path when I start them. After reconnecting, the SSH hook updates the symlink and those processes use the new socket for subsequent requests. Agents already running with an old socket path need to be restarted once with the stable path in their environment.
The SSH connection from the laptop still has to stay open. Requests fail while it's disconnected, and reconnecting starts a new lend session with fresh approvals and leases. The link points at one connection at a time, so the last update wins.
Secrets the agent never sees #
gh works because it's already logged in on my laptop. Some tools need a token passed in. For those, a command rule can read secrets with something like op read and hand them to the approved command as environment variables:
 1{
 2  "secret_reader": "/opt/homebrew/bin/op",
 3  "secret_reader_args": ["read", "--no-newline"],
 4  "commands": [
 5    {
 6      "executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh",
 7      "args_prefix": ["pr", "view"],
 8      "approval": "biometric",
 9      "secrets": {"GH_TOKEN": "op://Development/github/token"}
10    }
11  ]
12}
When the agent asks to run gh pr view and I approve it, lend reads the token from 1Password, runs gh with GH_TOKEN set, and sends back the output. The token stays on the laptop. The VM can't pick which variables get set or which references get read. The prompt shows the variable names and references, and the values never show up in prompts or history.
Here's the VM running gh api user with a rule that injects GH_TOKEN. After I approve in lend, 1Password asks for its own Touch ID before op read returns the token. The VM gets my login back, and its own environment has no GH_TOKEN:
There's one catch: this only works if the approved command doesn't print its environment. If you approve env or sh, you've handed the values right back. The same goes for allowing op itself as a command, since op read prints the secret and that output goes straight to the agent.
SSH keys #
Keys get their own policy too. Keys that aren't listed are hidden from the VM, and listed keys can be limited by what they're allowed to sign. max_signatures caps how many signatures a key can make in a session.
Leases #
A rule can offer a lease when I approve, like five minutes or three uses. Leases only exist inside a lend ssh session and only match the exact command and arguments I approved. They go away when the session ends or my screen locks.
Seeing what happened #
lend status --all --watch shows what's connected, what's waiting, what's running, and any active leases. lend pause --all cancels everything and refuses new requests until I resume. lend history keeps a record of what ran and how it was approved. It leaves out arguments, output, and secrets, and you can opt into logging arguments.
Answering agent prompts from the laptop #
Agents also ask permission for things that have nothing to do with my credentials, like running a shell command on the VM, editing a file, or fetching a URL. lend approve sends those questions to the same dialog on my Mac. It doesn't run anything on the laptop. It asks me, and the agent decides what to do with the answer.
For Claude Code, it's a PermissionRequest hook on the VM:
1{
2  "hooks": {
3    "PermissionRequest": [
4      {"matcher": "*", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "lend approve --hook claude-code"}]}
5    ]
6  }
7}
Now when Claude Code would normally stop and ask in the terminal, my Mac shows the command or tool input and I answer with Touch ID. The laptop policy lists which topics are allowed to ask, each with its own approval:
1"approvals": {
2  "topics": [{"name": "claude-code", "approval": "biometric:inline"}]
3}
There are adapters for Codex, Antigravity, and pi, plus a plain JSON format for anything else. You can use it in scripts too: lend approve --topic deploy --title "terraform apply" && terraform apply only applies after I approve on the laptop. If the laptop can't be reached, the hook stays out of the way and the agent asks in its own UI like it normally would.
What lend doesn't protect against #
An approved command runs as my user and can touch my files. Approval decides what runs, and lend doesn't sandbox it. If I approve a shell, an interpreter, or anything that reads instructions from stdin, I've basically approved running anything on my laptop, since stdin streams after approval and isn't shown in the prompt.
The caller details in the prompt come from the VM and can be faked. Anyone who can reach the forwarded socket on the VM, root included, can make requests while the session is open. The policy still limits what they can ask for, and every request still needs my approval.
lend is still early and runs on macOS and Linux. It doesn't allocate a PTY, so interactive programs won't work through it. On Linux, approval is a Zenity dialog or a terminal prompt, and biometric approval is macOS only.
Prior art #
ssh-rev-exec sends local execution requests through an SSH agent proxy, and op-forward forwards 1Password CLI commands to a machine with desktop authentication. lend is a separate implementation that uses the same agent extension trick and adds per-request policy, local approval, and key filtering.
Trying it #
Install lend on both your laptop and the remote host:
1brew install antoniomika/tap/lend
2# or
3curl -fsSL https://github.com/antoniomika/lend/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
Run lend doctor on the laptop to check your policy, executables, upstream agent, and approval setup. lend doctor --remote on the VM checks that the forwarded socket is actually lend. The getting started guide walks through a first session, and the docs cover policies, approval, and MCP. If you give it a try, I'd love to hear how it goes on GitHub.

articles.title: Running coding agents without handing them my credentials
articles.body:
Running coding agents without handing them my credentials
Table of Contents
I built lend to let remote agents use tools on my laptop with my approval. Here's how it fits into my workflow.
Background #
I use agents heavily these days as part of my toolchain. I usually have a few going at once: Claude Code working in one repo, Codex reviewing a branch in another, and something long-running in the background. I often have them review each other's work too. None of them run on my laptop. They run on VMs I can throw away, and my laptop keeps the stuff I care about: my SSH keys, my 1Password vault, and the gh and cloud CLIs that are logged in as me.
I run those agents on picd, our hosting service at pico.sh. It gives me my own VM with a Docker engine and a shell over SSH. I run herdr and the agents there, and my home directory persists across restarts so my dotfiles and tools stay in place.
This works great until an agent needs something on my laptop. In this post I'll go over how I run agents in parallel with herdr and Ovis, and the tool I wrote to deal with credentials, lend.
herdr #
herdr is a terminal multiplexer built for coding agents. You get the usual workspaces, tabs, and panes, and it also knows which agent is running in each pane and what it's doing. The sidebar shows whether each agent is working, waiting on me, or done, so I can tell at a glance which one needs attention.
The CLI talks to the running session, so agents can drive each other. An agent can start Codex in another pane, give it a prompt, wait for it to finish, and read what it said:
1herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane "$PANE"
2herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the diff on am/fix-retries" --wait --until done
3herdr agent read reviewer --source recent
Remote hosts work the same way. herdr machine add agent-vm sets up herdr on the VM and adds its sessions to my local client. Those sessions keep running after I disconnect.
Ovis #
Ovis is a browser and phone client for herdr. It shows each agent's transcript as a chat, with the live terminal a tap away. When an agent asks for approval or has a question, Ovis turns it into a card I can answer and sends me a push notification. It picks up the machines saved in herdr, so my VMs show up without any extra setup. I reach it over Tailscale.
If an agent gets stuck on a question while I'm away from my desk, I answer it from my phone and the other agents keep going.
The credential problem #
Agents on a VM still need to act as me. I use them to monitor CI with gh, call APIs with tokens from 1Password, and SSH into other hosts. There are two usual ways to make that work, and I don't love either of them.
The first is copying credentials onto the VM. A token in ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml can be read by every process on that machine, including the agent and anything it runs, for as long as the token is valid.
The second is forwarding my SSH agent with ssh -A. The private keys stay on my laptop, but the VM can use every key in the agent without asking and without any record of what it signed. It also only covers SSH keys.
What I wanted was for the credentials to stay on the laptop and for the commands that need them to run there too. The agent asks to run something, I approve it with Touch ID, and the agent gets the output back.
lend #
That's where lend comes in. lend is a proxy that sits in front of your existing SSH agent, and you forward its socket in place of the real one. SSH and Git keep working like normal, and lend adds a way to run commands through an SSH agent extension.
When an agent on the VM asks to run gh, the request goes over the socket and gh runs on my laptop with my login. The token never leaves the laptop, so the agent never has it. Every request, whether it's a signature or a command, is checked against a policy on the laptop and needs my approval before anything happens.
1Remote: lend exec -- command args
2                  |
3          forwarded SSH agent socket
4                  |
5Laptop: lend agent -> policy + local approval -> local command
6                                           -> original SSH agent (signing)
The policy lives on the laptop and lists what the VM is allowed to ask for. Everything else is denied. Mine is pretty short:
 1{
 2  "default": "deny",
 3  "commands": [
 4    {"executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh", "approval": "biometric:inline"}
 5  ],
 6  "ssh": {
 7    "default": "deny",
 8    "keys": [
 9      {"fingerprint": "SHA256:...", "approval": "biometric:inline"}
10    ]
11  }
12}
A rule can also take an args_prefix like ["pr", "view"] if you only want to allow some subcommands. biometric:inline puts Touch ID right in the request dialog, so I read the request and touch once to approve it. Plain biometric asks for Touch ID in a second prompt after I click Allow.
To connect, I run lend ssh from the laptop. It starts a proxy for that one connection and stops it when SSH exits:
1lend ssh --config ./policy.json -- agent-vm
I run herdr on the VM. Claude Code talks to lend through lend mcp, an MCP server with a single tool called run_local_command. The tool takes the command to run and a reason, and the reason is required:
1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "laptop": {"command": "lend", "args": ["mcp"]}
4  }
5}
Here I asked Claude Code on the VM for the lend repo's description. It called the tool with gh repo view, my Mac showed the request, and one touch approved it:
The dialog shows the full path to the executable, every argument, the directory it'll run in on the laptop, the reason, and what the remote process said about itself. Once I approve, gh runs on the laptop and stdout, stderr, and the exit code stream back to the agent. The reason and caller details come from the VM, so they're marked as unverified. They're there to help me decide and can't change what the policy allows.
If you'd rather skip MCP, the same request works as a plain CLI call on the VM:
1lend exec --reason "Read the repo description" -- gh repo view antoniomika/lend
Keeping the socket stable across reconnects #
herdr panes survive an SSH disconnect, but the forwarded socket belongs to that connection. When I reconnect, SSH gives me a new socket path. Agents still running in the panes keep the old SSH_AUTH_SOCK.
I use a symlink at a fixed path and update it from ~/.ssh/rc on the VM. SSH runs this before starting the shell, so it sees the socket forwarded by the new connection:
 1#!/bin/sh
 2
 3if [ -n "${SSH_AUTH_SOCK:-}" ] &&
 4    [ "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" != "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] &&
 5    "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
 6  install -d -m 700 "$HOME/.ssh/lend" &&
 7    ln -sfn -- "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock"
 8fi
 9
10if [ -n "${DISPLAY:-}" ] && read -r _ssh_proto _ssh_cookie; then
11  case $DISPLAY in
12    localhost:*) _ssh_display="unix:${DISPLAY#localhost:}" ;;
13    *) _ssh_display=$DISPLAY ;;
14  esac
15  printf 'add %s %s %s\n' "$_ssh_display" "$_ssh_proto" "$_ssh_cookie" | /usr/bin/xauth -q -
16fi
The check confirms the forwarded socket speaks lend before updating the link. The directory is private to my user and keeps this link separate from other agent sockets. I use lend's absolute path because this runs before my shell adds ~/.local/bin to PATH. The X11 block handles cookie setup, which SSH delegates to this file when it exists.
My ~/.bashrc checks the stable path before exporting it:
1if [ -S "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" ] &&
2    "$HOME/.local/bin/lend" doctor --remote --socket "$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock" --timeout 1s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
3  export SSH_AUTH_SOCK="$HOME/.ssh/lend/agent.sock"
4fi
New Bash shells in herdr panes pick up the stable path when it works. If the check fails, Bash leaves SSH_AUTH_SOCK alone. MCP, approval hooks, and Git inherit that path when I start them. After reconnecting, the SSH hook updates the symlink and those processes use the new socket for subsequent requests. Agents already running with an old socket path need to be restarted once with the stable path in their environment.
The SSH connection from the laptop still has to stay open. Requests fail while it's disconnected, and reconnecting starts a new lend session with fresh approvals and leases. The link points at one connection at a time, so the last update wins.
Secrets the agent never sees #
gh works because it's already logged in on my laptop. Some tools need a token passed in. For those, a command rule can read secrets with something like op read and hand them to the approved command as environment variables:
 1{
 2  "secret_reader": "/opt/homebrew/bin/op",
 3  "secret_reader_args": ["read", "--no-newline"],
 4  "commands": [
 5    {
 6      "executable": "/opt/homebrew/bin/gh",
 7      "args_prefix": ["pr", "view"],
 8      "approval": "biometric",
 9      "secrets": {"GH_TOKEN": "op://Development/github/token"}
10    }
11  ]
12}
When the agent asks to run gh pr view and I approve it, lend reads the token from 1Password, runs gh with GH_TOKEN set, and sends back the output. The token stays on the laptop. The VM can't pick which variables get set or which references get read. The prompt shows the variable names and references, and the values never show up in prompts or history.
Here's the VM running gh api user with a rule that injects GH_TOKEN. After I approve in lend, 1Password asks for its own Touch ID before op read returns the token. The VM gets my login back, and its own environment has no GH_TOKEN:
There's one catch: this only works if the approved command doesn't print its environment. If you approve env or sh, you've handed the values right back. The same goes for allowing op itself as a command, since op read prints the secret and that output goes straight to the agent.
SSH keys #
Keys get their own policy too. Keys that aren't listed are hidden from the VM, and listed keys can be limited by what they're allowed to sign. max_signatures caps how many signatures a key can make in a session.
Leases #
A rule can offer a lease when I approve, like five minutes or three uses. Leases only exist inside a lend ssh session and only match the exact command and arguments I approved. They go away when the session ends or my screen locks.
Seeing what happened #
lend status --all --watch shows what's connected, what's waiting, what's running, and any active leases. lend pause --all cancels everything and refuses new requests until I resume. lend history keeps a record of what ran and how it was approved. It leaves out arguments, output, and secrets, and you can opt into logging arguments.
Answering agent prompts from the laptop #
Agents also ask permission for things that have nothing to do with my credentials, like running a shell command on the VM, editing a file, or fetching a URL. lend approve sends those questions to the same dialog on my Mac. It doesn't run anything on the laptop. It asks me, and the agent decides what to do with the answer.
For Claude Code, it's a PermissionRequest hook on the VM:
1{
2  "hooks": {
3    "PermissionRequest": [
4      {"matcher": "*", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "lend approve --hook claude-code"}]}
5    ]
6  }
7}
Now when Claude Code would normally stop and ask in the terminal, my Mac shows the command or tool input and I answer with Touch ID. The laptop policy lists which topics are allowed to ask, each with its own approval:
1"approvals": {
2  "topics": [{"name": "claude-code", "approval": "biometric:inline"}]
3}
There are adapters for Codex, Antigravity, and pi, plus a plain JSON format for anything else. You can use it in scripts too: lend approve --topic deploy --title "terraform apply" && terraform apply only applies after I approve on the laptop. If the laptop can't be reached, the hook stays out of the way and the agent asks in its own UI like it normally would.
What lend doesn't protect against #
An approved command runs as my user and can touch my files. Approval decides what runs, and lend doesn't sandbox it. If I approve a shell, an interpreter, or anything that reads instructions from stdin, I've basically approved running anything on my laptop, since stdin streams after approval and isn't shown in the prompt.
The caller details in the prompt come from the VM and can be faked. Anyone who can reach the forwarded socket on the VM, root included, can make requests while the session is open. The policy still limits what they can ask for, and every request still needs my approval.
lend is still early and runs on macOS and Linux. It doesn't allocate a PTY, so interactive programs won't work through it. On Linux, approval is a Zenity dialog or a terminal prompt, and biometric approval is macOS only.
Prior art #
ssh-rev-exec sends local execution requests through an SSH agent proxy, and op-forward forwards 1Password CLI commands to a machine with desktop authentication. lend is a separate implementation that uses the same agent extension trick and adds per-request policy, local approval, and key filtering.
Trying it #
Install lend on both your laptop and the remote host:
1brew install antoniomika/tap/lend
2# or
3curl -fsSL https://github.com/antoniomika/lend/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
Run lend doctor on the laptop to check your policy, executables, upstream agent, and approval setup. lend doctor --remote on the VM checks that the forwarded socket is actually lend. The getting started guide walks through a first session, and the docs cover policies, approval, and MCP. If you give it a try, I'd love to hear how it goes on GitHub.

articles.title: My Quest to push native Three.js quality match AAA Game Engines
articles.body:
Building the AAA Lighting Pipeline in Three.js
From the G-buffer to temporal upscaling, here is each stage of the lightmap, probe and screen-space reflection pipeline measured against Three.js: what games require of it, what Three.js has today, and the pull requests in review or still to write.
Ben Houston • • 21 min read
Part 2 picked a pipeline for indoor scenes: lightmaps, light probes and reflection probes, with SSR, SSGI and ambient occlusion on top. Here I measure Three.js against it one stage at a time: what the games require, what Three.js has, and what is missing.
The pipeline#
The pipeline has two parts. The setup fills three caches: lightmaps for static meshes, a light probe grid for moving objects, and reflection probes for each room.
Each frame then reads those caches and adds the screen-space work on top:
Where things stand#
The biggest remaining gaps are in the SSR, SSGI and BRDF rows: Hi-Z tracing and coverage for SSR, the same coverage for SSGI, and above all the pluggable indirect lighting that ties both cascades into the BRDF.
It has moved this fast because of the Three.js maintainers. Michael Herzog (@Mugen87) has reviewed most of these PRs, and more than once has reworked one into a better design that fits how Three.js as a whole is built, adjusting the renderer's internals to make room for it. mrdoob has expressed strong support for many of them. I am very lucky to have both.
So far, though, these pieces have been proposed and reviewed one at a time. Nobody has been asked to sign up to the whole. This series is my attempt to put them together into one picture, so that each PR can be judged for where it fits as well as for what it does.
The pipeline, stage by stage#
The G-buffer#
What the games require. SSR, GTAO and the denoisers run in screen space before lighting, so they need per-pixel depth, normals, roughness, metalness and motion vectors. A deferred engine also stores base color and emissive, because its lighting pass reads only the G-buffer. Three.js renders forward and its beauty pass reads those from the material, so the G-buffer fits in 16 bytes per pixel. Part 2 has the layout and the memory budget for the whole frame.
What Three.js has. WebGPURenderer already renders a G-buffer prepass with multiple render targets, and the SSR examples use it today:
const scenePass = pass( scene, camera );
scenePass.setMRT( mrt( {
	output: output,
	diffuseColor: vec4( diffuseColor.rgb, materialMetalness ),
	normal: vec4( packNormalToRGB( normalView ).rgb, materialRoughness ),
	velocity: velocity
} ) );
What is missing. Normal precision. SSR is unforgiving of normal error: a ray reflected off a slightly wrong normal lands somewhere visibly wrong at the end of a long trace. With RGB8 normals, smooth curved surfaces snap to a limited set of directions, and their reflections show banding and clumping.
AAA G-buffers use octahedral encoding: fold the sphere of directions onto an octahedron, unfold it into a square, and store two coordinates. It is the most accurate of the encodings surveyed by Cigolle et al. for its size. PR #35480 adds packNormalToOctahedral() and unpackOctahedralToNormal():
RG16 snorm is the target, with RG16F as the fallback.
Global illumination#
What the games require. Bounce light baked into lightmaps for everything that does not move, and a probe volume to light dynamic objects, ideally one that does not leak light through walls.
What Three.js has. Every standard material takes a lightMap, and there is now a complete baking pipeline in the browser to make one; that is Part 4. For dynamic objects, LightProbeGrid places a grid of probes through a scene, each storing incoming light as L2 spherical harmonics, and lights each object from the probes around it (example).
The grid's limit was how long a capture took. Profiling showed the bake was CPU-bound on submitting render passes, so the batched capture renders eight probes per pass with one array camera, and a resolution-12 grid dropped from 5.6 s to 1.2 s. Culling each draw against its own sub-camera doubled that again. The grid now bakes about eight times faster than it did at the start of September, fast enough to re-capture a few probes per frame, and supports multi-bounce light. Integrating the spherical harmonics exactly also cut their error from 2.4% to 0.08%.
What is missing. Probes leak. A probe on one side of a wall can light an object on the other, so a dark room glows with the light of the bright room next door. DDGI solves this by storing, with each probe, the distance to the nearest surface in every direction, and ignoring probes that cannot see the point being lit. I have DDGI-style visibility weighting working as a draft PR. Testing visibility against all eight surrounding probes was costly, so the draft can use tetrahedral interpolation, which blends four:
Ambient and specular occlusion#
What the games require. Lightmaps are too coarse for contact shadows, and they know nothing about dynamic objects. Games add screen-space occlusion on top, and Activision's GTAO is the standard. It also produces a bent normal, the average open direction, which gives specular occlusion (GTSO): a reflection pointing into a fold of the surface is occluded, one pointing out of the opening is not.
Horizon-based SSGI, which is what Three.js has, runs the same depth-buffer search as GTAO and gathers light along the way. With SSGI on, its pass supplies the occlusion and the bent normal, and GTAO runs only when SSGI is off.
Which light the occlusion applies to matters as much as how it is computed. Occlusion is a shared buffer, set with builtinAOContext, and each source decides whether to read it:
- The lightmap, probe grid and environment apply AO to their indirect diffuse, combined with the material's AO map as min( materialAO, gtao ).
- The reflection probes and environment apply GTSO to their indirect specular.
- SSR and SSGI apply neither. A screen-space hit is something the ray found, so it is already correctly occluded.
- Behind SSGI, the diffuse sources skip AO. SSGI's coverage is the share of the hemisphere that something on screen blocks, which is the occlusion itself. The cascade already scales the lightmap or probe grid by 1 − coverage.
- Occlusion darkens a source's color and leaves its coverage alone. Lowering an occluded probe's coverage would let the next source's unoccluded light leak into the corner.
What Three.js has. GTAO already feeds the lighting through a context, which is the pattern the indirect lighting design in Part 5 extends:
const aoPass = ao( prePassDepth, prePassNormal, camera );
scenePass.contextNode = builtinAOContext( aoPass.getTextureNode().sample( screenUV ).r );
What is missing.
- Specular occlusion. GTAO outputs a single visibility value, and the lighting model turns it into specular occlusion with a heuristic. It does not know which directions are blocked, so metal keeps reflecting the sky inside folds. Bent normals and GTSO are up as a draft PR. The bent normal comes out of the same horizon search; the cost is an AO target that grows from one byte per pixel to four.
- Edge-aware upsampling. Half-resolution GTAO upsampled bilinearly leaves dark outlines around objects. jointBilateralUpsample() uses the full-resolution depth and normals as guides (Kopf et al. 2007), so the result stops at the edges. It is drafted and not yet submitted; half-resolution SSR and SSGI need the same filter.
- Bent normals from SSGINode, so that specular occlusion does not need a second pass when SSGI is on.
Screen-space reflections#
SSR has its own series, Fixing Three.js's Screen Space Reflections. This section is the summary.
What the games require. Shipped engines agree on a recipe, set out with its sources in How Games Do Screen-Space Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead. In a cascade, SSR has to:
- Trace the previous frame's lit image, so the reflection exists before the frame is shaded.
- Trace exactly over any distance, using a Hi-Z depth pyramid.
- Trace at half resolution and reuse rays between pixels, which is what brings the trace under a millisecond.
- Output radiance and coverage, so the probes can fill what it misses.
- Denoise that radiance and coverage, and leave the BRDF to the material.
What Three.js has. SSRNode importance-samples the full GGX lobe with correct Fresnel, can validate and refine its hits, and its result is reprojected and accumulated over time. The trace is a fixed-step march with short rays. The three SSR examples find 98%, 82% and 46% of the hits within their own ray length, in 2 to 3 ms, and the denoiser fills the gaps from neighbouring pixels. The result is composited over the image, as in the SSR example:
const litColor = scenePassColor.rgb.add( denoisedReflections.rgb );
What is missing. All five requirements, each prototyped or in review except ray reuse.
Exact tracing. A Hi-Z pyramid is a mip chain where each texel stores the nearest depth of the four below it. The ray takes large steps through empty space at coarse levels and single-pixel steps near surfaces, so it finds every hit the depth buffer contains and has no maximum distance to tune. My implementation adds a HiZNode that builds the pyramid in a compute pass. Trace time at 1920×1080, against the fixed-step march raised to the same hit rate:
That is still a ray for every pixel. Tracing at half resolution with a joint bilateral upsample is written, and ray reuse between pixels, as Frostbite does it, is still to build. Exact Screen-Space Reflections on a Budget has the full plan.
Coverage. Today a ray that misses samples an environment map inside SSR: an equirectangular texture passed in as environmentNode, which cannot be the PMREM-filtered scene.environment, let alone a local probe. Adding SSR over the image also counts the environment reflection twice. In a cascade, SSR outputs one thing: radiance premultiplied by coverage, with coverage 1 for a hit, 0 for a miss, and fading toward the screen border. The environment input and the BRDF estimate leave the node. This is prototyped as part of Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.
Tracing the previous frame. SSR cannot be part of the lighting while it reads the lighting's output. DOOM's answer is to trace the current depth buffer but read colors from the previous frame: reproject each hit point into last frame's TRAA output and sample it there. A hit that fails the check against last frame's depth gets zero coverage. Last frame's image already contained last frame's reflections, so a mirror facing a mirror gains a bounce each frame. Previous-frame tracing is in review.
The loop needs two rules. The image SSR reads must be linear HDR radiance, taken after TRAA but before tone mapping and bloom, or reflections pick up tone-mapped colors and bloom halos. And the fed-back radiance must be clamped, because each frame's reflections become the next frame's input and a single firefly compounds frame after frame.
Denoising. Three.js has two reflection denoisers. The pair the SSR example runs, TemporalReprojectNode and RecurrentDenoiseNode, reads every black pixel as missing data and fills it from its neighbours. That hides the tracer's misses and leaves nothing for the probes to answer. zalo's SVGF-based DenoiseNode replaced the pair in the SSR example and was taken back out five days later. I traced the flicker that caused it to the missing coverage: at the edge of a reflection a hit and a miss were averaged as two samples of one signal, and the history kept resetting.
My ssr-coverage branch carries coverage through every stage of DenoiseNode and takes its statistics from covered samples only. Still to do are a two-lookup history, a history cap that follows roughness, and skipping mirrors and matte pixels. The denoiser filters incoming light and the material applies its BRDF afterwards, so it needs no albedo in the G-buffer and no demodulation step. How Games Denoise Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead has the comparison and the plan.
Screen-space global illumination#
What the games require. Engines that use SSGI as part of their lighting put it in front of their baked light as the first stage of the diffuse cascade. That means SSGI has to output coverage, trace the previous frame's lit image, and accumulate over time at half resolution.
What Three.js has. SSGINode is built on the visibility-bitmask approach of SSRT3, which extends GTAO's horizon search to gather light as well as occlusion. One search of 24 depth samples yields a GI texture and an AO texture, and it is much less noisy than a single random ray, because each sample accounts for a whole arc of directions. The SSGI example traces the current frame's beauty pass and composites over it.
What is missing.
- Coverage output. The sectors the search marks as blocked are the directions in which it found a surface, so coverage is 1 − ao, and the node already computes it. What is missing is handing the GI and that coverage to the cascade as a pair, so SSGI can replace the baked bounce where it has an answer.
- Previous-frame tracing. SSR reads the previous frame once per pixel, where its ray lands. SSGI reads it at every sample that finds a surface, so reprojecting at each read is paid many times per pixel. A draft measures the options on an Apple M3:
The third option also follows moving objects, and shows no visible artifacts in the test scenes.
Reflection probes#
What the games require. Indoors, one environment map is wrong: walk from a red room into a blue corridor and the floor should reflect red, then blue. Every game in the survey, and Unreal's reflection captures, use local reflection probes: cubemaps captured inside each room, each with a box describing the volume it influences. Inside its box a probe is box-projected, which removes most of a cubemap's parallax error (Lagarde's write-up is the classic explanation). Where boxes overlap, probes blend.
What Three.js has. CubeCamera captures a cubemap, PMREMGenerator prefilters it, and getParallaxCorrectNormal() box-projects it, as the box-projected environment map example shows. That is one probe per material, set by hand.
What is missing.
- A probe system. Box-projected reflection probes for WebGPURenderer adds scene-level probes with influence boxes and blending, and is up as a draft PR.
- Fast access to many probes. Cube array textures put every probe in one texture; sampling them is merged, and the texture class is in review.
- Probe normalization. A probe is captured at one point in a room, so a dark corner or the inside of a cupboard reflects a brightly lit room. Call of Duty's fix, introduced in Black Ops II and carried into Infinite Warfare, is to scale the probe's reflection by the ratio of the diffuse light at the pixel to the diffuse light at the probe. The lightmaps and probe grid already provide both. Still to do.
- Small probes. PMREMGenerator has a minimum size of 256². A 128² probe is enough for blurry room reflections, since SSR handles the sharp ones, and takes a quarter of the memory. Still to do.
Indirect lighting in the BRDF#
What the games require. The bounced light has to go through the material's BRDF, so Fresnel, roughness and metalness apply to it as they do to direct light. In a forward renderer the beauty pass needs two inputs:
- Indirect diffuse: SSGI where it has coverage, then the lightmap on static meshes or the probe grid on everything else, then the environment map.
- Indirect specular: SSR, then the box-projected probes, then the environment map.
Three.js renders forward, so SSR, SSGI and AO are computed before the beauty pass and each material reads them while it shades. Tracing the previous frame is what makes that order possible.
What Three.js has. Indirect diffuse is mostly in place: lightMap, LightProbeGrid and scene.environment all feed it, and AO reaches it through builtinAOContext. Indirect specular comes only from scene.environment, or a material's own envMap.
What is missing. A way to plug a screen-space result, or a cascade of sources, into a material's indirect specular, the way AO is plugged into its diffuse. This is the biggest gap in the pipeline, and my proposed design is in Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.
TRAA and TAAU#
What the games require. Temporal anti-aliasing whose output can also be next frame's input to SSR and SSGI, so it has to stay sharp under motion and must not feed ghosts or fireflies back into the reflections. Every engine this series measures itself against also renders below the output resolution and reconstructs the difference over time: TSR in Unreal, FSR 2 in Godot, DLSS and FSR in Cyberpunk 2077.
What Three.js has. A TRAA node with Halton jitter, motion-vector reprojection and variance clipping of the history, and TAAUNode, which follows Karis's temporal supersampling and FSR 2. The TAAU example shows it at a quarter of the pixels:
scenePass.setResolutionScale( 0.5 );
const taauNode = taau( scenePassColor, scenePassDepth, scenePassVelocity, camera );
TAAU takes TRAA's place as the last stage of the frame. Everything before it runs at the render resolution, its linear HDR output is what the next frame's SSR and SSGI read, and bloom and tone mapping run after it. At a scale of 0.5, the screen buffers at 1080p drop from about 157 MB to 81 MB.
What is missing.
- Wider clipping at rest. Variance clipping stops ghosting by rejecting history that no longer matches the current frame, and it also rejects good history. TRAA tightens its clip box to 0.5σ under fast motion, but at rest the box was 1σ, tight enough to clip converged sub-pixel detail, so a still image never fully resolved and longer histories scored worse. A drafted change widens the box to 2σ at rest and adds a historyLength control. Against a supersampled reference:
- Sharper history. History sampled bilinearly blurs a little more every frame the camera moves. Catmull-Rom history sampling, a draft PR, keeps it sharp. Both refinements apply to TAAU as well.
- TAAU in the full pipeline. The example upscales a single scene pass. The pipeline has a prepass, half-resolution effects and a beauty pass that all have to agree on resolution and jitter, and none of that has been tried together yet. With TAAU at 0.5, half-resolution SSR and SSGI would run at a quarter of the output resolution on each axis, so it may be better to run them at the full render resolution and skip the bilateral upsample.
- Texture mip bias. Rendering at half resolution makes the GPU pick blurrier texture mips than the output deserves. Temporal upscalers pair with a negative mip bias of about log2 of the resolution scale, and Three.js does not apply one yet.
Future work#
- Cheaper noise. Houston Stratified Noise costs about 400 operations per sample, on every pixel, every frame. I want to move some of that into a small map generated at startup, so each sample is a lookup and a few adds.
- Auto-exposure. Walking from a dark room into a bright courtyard needs eye adaptation, and Three.js does not have it yet.
- A physically based sun and sky. A room lit through its windows needs a sun and sky in real units that agree with each other and with the exposure. A prototype does single scattering; multiple scattering and clouds are still to do.
- Reflection probes in glTF. There is no standard way to ship reflection probes. The minimum is each probe's position and influence box, so a loader can capture the probes on load.
- Directional lightmaps. The lightmaps here store one irradiance value per texel, so normal maps cannot respond to baked light. The options are an ambient term plus one dominant direction as in The Last of Us and Call of Duty, L1 spherical harmonics as in Frostbite, or spherical Gaussians as in The Order: 1886.

articles.title: My Quest to push native Three.js quality match AAA Game Engines
articles.body:
Building the AAA Lighting Pipeline in Three.js
From the G-buffer to temporal upscaling, here is each stage of the lightmap, probe and screen-space reflection pipeline measured against Three.js: what games require of it, what Three.js has today, and the pull requests in review or still to write.
Ben Houston • • 21 min read
Part 2 picked a pipeline for indoor scenes: lightmaps, light probes and reflection probes, with SSR, SSGI and ambient occlusion on top. Here I measure Three.js against it one stage at a time: what the games require, what Three.js has, and what is missing.
The pipeline#
The pipeline has two parts. The setup fills three caches: lightmaps for static meshes, a light probe grid for moving objects, and reflection probes for each room.
Each frame then reads those caches and adds the screen-space work on top:
Where things stand#
The biggest remaining gaps are in the SSR, SSGI and BRDF rows: Hi-Z tracing and coverage for SSR, the same coverage for SSGI, and above all the pluggable indirect lighting that ties both cascades into the BRDF.
It has moved this fast because of the Three.js maintainers. Michael Herzog (@Mugen87) has reviewed most of these PRs, and more than once has reworked one into a better design that fits how Three.js as a whole is built, adjusting the renderer's internals to make room for it. mrdoob has expressed strong support for many of them. I am very lucky to have both.
So far, though, these pieces have been proposed and reviewed one at a time. Nobody has been asked to sign up to the whole. This series is my attempt to put them together into one picture, so that each PR can be judged for where it fits as well as for what it does.
The pipeline, stage by stage#
The G-buffer#
What the games require. SSR, GTAO and the denoisers run in screen space before lighting, so they need per-pixel depth, normals, roughness, metalness and motion vectors. A deferred engine also stores base color and emissive, because its lighting pass reads only the G-buffer. Three.js renders forward and its beauty pass reads those from the material, so the G-buffer fits in 16 bytes per pixel. Part 2 has the layout and the memory budget for the whole frame.
What Three.js has. WebGPURenderer already renders a G-buffer prepass with multiple render targets, and the SSR examples use it today:
const scenePass = pass( scene, camera );
scenePass.setMRT( mrt( {
	output: output,
	diffuseColor: vec4( diffuseColor.rgb, materialMetalness ),
	normal: vec4( packNormalToRGB( normalView ).rgb, materialRoughness ),
	velocity: velocity
} ) );
What is missing. Normal precision. SSR is unforgiving of normal error: a ray reflected off a slightly wrong normal lands somewhere visibly wrong at the end of a long trace. With RGB8 normals, smooth curved surfaces snap to a limited set of directions, and their reflections show banding and clumping.
AAA G-buffers use octahedral encoding: fold the sphere of directions onto an octahedron, unfold it into a square, and store two coordinates. It is the most accurate of the encodings surveyed by Cigolle et al. for its size. PR #35480 adds packNormalToOctahedral() and unpackOctahedralToNormal():
RG16 snorm is the target, with RG16F as the fallback.
Global illumination#
What the games require. Bounce light baked into lightmaps for everything that does not move, and a probe volume to light dynamic objects, ideally one that does not leak light through walls.
What Three.js has. Every standard material takes a lightMap, and there is now a complete baking pipeline in the browser to make one; that is Part 4. For dynamic objects, LightProbeGrid places a grid of probes through a scene, each storing incoming light as L2 spherical harmonics, and lights each object from the probes around it (example).
The grid's limit was how long a capture took. Profiling showed the bake was CPU-bound on submitting render passes, so the batched capture renders eight probes per pass with one array camera, and a resolution-12 grid dropped from 5.6 s to 1.2 s. Culling each draw against its own sub-camera doubled that again. The grid now bakes about eight times faster than it did at the start of September, fast enough to re-capture a few probes per frame, and supports multi-bounce light. Integrating the spherical harmonics exactly also cut their error from 2.4% to 0.08%.
What is missing. Probes leak. A probe on one side of a wall can light an object on the other, so a dark room glows with the light of the bright room next door. DDGI solves this by storing, with each probe, the distance to the nearest surface in every direction, and ignoring probes that cannot see the point being lit. I have DDGI-style visibility weighting working as a draft PR. Testing visibility against all eight surrounding probes was costly, so the draft can use tetrahedral interpolation, which blends four:
Ambient and specular occlusion#
What the games require. Lightmaps are too coarse for contact shadows, and they know nothing about dynamic objects. Games add screen-space occlusion on top, and Activision's GTAO is the standard. It also produces a bent normal, the average open direction, which gives specular occlusion (GTSO): a reflection pointing into a fold of the surface is occluded, one pointing out of the opening is not.
Horizon-based SSGI, which is what Three.js has, runs the same depth-buffer search as GTAO and gathers light along the way. With SSGI on, its pass supplies the occlusion and the bent normal, and GTAO runs only when SSGI is off.
Which light the occlusion applies to matters as much as how it is computed. Occlusion is a shared buffer, set with builtinAOContext, and each source decides whether to read it:
- The lightmap, probe grid and environment apply AO to their indirect diffuse, combined with the material's AO map as min( materialAO, gtao ).
- The reflection probes and environment apply GTSO to their indirect specular.
- SSR and SSGI apply neither. A screen-space hit is something the ray found, so it is already correctly occluded.
- Behind SSGI, the diffuse sources skip AO. SSGI's coverage is the share of the hemisphere that something on screen blocks, which is the occlusion itself. The cascade already scales the lightmap or probe grid by 1 − coverage.
- Occlusion darkens a source's color and leaves its coverage alone. Lowering an occluded probe's coverage would let the next source's unoccluded light leak into the corner.
What Three.js has. GTAO already feeds the lighting through a context, which is the pattern the indirect lighting design in Part 5 extends:
const aoPass = ao( prePassDepth, prePassNormal, camera );
scenePass.contextNode = builtinAOContext( aoPass.getTextureNode().sample( screenUV ).r );
What is missing.
- Specular occlusion. GTAO outputs a single visibility value, and the lighting model turns it into specular occlusion with a heuristic. It does not know which directions are blocked, so metal keeps reflecting the sky inside folds. Bent normals and GTSO are up as a draft PR. The bent normal comes out of the same horizon search; the cost is an AO target that grows from one byte per pixel to four.
- Edge-aware upsampling. Half-resolution GTAO upsampled bilinearly leaves dark outlines around objects. jointBilateralUpsample() uses the full-resolution depth and normals as guides (Kopf et al. 2007), so the result stops at the edges. It is drafted and not yet submitted; half-resolution SSR and SSGI need the same filter.
- Bent normals from SSGINode, so that specular occlusion does not need a second pass when SSGI is on.
Screen-space reflections#
SSR has its own series, Fixing Three.js's Screen Space Reflections. This section is the summary.
What the games require. Shipped engines agree on a recipe, set out with its sources in How Games Do Screen-Space Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead. In a cascade, SSR has to:
- Trace the previous frame's lit image, so the reflection exists before the frame is shaded.
- Trace exactly over any distance, using a Hi-Z depth pyramid.
- Trace at half resolution and reuse rays between pixels, which is what brings the trace under a millisecond.
- Output radiance and coverage, so the probes can fill what it misses.
- Denoise that radiance and coverage, and leave the BRDF to the material.
What Three.js has. SSRNode importance-samples the full GGX lobe with correct Fresnel, can validate and refine its hits, and its result is reprojected and accumulated over time. The trace is a fixed-step march with short rays. The three SSR examples find 98%, 82% and 46% of the hits within their own ray length, in 2 to 3 ms, and the denoiser fills the gaps from neighbouring pixels. The result is composited over the image, as in the SSR example:
const litColor = scenePassColor.rgb.add( denoisedReflections.rgb );
What is missing. All five requirements, each prototyped or in review except ray reuse.
Exact tracing. A Hi-Z pyramid is a mip chain where each texel stores the nearest depth of the four below it. The ray takes large steps through empty space at coarse levels and single-pixel steps near surfaces, so it finds every hit the depth buffer contains and has no maximum distance to tune. My implementation adds a HiZNode that builds the pyramid in a compute pass. Trace time at 1920×1080, against the fixed-step march raised to the same hit rate:
That is still a ray for every pixel. Tracing at half resolution with a joint bilateral upsample is written, and ray reuse between pixels, as Frostbite does it, is still to build. Exact Screen-Space Reflections on a Budget has the full plan.
Coverage. Today a ray that misses samples an environment map inside SSR: an equirectangular texture passed in as environmentNode, which cannot be the PMREM-filtered scene.environment, let alone a local probe. Adding SSR over the image also counts the environment reflection twice. In a cascade, SSR outputs one thing: radiance premultiplied by coverage, with coverage 1 for a hit, 0 for a miss, and fading toward the screen border. The environment input and the BRDF estimate leave the node. This is prototyped as part of Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.
Tracing the previous frame. SSR cannot be part of the lighting while it reads the lighting's output. DOOM's answer is to trace the current depth buffer but read colors from the previous frame: reproject each hit point into last frame's TRAA output and sample it there. A hit that fails the check against last frame's depth gets zero coverage. Last frame's image already contained last frame's reflections, so a mirror facing a mirror gains a bounce each frame. Previous-frame tracing is in review.
The loop needs two rules. The image SSR reads must be linear HDR radiance, taken after TRAA but before tone mapping and bloom, or reflections pick up tone-mapped colors and bloom halos. And the fed-back radiance must be clamped, because each frame's reflections become the next frame's input and a single firefly compounds frame after frame.
Denoising. Three.js has two reflection denoisers. The pair the SSR example runs, TemporalReprojectNode and RecurrentDenoiseNode, reads every black pixel as missing data and fills it from its neighbours. That hides the tracer's misses and leaves nothing for the probes to answer. zalo's SVGF-based DenoiseNode replaced the pair in the SSR example and was taken back out five days later. I traced the flicker that caused it to the missing coverage: at the edge of a reflection a hit and a miss were averaged as two samples of one signal, and the history kept resetting.
My ssr-coverage branch carries coverage through every stage of DenoiseNode and takes its statistics from covered samples only. Still to do are a two-lookup history, a history cap that follows roughness, and skipping mirrors and matte pixels. The denoiser filters incoming light and the material applies its BRDF afterwards, so it needs no albedo in the G-buffer and no demodulation step. How Games Denoise Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead has the comparison and the plan.
Screen-space global illumination#
What the games require. Engines that use SSGI as part of their lighting put it in front of their baked light as the first stage of the diffuse cascade. That means SSGI has to output coverage, trace the previous frame's lit image, and accumulate over time at half resolution.
What Three.js has. SSGINode is built on the visibility-bitmask approach of SSRT3, which extends GTAO's horizon search to gather light as well as occlusion. One search of 24 depth samples yields a GI texture and an AO texture, and it is much less noisy than a single random ray, because each sample accounts for a whole arc of directions. The SSGI example traces the current frame's beauty pass and composites over it.
What is missing.
- Coverage output. The sectors the search marks as blocked are the directions in which it found a surface, so coverage is 1 − ao, and the node already computes it. What is missing is handing the GI and that coverage to the cascade as a pair, so SSGI can replace the baked bounce where it has an answer.
- Previous-frame tracing. SSR reads the previous frame once per pixel, where its ray lands. SSGI reads it at every sample that finds a surface, so reprojecting at each read is paid many times per pixel. A draft measures the options on an Apple M3:
The third option also follows moving objects, and shows no visible artifacts in the test scenes.
Reflection probes#
What the games require. Indoors, one environment map is wrong: walk from a red room into a blue corridor and the floor should reflect red, then blue. Every game in the survey, and Unreal's reflection captures, use local reflection probes: cubemaps captured inside each room, each with a box describing the volume it influences. Inside its box a probe is box-projected, which removes most of a cubemap's parallax error (Lagarde's write-up is the classic explanation). Where boxes overlap, probes blend.
What Three.js has. CubeCamera captures a cubemap, PMREMGenerator prefilters it, and getParallaxCorrectNormal() box-projects it, as the box-projected environment map example shows. That is one probe per material, set by hand.
What is missing.
- A probe system. Box-projected reflection probes for WebGPURenderer adds scene-level probes with influence boxes and blending, and is up as a draft PR.
- Fast access to many probes. Cube array textures put every probe in one texture; sampling them is merged, and the texture class is in review.
- Probe normalization. A probe is captured at one point in a room, so a dark corner or the inside of a cupboard reflects a brightly lit room. Call of Duty's fix, introduced in Black Ops II and carried into Infinite Warfare, is to scale the probe's reflection by the ratio of the diffuse light at the pixel to the diffuse light at the probe. The lightmaps and probe grid already provide both. Still to do.
- Small probes. PMREMGenerator has a minimum size of 256². A 128² probe is enough for blurry room reflections, since SSR handles the sharp ones, and takes a quarter of the memory. Still to do.
Indirect lighting in the BRDF#
What the games require. The bounced light has to go through the material's BRDF, so Fresnel, roughness and metalness apply to it as they do to direct light. In a forward renderer the beauty pass needs two inputs:
- Indirect diffuse: SSGI where it has coverage, then the lightmap on static meshes or the probe grid on everything else, then the environment map.
- Indirect specular: SSR, then the box-projected probes, then the environment map.
Three.js renders forward, so SSR, SSGI and AO are computed before the beauty pass and each material reads them while it shades. Tracing the previous frame is what makes that order possible.
What Three.js has. Indirect diffuse is mostly in place: lightMap, LightProbeGrid and scene.environment all feed it, and AO reaches it through builtinAOContext. Indirect specular comes only from scene.environment, or a material's own envMap.
What is missing. A way to plug a screen-space result, or a cascade of sources, into a material's indirect specular, the way AO is plugged into its diffuse. This is the biggest gap in the pipeline, and my proposed design is in Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.
TRAA and TAAU#
What the games require. Temporal anti-aliasing whose output can also be next frame's input to SSR and SSGI, so it has to stay sharp under motion and must not feed ghosts or fireflies back into the reflections. Every engine this series measures itself against also renders below the output resolution and reconstructs the difference over time: TSR in Unreal, FSR 2 in Godot, DLSS and FSR in Cyberpunk 2077.
What Three.js has. A TRAA node with Halton jitter, motion-vector reprojection and variance clipping of the history, and TAAUNode, which follows Karis's temporal supersampling and FSR 2. The TAAU example shows it at a quarter of the pixels:
scenePass.setResolutionScale( 0.5 );
const taauNode = taau( scenePassColor, scenePassDepth, scenePassVelocity, camera );
TAAU takes TRAA's place as the last stage of the frame. Everything before it runs at the render resolution, its linear HDR output is what the next frame's SSR and SSGI read, and bloom and tone mapping run after it. At a scale of 0.5, the screen buffers at 1080p drop from about 157 MB to 81 MB.
What is missing.
- Wider clipping at rest. Variance clipping stops ghosting by rejecting history that no longer matches the current frame, and it also rejects good history. TRAA tightens its clip box to 0.5σ under fast motion, but at rest the box was 1σ, tight enough to clip converged sub-pixel detail, so a still image never fully resolved and longer histories scored worse. A drafted change widens the box to 2σ at rest and adds a historyLength control. Against a supersampled reference:
- Sharper history. History sampled bilinearly blurs a little more every frame the camera moves. Catmull-Rom history sampling, a draft PR, keeps it sharp. Both refinements apply to TAAU as well.
- TAAU in the full pipeline. The example upscales a single scene pass. The pipeline has a prepass, half-resolution effects and a beauty pass that all have to agree on resolution and jitter, and none of that has been tried together yet. With TAAU at 0.5, half-resolution SSR and SSGI would run at a quarter of the output resolution on each axis, so it may be better to run them at the full render resolution and skip the bilateral upsample.
- Texture mip bias. Rendering at half resolution makes the GPU pick blurrier texture mips than the output deserves. Temporal upscalers pair with a negative mip bias of about log2 of the resolution scale, and Three.js does not apply one yet.
Future work#
- Cheaper noise. Houston Stratified Noise costs about 400 operations per sample, on every pixel, every frame. I want to move some of that into a small map generated at startup, so each sample is a lookup and a few adds.
- Auto-exposure. Walking from a dark room into a bright courtyard needs eye adaptation, and Three.js does not have it yet.
- A physically based sun and sky. A room lit through its windows needs a sun and sky in real units that agree with each other and with the exposure. A prototype does single scattering; multiple scattering and clouds are still to do.
- Reflection probes in glTF. There is no standard way to ship reflection probes. The minimum is each probe's position and influence box, so a loader can capture the probes on load.

The options are an ambient term plus one dominant direction as in The Last of Us and Call of Duty, L1 spherical harmonics as in Frostbite, or spherical Gaussians as in The Order: 1886.

articles.title: 17 Thanksgiving Salads
articles.body:
17 Thanksgiving Salads
Posted by Kathryne Taylor on November 16, 2026
Thanksgiving is coming right up! Your feast isn’t complete without a fresh salad or two to balance the mashed potatoes. While they’re often overlooked amongst more indulgent options, I’ll warn you that these salad recipes could steal the show.
Below, you’ll find seventeen great candidates for Thanksgiving Day. These recipes feature ingredients like fresh greens, vibrant fall produce, freshly toasted nuts or seeds, and zippy homemade dressings. Some include whole grains like wild rice or farro, which make nice leftovers for light post-holiday meals (store the dressing on the side so the lettuce doesn’t wilt).
I’ve brought my Favorite Green Salad with Apples to Friendsgivings, and I bring my Farro and Kale Salad with Goat Cheese every year to our family’s big celebration. The latter is hearty enough to serve as a vegetarian main dish, since there’s so much else to load onto the plate! You can peruse all of my Thanksgiving recipes here, from appetizers through dessert.
Favorite Green Salad with Apples, Cranberries and Pepitas
My favorite fresh salad featuring healthy greens, sliced apple, toasted pepitas, dried cranberries and crumbled goat cheese. Toss with my simple apple cider vinaigrette (recipe below) or use balsamic dressing in a pinch. Recipe yields 2 full-sized salads or 4 to 6 side salads.
Honey Mustard Brussels Sprout Slaw
This delicious slaw recipe features shredded Brussels sprouts tossed with tangy honey mustard dressing, toasted almonds and dried cherries (or cranberries). Recipe yields 4 substantial side servings; double if desired.
Pomegranate & Pear Green Salad with Ginger Dressing
This gorgeous green salad recipe is bursting with fresh pomegranate, Bartlett pear and Honeycrisp apple! This salad will brighten up your holiday table, and liven up a regular weeknight dinner. Recipe yields 4 to 6 side salads.
Roasted Beet Salad with Goat Cheese & Pistachios
This classic roasted beet salad recipe is like my favorite French restaurants’ beet salads! This salad features goat cheese, pistachios and arugula with a zippy Dijon dressing. Recipe yields 4 to 6 side servings.
Hearty Sweet Potato, Arugula & Wild Rice Salad with Ginger Dressing
This delicious salad recipe features roasted sweet potato, wild rice and arugula. It’s fresh, filling and nutritious! Enjoy this salad all week long. This recipe yields a lot of salad (6 generous servings) and is easily halved.
Farro and Kale Salad with Goat Cheese
You’re going to love this delicious and nutritious kale and farro salad recipe! It’s full of hearty greens and chewy whole grains, plus flavorful toasted almonds, crumbled goat cheese, dried cherries and tangy vinaigrette. Recipe yields 4 large salads or up to 8 side salads.
Spinach Salad
Make this delicious spinach salad recipe to serve with your main dish! It features fresh spinach, creamy goat cheese and seasonal fruit. Recipe yields 6 side salads.
Roasted Delicata Squash, Pomegranate and Arugula Salad
This vibrant salad features delicata squash, pomegranate, arugula, pepitas and feta tossed in a maple balsamic vinaigrette. If you are preparing this salad in advance, reserve the dressing on the side until you are ready to serve. Recipe yields 6 substantial side salads or up to 10 small salads; cut the recipe in half if desired.
Arugula and Wild Rice Salad with Zippy Lemon Dressing
This wild rice salad includes arugula, dried cherries, toasted almonds and feta, tossed in a zippy lemon dressing! It’s gluten free, filling and delicious. Recipe yields 4 medium salads, or 8 small side servings.
Kale, Apple & Goat Cheese Salad with Granola “Croutons”
Nutty granola croutons complete this salad made with massaged raw kale, crisp chopped apple, and crumbled goat cheese tossed in a tangy lemon dressing. This recipe yields 4 medium salads, and twice as much granola as you’ll need—it stores well for future salads.
Shredded Brussels Sprouts & Arugula Salad with Sunshine Dressing
This shredded Brussels sprout and arugula salad is crisp, refreshing and filling. Enjoy this simple recipe for dinner, pack it for lunch tomorrow, make it for the holidays! Recipe yields 4 large portions or 6 to 8 side salads.
Pear Salad with Walnuts
This fresh green salad with pears, walnuts, dates and blue cheese is a fresh option for your holiday table! It’s a great side salad for fall dinners, too. Recipe yields 4 side salads.
Butternut Tabbouleh
This fresh winter tabbouleh salad recipe features butternut squash instead of tomatoes, along with some dried cranberries for complementary flavor. This recipe yields 4 side salads. Feel free to double the recipe; if you do, you’ll likely need to cook the butternut squash longer than indicated below.
Autumn Kale Salad with Fennel, Honeycrisp and Goat Cheese
Healthy kale salad featuring shaved fennel, chopped honeycrisp apple, toasted pepitas, dried cranberries and goat cheese, tossed in a lemony dressing. This recipe yields 2 large, full-meal salads or 4 side salads.
The Little Green Salad
This simple green side salad is made with Parmesan and toasted nuts, tossed in lemon dressing. It’s wonderful in its simplest form, but you can add my suggested seasonal variations or put your own spin on it. Recipe yields 6 to 8 side salads.
Balsamic Butternut, Kale and Cranberry Panzanella
This winter panzanella salad features roasted butternut squash, kale, toasted croutons, cranberries and shallots tossed in homemade balsamic vinaigrette. Recipe yields 3 to 4 meal-sized salads.
More Thanksgiving recipe resources:
- 35+ Meatless Thanksgiving Recipes organized by course
- 16 Healthy Thanksgiving Side Dishes
- Thanksgiving Recipes category with filters for special diets, course, and more

articles.title: Caltech professor no longer grades homework's because everyone uses AI
articles.body:
Professor Yi Ni had no laptop or projector. He instead rapidly filled eight blackboards with chalk scrawl during an introductory math class at Caltech on Friday.
Though the instruction was entirely analog, the specter of AI loomed large.
Ni, a professor at Caltech for 17 years, told me that he no longer grades homework on accuracy because students are using AI to complete it. Now, he grades it only on completion.
"There is a problem in the education process," Ni said. "Virtually all the homework in college math, you can use AI."
Chatbots, once derided for their inability to perform such basic tasks as counting the r's in "strawberry," can now do math as well as a graduate student.
And if you're an undergraduate student, that's kind of a big deal. Some, Business Insider has reported, are reconsidering whether to study math at all.
From my perch near the back of the lecture hall on Friday, however, I didn't see any students prompting ChatGPT.
In many ways, the class resembled a typical early morning university lecture (for undergrads, 10 a.m. is basically the crack of dawn). Sweatshirted students arrived late and filtered in the upper rows, while the overachievers sat in the front and asked questions.
Many bent their heads over large iPads and took furious notes while Yi filled up blackboard after blackboard with formulas and practice problems. Some had no note-taking materials to speak of. A couple closed their eyes for extended periods.
The class is a "core requirement" in Caltech's curriculum, meaning everyone at the school has to take it. Students I spoke to afterward gave a variety of majors, but none said they were comfortable speaking on the record.
So later on I spoke with Sathvik Redrouthu, a sophomore who'd taken the class last year. Redrouthu, a math major, said he didn't use AI because he wanted to understand the concepts.
"I was interested in the class," he said, adding that mainlining the homework with AI is like "shooting yourself in the foot" for when an in-person exam comes around.
"I personally think that if you leave AI out, then it pushes the average student to learn properly," he said.
If you're not interested in math, though, Redrouthu said you'd probably turn to AI — and you'd get away with it, until the exam at least.
Ni told me that, as a professor, he can't tell whether a problem set he assigns is completed using AI. It's unlike AI-generated writing, which is usually a pretty obvious amalgamation of short sentences, em dashes, and hypophora.
But math is all numbers: the specialty of AI programs.
Caltech has no unified guidance for how math professors should plan around AI now. Redrouthu said that this year, some of his classes come with an auspicious caveat: "AI allowed."
"Syllabuses are changing," he said.
