based on whether that entry is a human or a cat. But this means you have to
account for mixed groups of humans and cats, even though we just said those
don't actually exist.
Instead, you can express this differently in Rust. You still have a Person
interface (trait), but you compose your individual type of Person (Human or
Cat) during compile time.
struct Group<T> {
   // some fields	
}
// compile time assembly, 
// then runtime creation of the assembled group of cats
let cat_group: Group<Cat> = Group::new();
Rust now refuses to compile if you use non-cat operations on items in the group, That's an invariant you now do not need to worry about anymore. This will be familiar to you with generics in other languages like TypeScript or Python.
In Rust, when you process your group of cats, there is no individual check somewhere whether an entry is a human or a cat, as it already knows it's all cats before the program even ran. Rust directly dispatches to the cat code, and the human code is not play. You avoid indirect dispatch for every group member, which can matter in situations where performance is important.
Rust made me a better programmer as I now better understand the connection between dispatch and performance.
Type driven development
When I discovered Python coming from C++ back in the late 1990s, dynamic typing was a revelation. You could so much with so little ceremony. For the last decade or so I have been on a long winding road back to types (far more ergonomic types) and more ceremony. I have the impression many have been on this journey along with me 4.
Types can statically check your code before it runs. In Rust, they can help the compiler compile stuff down to really high performance code. Both are great. But types can also have more subtle benefits. Let me get into this by analogy.
Why create automated tests?
Obvious: Automated tests ensure various properties of your code work and remain working.
Subtle: Writing tests forces you to think about the architecture and APIs you're implementing more carefully. Making code testable can lead to better architecture. This is the insight of test driven development.
Why write documentation?
Obvious: People (and now machines) can understand 5 the why and what of your software by reading the documentation.
Subtle: The act of writing the documentation can force you think about the architecture and APIs of your software. If you can't write about it, maybe you haven't gotten it right yet? That's documentation driven development.
Why write types?
Obvious: Statically check your code before it runs! Prevent runtime errors! Performance!
Subtle: You model the domain model using types, trying to make sure it hangs together. Enums are really valuable here. You express parse, don't validate in them. The types guide the architecture and APIs of your software.
This perhaps sounds like big design up front processes where people write all the tests, or all the docs, or all the types, in advance, and then do the implementation. 6 I'm not talking about this -- I'm talking about iterative development where you keep going back to tests, docs and types as you learn.
Rust brought into focus how types are yet another tool to help me think while I develop.
Rust made me a better programmer as it let me fully embrace type driven development.
The Biggest Surprise
Here is the biggest surprise I had coming to Rust. Much of the behavior I associated with dynamic interpreted languages with a rich runtime like Python can actually be done statically in Rust using macros.
Let's talk about magic.
Say you want to dump the state of a Python object -- you inspect all its fields, look at their type, turn each into a string, combine all the strings together into a big one. Now you can store it somewhere. Later on you restore that string back into an object. You can save and load any objects: magic! Python calls this pickle.
What if you need to serialize to JSON? Python has a type system, and a library like Pydantic inspects the type objects during runtime and then uses this information to let you automatically serialize a Python object to JSON, or parse it back into Python again. More magic!
Rust is a compiled language. Types aren't runtime objects. Without reflection, which takes special effort, runtime introspection of types is not a thing in Rust.
But Rust can still do what Pickle and Pydantic do, at compile time.
With serde, Rust's answer to pickle and Pydantic, you use a normal Rust type, annotate it with a few declarations, and then you can serialize it to JSON, or toml config format, and many other formats, and load it back again. The annotation looks like this:
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Human {
    first_name: String,
    last_name: String
}
With clap, you create the type that
expresses exactly what command line arguments you expect (with enums too!),
document it using the normal way you document any API in Rust, and boom, you
have a CLI with built in help. The code that handles the various cases gets
well-typed data - at that point it's been parsed correctly already, using the
same type you used to express the CLI.
Like this:
/// My first CLI
#[derive(Parser)]
struct MyFirstCli {
    /// How many cats do you want?
    #[arg(long, short)]
    amount_of_cats: usize
}
Again declarative #[] stuff going on. It looks a lot like decorators in
Python. But Python decorators are executed during runtime, and we just said Rust
doesn't normally let you do that.
How does that work in Rust? Macros! Macros lets you write code that generates code during compile time. With serde, the macro generates a whole bunch of serialization code and deserialization code for the types annotated with it. This generated code gets compiled along with the rest of your code. The compiler can optimize it just like any other code.
Code generation is scary. Macros are scary. Doing introspection in a dynamically typed language is a lot easier than using Rust macros, where code is parsed and generated. Macros shouldn't be randomly mixed with application code; macros belong in frameworks. That said, something being easy doesn't mean it should be used casually: in Python you typically want to carefully encapsulate your magic in a declarative framework too.
Rust made me a better programmer as I learned about a new class of framework patterns.
Ownership and Architecture
Rust famously lets you write code without memory leaks that doesn't use a garbage collector. It also stops you from mutating data you're also reading elsewhere, making it impossible to stumble into whole classes of weird undefined behavior, especially with code that runs in parallel.
Rust's ownership system is one of the main things that makes learning Rust hard. Python, JavaScript, Java and many other languages have mutable references everywhere, and you can just create cyclic data structures. Rust won't let you do either out of the box.
The equivalent of this does not compile in Rust:
class Item:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
      
class Container:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = items
my_item = Item()
my_container = Container()
my_container.items.append(my_item)
my_item.value = "I change you!"
This also doesn't compile:
class Node:
   def __init__(self, parent, value):
       self.parent = parent
       self.value = value
       self.children = []
   def add_child(self, node):
       node.parent = self
       self.children.append(node)
Rust won't just let you have circular references, in this case both children and a parent reference.
This feels very limiting at first! What do you do instead? For mutating stuff, you learn how to separate mutation (often during construction) from using your data. That is a thing that's good to do in many contexts -- less invariants makes it's easier to reason about, but it takes a bit of getting used to Rust strictly enforcing it.
For circular references it's trickier. I will go into it next, when I discuss arenas.
A weird thing happens: if you lean into this friction it can improve the architecture of your codebase. Code becomes less coupled. It's hard to create weird backchannels with action at a distance that makes code difficult to understand, test and debug 7.
Rust code locally can be difficult to understand. But how the data flows, what does what, in the larger codebase, tends to be cleaner.
Rust made me a better programmer as I now think about ownership more carefully, which has a positive impact on architecture.
The arena pattern everywhere
A few years ago I analyzed a bunch of XML tree libraries in Rust. The best I found, roxmltrree, has an immutable tree. But I needed a mutable tree. I found quite a few libraries that did support mutability, but many did not support parent references. You couldn't walk up the ancestor chain of a node. This, along with missing support for some XML features, is why I created my own in the form of Xot.
The reason for this surprising lack of parent references is the ownership limitation I discussed before: Rust makes circular references difficult. You can get around it using reference counted types and internal mutability, but in a lot of cases this pattern isn't really optimal -- it's verbose, less performant, and reference count cycles risk memory leaks. What you do instead is store nodes in an array and you use the array indexes to node as your reference. You can then have an index referencing your parent, and use index references to your children, or any other circular reference.
A fancy word for this pattern is an 'arena' and in Rust they show up everywhere.
In an arena, you store a lot of objects together in the same region of memory (in an array). What does it let you do?
- iterate fast over its contents. Objects being in the same memory region means the CPU can use its cache effectively. This is much faster than arbitrary main memory access and loops really benefit.
- fast allocation. The arena is allocated from the heap as a block, and after that your allocations may just be a few increments.
- interning: you store something once in the arena and use it in many places, so you don't duplicate data.
- the arena owns its stuff. Everything in the arena has the same lifetime. Indexes between objects in an arena can be circular without worrying.
Rust pushes you to use arenas. This involves more ceremony than just using a direct reference, but it also means Rust pushes you to write code that computers can execute really efficiently.
Performance has a quality all its own
I mentioned performance a number of times. But what about premature
optimization? The
great irony of this quote is that it comes from a paper where the author, Knuth,
argues in favor of keeping the goto statement around, as it's essential for
writing efficient software.
Rust lets you know what you pay for. Reference counting? Dynamic dispatch? You can do it, but it's going to be visible in your code. Rust also often lets you know when you don't want to pay for it: just look at tower middleware and despair about all the generic types and type constraints that get piled onto a relatively simple abstraction.
When you have these tools available, need to develop new wisdom about tradeoffs that never seemed to matter. If you write Python code you're not too worried about hash tables being a performance bottle neck, but in Rust code they certainly can be. You can get lost along the way into hyper optimization land. Often you need to just get go 8. Many patterns that are just plain readable Rust code anyway happen to also be friendly to the CPU executing it.
But Rust overwhelming you with details you may not want to think about is not the whole story, because performance is not just quantitative: if your code can truly be more performance, it can access new qualities. When you can write code that uses no memory and no CPU time 9, it changes how you think. It changes what's possible.
Sometimes the quality of performance is obvious: if you write numerical code, or a simulation, of course you don't want to wait for the answer. Being able to do many computations really fast is key to making AI possible.
But it's more subtle that that: modern computers are really powerful, and ridicously fast, and we generally ignore that and just throw more resources at our problems. There are good reasons why this happens. But if we open our eyes a little, there are new architectural possibilities we can explore.
While the power of macros were the biggest language surprise, I think this is the biggest shift in my thinking: access to performance unlocks possibilities I hadn't considered before. Take my experiment Colchis: a library can store vast amounts of JSON in memory, while retaining full access, even indexed access (I still hope to add jsonpath one day!), to JSON data. Before Rust, this was a possibility that wasn't even on my radar.
Rust made me a better programmer because I can make the computer do more with less, opening up new areas of opportunity.
Conclusion
Rust is one of the most difficult programming languages I've learned -- and thus
one of the languages that changed me the most. There's a simple part of Rust
that isn't much harder to manage than any language, and in some cases may
actually make your life easier -- enums, declarative type-driven frameworks,
and the excellent dev tooling come to mind. Even arenas are fundamentally not
that difficult to understand. The complexity is in unlearning some habits and
learning new ones. And then there's a more challenging complex Rust, mostly, but
not always under the surface, there when you need it.
Rust expands the reach of what I can build. That's what makes me happy I went on this journey. 10
AI agents write a lot of code. They know the programming language, so do you need to know it? Does the language still affect the developer? If you share my belief it's good to look at the code, then it helps if you understand the code you're reading. I also think it's never been more important to think about how the systems you use affect the way you think and behave.
If you don't know what a struct is, just call it a class in your head, and you're good.
You have them in many languages but in impoverished forms, like
true/false, or C's enum.
If you're going to do static type checking anyway for the guarantees it brings, perhaps use a language designed around it (enums!) that also gives you performance benefits?
Does AI truly understand? Do you want to have a philosophical debate? What do we mean by understand? Natural language is inherently stretchable.
With AI we've seen the return of big design up front. I may be wrong, but I'm still skeptical of this approach, and still a fan of iterative development and incremental learning and theory building.
Not impossible. I've seen it. People can do it if they really try, and it still makes life harder; it makes it much harder to test. But at least it's more obvious and more difficult to do.
Clone and own all the stuff! Which incidentally can also lead to more contiguous memory layouts...
No memory and no CPU time is an exaggeration, but little Rust programs sometimes feel that way.
AI development is shifting all the tradeoffs in software development - they're not gone, but they have shifted. The AI can write Rust, even if you don't know it. But I trust plenty of contexts remain where my Rust experience plus AI leads to a better outcome than AI by itself.

articles.title: How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack
articles.body:
How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and QPACK
A hands-on look at intercepting HTTP/3. How QUIC streams and QPACK work, what a proxy really sees, how to read and edit a request, and why the QPACK dynamic table makes some requests hard to read.
InterceptSuite Team
Short answer: HTTP/3 does not go through an HTTP proxy, because it runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP. Most HTTP proxies, such as Burp Suite, are built on HTTP over TCP, so they never see it. To intercept HTTP/3 you need a proxy that can relay UDP and can act as a man in the middle for QUIC. After that, the work is about streams and header compression: the request is not text any more, it is bytes on a QUIC stream, compressed with QPACK.
In this post: curl is easy to edit because it does not use QPACK's dynamic table. Browsers do, so later requests arrive as table references you cannot read one row at a time. You can still forward, drop and replay them, and an edited request works on a fresh connection.
In this post we intercept real HTTP/3 traffic from curl and from Microsoft Edge. Then we use a small lab server to look at every byte, so the QUIC and QPACK parts are easy to follow.
Table of contents
A note on the tool: it shows raw bytes, and an extension decodes HTTP/3
This post uses InterceptSuite, so you should know what it is and what it is not. It is not built for HTTP. It is built for raw network traffic: TCP, TLS, UDP, DTLS and QUIC. Because it can intercept UDP and QUIC, it can handle HTTP/3 too. But it does not come with an HTTP parser, and that is also true for HTTP/3. The core shows raw bytes.
To read and edit those bytes as HTTP, InterceptSuite has an extension API, and there is an official, open source HTTP/3 extension that decodes the QUIC stream and QPACK headers into text. You can read the code, change it, or send a fix. The decoding in the screenshots below comes from that extension, not from the core.
What changes with HTTP/3
If you have only used HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, three things are different.
1. It runs on QUIC, not TCP. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) is HTTP carried over QUIC (RFC 9000). QUIC packets travel inside UDP datagrams. TLS 1.3 is part of the QUIC handshake (RFC 9001), so there is no separate "TCP then TLS" step.
2. The client has to learn that the server speaks HTTP/3. The ALPN name for HTTP/3 is h3. A server can advertise it with an Alt-Svc response header, and a DNS HTTPS record can advertise it too (RFC 9460). So a browser often makes its first request over TCP, then moves to QUIC.
3. Everything is a stream. A QUIC connection carries many streams. The two lowest bits of a stream ID tell you what it is (RFC 9000, section 2.1):
In HTTP/3, every client-started two-way stream is one request and its response (stream 0, 4, 8 and so on). The one-way streams are for housekeeping: a control stream, and two QPACK streams. Their type is the first byte on the stream: 0x00 control, 0x02 QPACK encoder, 0x03 QPACK decoder (RFC 9114, section 6.2 and RFC 9204, section 4.2).
One more detail that matters for interception. The first packets of a QUIC connection (the Initial packets) are protected with keys that anyone can calculate from the connection ID, so they have no real secrecy (RFC 9001, section 5). That is why a passive observer can still see things like the server name in the handshake. Everything after the handshake is encrypted with keys from the TLS 1.3 exchange. You cannot read it without being one of the two ends. A proxy that wants to read HTTP/3 has to be one of the two ends.
Why your usual proxy setup does not work
HTTP proxies use CONNECT to open a tunnel. In HTTP/3, CONNECT still builds a tunnel to a TCP connection (RFC 9114, section 4.4). To tunnel UDP over HTTP there is a different method, CONNECT-UDP (RFC 9298), and most tools and apps do not use it.
SOCKS5 can relay UDP. The command is UDP ASSOCIATE (RFC 1928). But many clients never use it. For example, the Chromium network docs say that in Chrome, SOCKSv5 is only used to proxy TCP-based requests and cannot relay UDP (Chromium proxy docs). So pointing a browser at a SOCKS5 proxy does not send its QUIC traffic through that proxy, and you are not testing the QUIC path.
That leaves two practical ways to get QUIC traffic into a proxy:
- The app (or a library) speaks SOCKS5 UDP itself. The lab client later in this post does this, so you can see exactly what the proxy receives.
- You redirect the app's traffic from outside the app, so it does not need to know about the proxy. This is what we use for curl and Edge. ProxyBridge does this on its own. InterceptSuite also has a Redirect tab, which is built on ProxyBridge and works inside the app.
For how this compares with mitmproxy, see the QUIC interception post.
Setup: the Redirect tab
Open Proxy, then Redirect, click Add, type the program name (for example curl.exe), leave the action on Proxy, and save. Then click Start Redirect. The status line says Redirecting through the proxy at 127.0.0.1:4444, and the program's TCP and UDP traffic goes through InterceptSuite without changing any setting in the program.
A rule can also limit the destination hosts and ports. The first matching rule decides, and programs that match no rule are left alone. Remember to trust the InterceptSuite CA on the machine, as in the quick start.
These two demos show the Redirect tab and the CA install on each system:
Want to follow along? There is a 7-day trial for Windows, macOS and Linux.
Real traffic 1: curl
curl is a good first test because it is simple and does exactly what you tell it. It needs a build with HTTP/3 support. This example runs on Windows. The curl that ships with Windows (8.21.0 here) does not support HTTP/3: curl -V does not list HTTP3 in its features. So we installed a second curl build that does:
winget install cURL.cURL
The new build (8.23.0) lists HTTP3, ngtcp2 and nghttp3 in curl -V. Check yours the same way before you test, and make sure the new curl is the one that runs (open a new terminal after the install).
curl --http3-only -sS -D - https://cloudflare-quic.com/cdn-cgi/trace
--http3-only makes curl use HTTP/3 and nothing else, so it cannot quietly fall back to TCP. With the Redirect rule on, curl worked without any proxy option and its output showed HTTP/3 200. No -k was needed, because curl used the Windows trust store, where the InterceptSuite CA is installed.
In Proxy History the connection appeared as QUIC with host cloudflare-quic.com and ALPN h3:
The first client packet (46 bytes) is the request. With the HTTP/3 tab it reads like this:
Now turn Intercept ON, run curl again, and change the request while it is held. Replace user-agent: curl/8.23.0 with user-agent: edited-by-proxy and press Forward:
The test site prints back what it saw. The first run says uag=curl/8.23.0. The run with the edit says:
uag=edited-by-proxy
So the server got the edited header, and curl never knew. The response is readable too:
Look at curl's SETTINGS frame, from the client:
QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY: 0 means curl does not use the QPACK dynamic table at all. That is why every curl request is easy to read and edit. We will see the opposite case later.
Real traffic 2: Browser traffic
Browsers are harder, for two reasons.
- ECH (Encrypted Client Hello). The real site name is hidden inside the handshake. The proxy only sees the CDN's public name, so it makes a certificate for the wrong name and the browser rejects it.
- Chromium does not run QUIC with a locally added CA. Even when Windows trusts the CA, Chromium refuses QUIC on a certificate that chains to a user-installed CA.
The fix is to start the browser with three flags:
msedge.exe --disable-features=EncryptedClientHello,UseDnsHttpsSvcb
           --ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list=<hash>
           --origin-to-force-quic-on=*
- --disable-features=... turns off ECH and stops the browser from reading HTTPS DNS records, where the ECH keys come from.
- --origin-to-force-quic-on=* makes Edge try QUIC straight away, instead of waiting for an Alt-Svc header. * means every host. Use host:443 for one site.
- --ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list=<hash> trusts QUIC connections signed by the InterceptSuite CA. Use this flag and not --ignore-certificate-errors.
<hash> is the base64 SHA-256 of the CA's public key. You calculate it from your own CA file:
openssl x509 -in intercept-ca.pem -pubkey -noout | openssl pkey -pubin -outform der | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl enc -base64
Edge shows a bar saying the flag is unsupported. That is expected, and it is why you should use a test profile and not your daily one. Close all Edge windows before you start it, or the flags are ignored.
With the Redirect rule for msedge.exe on, open https://cloudflare-quic.com/. The page says "your browser used HTTP/3":
In InterceptSuite the same visit was a QUIC connection with ALPN h3. The request from Edge, decoded by the extension:
And the response, with the alt-svc: h3=":443" header the site uses to advertise HTTP/3:
The response body here is content-encoding: gzip. The extension decompresses it for display, so the body shows as HTML.
Edge's SETTINGS are very different from curl's:
Edge offers a 64 KB dynamic table and up to 100 blocked streams, so after the first request, Edge can send headers as table references. The QPACK section below explains what that means for reading and editing.
How SOCKS5 carries UDP
UDP ASSOCIATE works in two parts.
- The client opens a normal TCP connection to the proxy, does the SOCKS5 greeting, and sends the command 03 (UDP ASSOCIATE). The proxy answers with an address and a port. This is the UDP relay.
- The client sends UDP datagrams to that relay address. Each datagram starts with a small header, then the real payload.
The header, from RFC 1928 section 7:
RSV (2 bytes) | FRAG (1) | ATYP (1) | DST.ADDR (variable) | DST.PORT (2) | DATA
The association lives as long as the TCP connection that asked for it. If that TCP connection closes, the UDP association ends (RFC 1928, section 6). This is easy to forget when you write your own client.
InterceptSuite listens on 127.0.0.1:4444 for SOCKS5 over TCP and 127.0.0.1:4445 for the UDP relay (see the quick start). The reply to UDP ASSOCIATE points to 127.0.0.1:4445.
The lab: seeing every byte
Real servers make it hard to see what is going on, so here is a small lab. Both sides use Python and aioquic.
- Server: a small HTTP/3 server on 127.0.0.1:4433 with a self-signed certificate. It answers with JSON that repeats what it received (method, path, one custom header, and the body). It also prints what it got, so you can see what actually arrived.
- Client: an HTTP/3 client that sends its datagrams through the SOCKS5 UDP relay. aioquic does not know about SOCKS5, so the client wraps its datagrams itself. This is the whole trick:
class Shim(asyncio.DatagramProtocol):
    """Wraps each QUIC datagram in the SOCKS5 UDP header."""
    def sendto(self, data, addr=None):
        hdr = b'\x00\x00\x00\x01' + socket.inet_aton(SERVER[0]) + struct.pack('!H', SERVER[1])
        self.t.sendto(hdr + data, self.relay)
    def datagram_received(self, d, addr):
        if d[0:3] != b'\x00\x00\x00' or d[3] != 1:
            return
        self.proto.datagram_received(d[10:], SERVER)   # strip the 10 byte header
The lab client skips certificate checks. That is fine for a lab. A real app must trust the proxy's CA certificate, or it will close the connection when it sees the forged certificate. See Install the CA certificate for that step.
The lab client sent one request:
POST /login   (body: user=alice&pw=hunter2)
user-agent: h3-lab-client/1.0
accept: application/json
authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.demo.token
cookie: session=abc123def456; theme=dark
x-demo: first
What the proxy sees: ten rows for one request
Here is Proxy History after the client connected, sent requests, and closed.
The host column shows h3.lab.test. That is the server name from the TLS handshake. The ALPN column shows h3. The Protocol column says QUIC.
The thing most people do not expect is the number of rows. One request gave 10 entries, not 2. Each row is a chunk of data from one QUIC stream, in the order the proxy saw it. The small ones are all HTTP/3 housekeeping:
The client's control stream is three bytes longer than the server's: 0D 01 08 at the end, which is a MAX_PUSH_ID frame.
Filtering helps a lot here. The filter box understands things like connection_id == 3 and size > 100. The available fields are src_ip, dst_ip, port, direction, protocol, size, modified, connection_id, type, data, host and alpn.
The SETTINGS frame
With the HTTP/3 extension loaded, the control stream entry is shown as text:
Read it against the bytes:
00            stream type: control
04 09         frame type SETTINGS, length 9
01 50 00      setting 0x01 (QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY) = 4096
07 10         setting 0x07 (QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS)    = 16
08 01         setting 0x08 (ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL)  = 1
21 01         a reserved ("GREASE") setting
The 50 00 part is a QUIC variable-length integer. The first two bits (01) say it uses two bytes, and the value is 0x1000, which is 4096. This one matters later, because QPACK's dynamic table is off by default. Both QPACK settings default to zero (RFC 9204, section 5). This server turned it on and allowed 16 blocked streams.
Reading the request
Now the request itself. This is the raw view of the held request packet:
You can see the body (user=alice&pw=hunter2), because the body is not compressed. The headers are unreadable. This is QPACK. It is HPACK's cousin for HTTP/3 (RFC 9204), and it does three things:
- A static table. 99 predefined header fields, for example :method GET or content-type application/json. A whole header becomes one small number.
- Huffman coding for strings that are not in the table. QPACK uses the Huffman table from HPACK without changes.
- A dynamic table. A table that grows during the connection. Both ends fill it in using the two QPACK streams (02 and 03). We will come back to this.
The HTTP/3 extension from the Extension repository decodes all of this into text. Open the HTTP/3 tab on the same packet:
The core of InterceptSuite shows HTTP/3 as raw bytes. The decoded view comes from this extension. The extension is a normal Python file, and you can read it. Its _decode function parses the QUIC variable-length integers, the HTTP/3 frames, then the QPACK block with the static table and Huffman decoder.
Editing the request in flight
Turn Intercept ON. By default it holds client-to-server packets. There is also an Intercept response option for the other direction.
When the client sends its request, the request packet is held and the queue says 1 packet(s) waiting. Change two things in the HTTP/3 tab: the x-demo header and the body.
Then press Forward. The server printed this:
SERVER got POST /login x-demo= tampered body= b'user=admin&pw=letmein'
So the server received the edited request. The client got a normal 200 answer from the server, and its own copy of the request was never changed.
In Proxy History, the row shows Modified: Yes, and the viewer can show the Original and Edited versions:
Two practical points from doing this:
- Every chunk is held, not only the request. The small stream packets (02, 03, the control stream) are held too, one by one. After you forward the request, the queue still has items. Press Forward until it is empty.
- Your client has its own timeouts. If you take too long to edit, the client may give up and close the connection. Edit fast, or raise the timeout in the client you test.
What happens to the bytes when you edit
The extension does not patch the old bytes. It builds a new HEADERS frame. From the source, the rules are:
- The headers are written again with the static table only and plain (not Huffman) strings. Required Insert Count is set to zero. This means the new header block does not depend on the dynamic table.
- If the body changes, it builds a new DATA frame. If the request has a content-length header, it updates that number too. If there is a content-encoding, it compresses the new body again.
- The frame lengths are calculated again, so the HTTP/3 framing stays valid.
- If it cannot do this safely (for example the body is binary, or it is cut off, or it continues in a later entry), it changes nothing. It never sends half-built bytes.
The hard part: the QPACK dynamic table
This is the part that needs care. So far everything decoded nicely. Now send more requests on the same connection (same headers, different path) and look again.
The sizes tell the story. Requests 1 and 2 were 122 bytes each. Request 3 was 13 bytes. And at some point, a 114-byte entry showed up on the client's QPACK encoder stream.
Here are the 13 bytes of request 3, the way they were on the wire:
01 0B 08 86 D1 D7 10 11 12 13 14 15 16
- 01 0B is a HEADERS frame, 11 bytes long.
- 08 86 is the QPACK block prefix: the Required Insert Count and the Delta Base. A Required Insert Count that is not zero means this header block needs entries from the dynamic table.
- D1 and D7 are two entries from the static table (:method GET and :scheme https).
- 10 11 12 13 14 15 16 are seven "indexed field line with post-base index" instructions. Each one points to an entry in the dynamic table. The request says "use entries 0 to 6" and nothing else.
Where are the entries? In the 114-byte entry on the encoder stream. Its first bytes are C0 88 9D 95 E8 1C 6B A4 A8 4F, which is "insert :authority, with a Huffman-coded value" (the value decodes to h3.lab.test). The client sent the long header values once, and every later request only sends numbers. This is a good design. It is also what makes interception harder.
Look at what the HTTP/3 tab shows for request 3:
GET https:// HTTP/3
[dynamic table entry (post-base) 0]:
[dynamic table entry (post-base) 1]:
...
[dynamic table entry (post-base) 6]:
The path, the host, the cookie and the token are gone. That is not a bug in the display, it is the nature of QPACK. The values for these entries were sent earlier, on a different stream. A single history row does not contain them. The extension decodes one entry at a time and does not keep the QPACK table of the connection, so it can only show placeholders.
The server's response did the same thing. After a few responses, its header block started using the dynamic table, and the HTTP/3 tab shows the body but only placeholders for two of the headers:
There is one more thing to see here. In the capture, the 13-byte request (row 30) arrived before the 114-byte encoder stream entry (row 31). That is allowed by design. QPACK lets a request stream wait ("block") until the inserts it needs have arrived. The server announced it could keep up to 16 blocked streams (the QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS setting we saw above). Later a single byte 88 comes back from the server on its decoder stream. That is a Section Acknowledgment for stream 8, which was the third request: the decoder tells the encoder it processed a header block that needed the table (RFC 9204, section 4.4.1).
So two things follow for a tester:
- You cannot edit these requests with the extension. From the source: if a header block uses the dynamic table, the extension does not rebuild it, and your edit is not applied.
- The data is not lost. The values are in the encoder stream entry in Hex view, and in the raw bytes. You can still forward, drop, and replay them. You just cannot read them as text.
How do you work around it?
- Use the start of a connection. In the lab, the first two requests did not use the table at all, because the client had not inserted anything yet. Whether that holds for your client depends on its QPACK encoder, so check it.
- Replay on a fresh connection, with an edit. A new QUIC connection starts with an empty table. When you edit a request in the HTTP/3 tab, the extension writes it with the static table only, so it does not depend on any earlier state. The next section does exactly this, and the server answers.
- Do not replay a dynamic-table request unchanged. If you send the 13-byte request from Replay on a new connection, the server never answers and never logs the request. That fits how QPACK works. The request points to table entries that this new connection never received, so it cannot be read.
- Look at the encoder stream. It has the real values, in Huffman form. If you must read them, decode the Huffman strings by hand or write a small extension that tracks the table.
Replay: send your own HTTP/3 request
Right-click a row in Proxy History and choose Send to Replay.
The session opens with the details filled in: host, port, protocol QUIC, ALPN h3, New bidirectional stream, and End stream (FIN) ticked. HTTP/3 request streams are client-started two-way streams, so that is the correct choice. The FIN flag matters because the lab server only answers after it sees the end of the request.
In the lab the host name h3.lab.test is only a name in the TLS handshake and does not resolve, so change the host to 127.0.0.1. In the HTTP/3 tab, change the path to /admin and x-demo to replayed, then press Send.
The conversation shows what happened on the wire:
- Three packets came from the server on its one-way streams: stream 3 (12 bytes, its control stream), stream 7 (1 byte, QPACK encoder) and stream 11 (1 byte, QPACK decoder). The stream numbers match the rule from the table at the start: they end in 11 in binary, so they are server-started one-way streams.
- SENT 158 bytes on stream 0 with FIN is the request.
- RECV 152 bytes on stream 0 with FIN is the response.
The server printed GET /admin x-demo= replayed, and the response JSON shows "path": "/admin" and "x_demo": "replayed".
What a broken request looks like
If the edited text leaves a broken header block, Replay sends only a few bytes (25 here) and the server closes the connection:
0x106 is H3_FRAME_ERROR. RFC 9114 says that if a stream ends and the last frame on it is cut short, the receiver must treat it as a connection error of this type (RFC 9114, section 7.1). In plain words: the frame header promised more bytes than the stream delivered. If you hand-craft HTTP/3 bytes in the Raw or Hex tab, this is the error you will meet first. It means your frame length does not match your data.
Limits to know
- QUIC version 1 only. QUIC version 2 is not supported yet.
- ECH. If a connection uses Encrypted Client Hello, it cannot be intercepted.
- The client must trust the CA. QUIC always uses TLS. If the app pins its certificate, or does not trust your CA, it will refuse the proxy's certificate.
- The UDP path must reach the proxy. If the app does not speak SOCKS5 UDP, redirect it from outside, for example with ProxyBridge UDP rules.
- The extension reads one entry at a time. It decodes request and response streams and the control stream. It does not track the QPACK table, so dynamic-table headers show as placeholders and cannot be edited.
- Large bodies. A body that continues in later entries cannot be edited as text.
You can find the current list in the protocol compatibility matrix.
A short checklist
- Route the UDP traffic into the proxy (SOCKS5 UDP, or redirect it).
- Trust the proxy CA on the machine that runs the client.
- Look at the history first. Expect many small rows per request.
- Use the HTTP/3 tab to read and edit requests that use only the static table.
- If you see [dynamic table entry ...], look at the encoder stream entry in Hex, or test on a fresh connection.
- Use Replay to resend and change a request without the client.
Related reading: Replay documentation, Proxy History documentation, the HTTP/3 extension source, and Intercepting QUIC and HTTP/3 when mitmproxy isn't enough.
You can reproduce every step here on your own test server with the 7-day trial. Only test servers you own or are allowed to test.
Updates and new write-ups: @InterceptSuite on X.

articles.title: How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack
articles.body:
How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and QPACK
A hands-on look at intercepting HTTP/3. How QUIC streams and QPACK work, what a proxy really sees, how to read and edit a request, and why the QPACK dynamic table makes some requests hard to read.
InterceptSuite Team
Short answer: HTTP/3 does not go through an HTTP proxy, because it runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP. Most HTTP proxies, such as Burp Suite, are built on HTTP over TCP, so they never see it. To intercept HTTP/3 you need a proxy that can relay UDP and can act as a man in the middle for QUIC. After that, the work is about streams and header compression: the request is not text any more, it is bytes on a QUIC stream, compressed with QPACK.
In this post: curl is easy to edit because it does not use QPACK's dynamic table. Browsers do, so later requests arrive as table references you cannot read one row at a time. You can still forward, drop and replay them, and an edited request works on a fresh connection.
In this post we intercept real HTTP/3 traffic from curl and from Microsoft Edge. Then we use a small lab server to look at every byte, so the QUIC and QPACK parts are easy to follow.
Table of contents
A note on the tool: it shows raw bytes, and an extension decodes HTTP/3
This post uses InterceptSuite, so you should know what it is and what it is not. It is not built for HTTP. It is built for raw network traffic: TCP, TLS, UDP, DTLS and QUIC. Because it can intercept UDP and QUIC, it can handle HTTP/3 too. But it does not come with an HTTP parser, and that is also true for HTTP/3. The core shows raw bytes.
To read and edit those bytes as HTTP, InterceptSuite has an extension API, and there is an official, open source HTTP/3 extension that decodes the QUIC stream and QPACK headers into text. You can read the code, change it, or send a fix. The decoding in the screenshots below comes from that extension, not from the core.
What changes with HTTP/3
If you have only used HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, three things are different.
1. It runs on QUIC, not TCP. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) is HTTP carried over QUIC (RFC 9000). QUIC packets travel inside UDP datagrams. TLS 1.3 is part of the QUIC handshake (RFC 9001), so there is no separate "TCP then TLS" step.
2. The client has to learn that the server speaks HTTP/3. The ALPN name for HTTP/3 is h3. A server can advertise it with an Alt-Svc response header, and a DNS HTTPS record can advertise it too (RFC 9460). So a browser often makes its first request over TCP, then moves to QUIC.
3. Everything is a stream. A QUIC connection carries many streams. The two lowest bits of a stream ID tell you what it is (RFC 9000, section 2.1):
In HTTP/3, every client-started two-way stream is one request and its response (stream 0, 4, 8 and so on). The one-way streams are for housekeeping: a control stream, and two QPACK streams. Their type is the first byte on the stream: 0x00 control, 0x02 QPACK encoder, 0x03 QPACK decoder (RFC 9114, section 6.2 and RFC 9204, section 4.2).
One more detail that matters for interception. The first packets of a QUIC connection (the Initial packets) are protected with keys that anyone can calculate from the connection ID, so they have no real secrecy (RFC 9001, section 5). That is why a passive observer can still see things like the server name in the handshake. Everything after the handshake is encrypted with keys from the TLS 1.3 exchange. You cannot read it without being one of the two ends. A proxy that wants to read HTTP/3 has to be one of the two ends.
Why your usual proxy setup does not work
HTTP proxies use CONNECT to open a tunnel. In HTTP/3, CONNECT still builds a tunnel to a TCP connection (RFC 9114, section 4.4). To tunnel UDP over HTTP there is a different method, CONNECT-UDP (RFC 9298), and most tools and apps do not use it.
SOCKS5 can relay UDP. The command is UDP ASSOCIATE (RFC 1928). But many clients never use it. For example, the Chromium network docs say that in Chrome, SOCKSv5 is only used to proxy TCP-based requests and cannot relay UDP (Chromium proxy docs). So pointing a browser at a SOCKS5 proxy does not send its QUIC traffic through that proxy, and you are not testing the QUIC path.
That leaves two practical ways to get QUIC traffic into a proxy:
- The app (or a library) speaks SOCKS5 UDP itself. The lab client later in this post does this, so you can see exactly what the proxy receives.
- You redirect the app's traffic from outside the app, so it does not need to know about the proxy. This is what we use for curl and Edge. ProxyBridge does this on its own. InterceptSuite also has a Redirect tab, which is built on ProxyBridge and works inside the app.
For how this compares with mitmproxy, see the QUIC interception post.
Setup: the Redirect tab
Open Proxy, then Redirect, click Add, type the program name (for example curl.exe), leave the action on Proxy, and save. Then click Start Redirect. The status line says Redirecting through the proxy at 127.0.0.1:4444, and the program's TCP and UDP traffic goes through InterceptSuite without changing any setting in the program.
A rule can also limit the destination hosts and ports. The first matching rule decides, and programs that match no rule are left alone. Remember to trust the InterceptSuite CA on the machine, as in the quick start.
These two demos show the Redirect tab and the CA install on each system:
Want to follow along? There is a 7-day trial for Windows, macOS and Linux.
Real traffic 1: curl
curl is a good first test because it is simple and does exactly what you tell it. It needs a build with HTTP/3 support. This example runs on Windows. The curl that ships with Windows (8.21.0 here) does not support HTTP/3: curl -V does not list HTTP3 in its features. So we installed a second curl build that does:
winget install cURL.cURL
The new build (8.23.0) lists HTTP3, ngtcp2 and nghttp3 in curl -V. Check yours the same way before you test, and make sure the new curl is the one that runs (open a new terminal after the install).
curl --http3-only -sS -D - https://cloudflare-quic.com/cdn-cgi/trace
--http3-only makes curl use HTTP/3 and nothing else, so it cannot quietly fall back to TCP. With the Redirect rule on, curl worked without any proxy option and its output showed HTTP/3 200. No -k was needed, because curl used the Windows trust store, where the InterceptSuite CA is installed.
In Proxy History the connection appeared as QUIC with host cloudflare-quic.com and ALPN h3:
The first client packet (46 bytes) is the request. With the HTTP/3 tab it reads like this:
Now turn Intercept ON, run curl again, and change the request while it is held. Replace user-agent: curl/8.23.0 with user-agent: edited-by-proxy and press Forward:
The test site prints back what it saw. The first run says uag=curl/8.23.0. The run with the edit says:
uag=edited-by-proxy
So the server got the edited header, and curl never knew. The response is readable too:
Look at curl's SETTINGS frame, from the client:
QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY: 0 means curl does not use the QPACK dynamic table at all. That is why every curl request is easy to read and edit. We will see the opposite case later.
Real traffic 2: Browser traffic
Browsers are harder, for two reasons.
- ECH (Encrypted Client Hello). The real site name is hidden inside the handshake. The proxy only sees the CDN's public name, so it makes a certificate for the wrong name and the browser rejects it.
- Chromium does not run QUIC with a locally added CA. Even when Windows trusts the CA, Chromium refuses QUIC on a certificate that chains to a user-installed CA.
The fix is to start the browser with three flags:
msedge.exe --disable-features=EncryptedClientHello,UseDnsHttpsSvcb
           --ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list=<hash>
           --origin-to-force-quic-on=*
- --disable-features=... turns off ECH and stops the browser from reading HTTPS DNS records, where the ECH keys come from.
- --origin-to-force-quic-on=* makes Edge try QUIC straight away, instead of waiting for an Alt-Svc header. * means every host. Use host:443 for one site.
- --ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list=<hash> trusts QUIC connections signed by the InterceptSuite CA. Use this flag and not --ignore-certificate-errors.
<hash> is the base64 SHA-256 of the CA's public key. You calculate it from your own CA file:
openssl x509 -in intercept-ca.pem -pubkey -noout | openssl pkey -pubin -outform der | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl enc -base64
Edge shows a bar saying the flag is unsupported. That is expected, and it is why you should use a test profile and not your daily one. Close all Edge windows before you start it, or the flags are ignored.
With the Redirect rule for msedge.exe on, open https://cloudflare-quic.com/. The page says "your browser used HTTP/3":
In InterceptSuite the same visit was a QUIC connection with ALPN h3. The request from Edge, decoded by the extension:
And the response, with the alt-svc: h3=":443" header the site uses to advertise HTTP/3:
The response body here is content-encoding: gzip. The extension decompresses it for display, so the body shows as HTML.
Edge's SETTINGS are very different from curl's:
Edge offers a 64 KB dynamic table and up to 100 blocked streams, so after the first request, Edge can send headers as table references. The QPACK section below explains what that means for reading and editing.
How SOCKS5 carries UDP
UDP ASSOCIATE works in two parts.
- The client opens a normal TCP connection to the proxy, does the SOCKS5 greeting, and sends the command 03 (UDP ASSOCIATE). The proxy answers with an address and a port. This is the UDP relay.
- The client sends UDP datagrams to that relay address. Each datagram starts with a small header, then the real payload.
The header, from RFC 1928 section 7:
RSV (2 bytes) | FRAG (1) | ATYP (1) | DST.ADDR (variable) | DST.PORT (2) | DATA
The association lives as long as the TCP connection that asked for it. If that TCP connection closes, the UDP association ends (RFC 1928, section 6). This is easy to forget when you write your own client.
InterceptSuite listens on 127.0.0.1:4444 for SOCKS5 over TCP and 127.0.0.1:4445 for the UDP relay (see the quick start). The reply to UDP ASSOCIATE points to 127.0.0.1:4445.
The lab: seeing every byte
Real servers make it hard to see what is going on, so here is a small lab. Both sides use Python and aioquic.
- Server: a small HTTP/3 server on 127.0.0.1:4433 with a self-signed certificate. It answers with JSON that repeats what it received (method, path, one custom header, and the body). It also prints what it got, so you can see what actually arrived.
- Client: an HTTP/3 client that sends its datagrams through the SOCKS5 UDP relay. aioquic does not know about SOCKS5, so the client wraps its datagrams itself. This is the whole trick:
class Shim(asyncio.DatagramProtocol):
    """Wraps each QUIC datagram in the SOCKS5 UDP header."""
    def sendto(self, data, addr=None):
        hdr = b'\x00\x00\x00\x01' + socket.inet_aton(SERVER[0]) + struct.pack('!H', SERVER[1])
        self.t.sendto(hdr + data, self.relay)
    def datagram_received(self, d, addr):
        if d[0:3] != b'\x00\x00\x00' or d[3] != 1:
            return
        self.proto.datagram_received(d[10:], SERVER)   # strip the 10 byte header
The lab client skips certificate checks. That is fine for a lab. A real app must trust the proxy's CA certificate, or it will close the connection when it sees the forged certificate. See Install the CA certificate for that step.
The lab client sent one request:
POST /login   (body: user=alice&pw=hunter2)
user-agent: h3-lab-client/1.0
accept: application/json
authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.demo.token
cookie: session=abc123def456; theme=dark
x-demo: first
What the proxy sees: ten rows for one request
Here is Proxy History after the client connected, sent requests, and closed.
The host column shows h3.lab.test. That is the server name from the TLS handshake. The ALPN column shows h3. The Protocol column says QUIC.
The thing most people do not expect is the number of rows. One request gave 10 entries, not 2. Each row is a chunk of data from one QUIC stream, in the order the proxy saw it. The small ones are all HTTP/3 housekeeping:
The client's control stream is three bytes longer than the server's: 0D 01 08 at the end, which is a MAX_PUSH_ID frame.
Filtering helps a lot here. The filter box understands things like connection_id == 3 and size > 100. The available fields are src_ip, dst_ip, port, direction, protocol, size, modified, connection_id, type, data, host and alpn.
The SETTINGS frame
With the HTTP/3 extension loaded, the control stream entry is shown as text:
Read it against the bytes:
00            stream type: control
04 09         frame type SETTINGS, length 9
01 50 00      setting 0x01 (QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY) = 4096
07 10         setting 0x07 (QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS)    = 16
08 01         setting 0x08 (ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL)  = 1
21 01         a reserved ("GREASE") setting
The 50 00 part is a QUIC variable-length integer. The first two bits (01) say it uses two bytes, and the value is 0x1000, which is 4096. This one matters later, because QPACK's dynamic table is off by default. Both QPACK settings default to zero (RFC 9204, section 5). This server turned it on and allowed 16 blocked streams.
Reading the request
Now the request itself. This is the raw view of the held request packet:
You can see the body (user=alice&pw=hunter2), because the body is not compressed. The headers are unreadable. This is QPACK. It is HPACK's cousin for HTTP/3 (RFC 9204), and it does three things:
- A static table. 99 predefined header fields, for example :method GET or content-type application/json. A whole header becomes one small number.
- Huffman coding for strings that are not in the table. QPACK uses the Huffman table from HPACK without changes.
- A dynamic table. A table that grows during the connection. Both ends fill it in using the two QPACK streams (02 and 03). We will come back to this.
The HTTP/3 extension from the Extension repository decodes all of this into text. Open the HTTP/3 tab on the same packet:
The core of InterceptSuite shows HTTP/3 as raw bytes. The decoded view comes from this extension. The extension is a normal Python file, and you can read it. Its _decode function parses the QUIC variable-length integers, the HTTP/3 frames, then the QPACK block with the static table and Huffman decoder.
Editing the request in flight
Turn Intercept ON. By default it holds client-to-server packets. There is also an Intercept response option for the other direction.
When the client sends its request, the request packet is held and the queue says 1 packet(s) waiting. Change two things in the HTTP/3 tab: the x-demo header and the body.
Then press Forward. The server printed this:
SERVER got POST /login x-demo= tampered body= b'user=admin&pw=letmein'
So the server received the edited request. The client got a normal 200 answer from the server, and its own copy of the request was never changed.
In Proxy History, the row shows Modified: Yes, and the viewer can show the Original and Edited versions:
Two practical points from doing this:
- Every chunk is held, not only the request. The small stream packets (02, 03, the control stream) are held too, one by one. After you forward the request, the queue still has items. Press Forward until it is empty.
- Your client has its own timeouts. If you take too long to edit, the client may give up and close the connection. Edit fast, or raise the timeout in the client you test.
What happens to the bytes when you edit
The extension does not patch the old bytes. It builds a new HEADERS frame. From the source, the rules are:
- The headers are written again with the static table only and plain (not Huffman) strings. Required Insert Count is set to zero. This means the new header block does not depend on the dynamic table.
- If the body changes, it builds a new DATA frame. If the request has a content-length header, it updates that number too. If there is a content-encoding, it compresses the new body again.
- The frame lengths are calculated again, so the HTTP/3 framing stays valid.
- If it cannot do this safely (for example the body is binary, or it is cut off, or it continues in a later entry), it changes nothing. It never sends half-built bytes.

[dynamic table entry (post-base) 1]:

- Large bodies. A body that continues in later entries cannot be edited as text.
You can find the current list in the protocol compatibility matrix.
A short checklist
- Route the UDP traffic into the proxy (SOCKS5 UDP, or redirect it).
- Trust the proxy CA on the machine that runs the client.
- Look at the history first. Expect many small rows per request.
- Use the HTTP/3 tab to read and edit requests that use only the static table.
- If you see [dynamic table entry ...], look at the encoder stream entry in Hex, or test on a fresh connection.
- Use Replay to resend and change a request without the client.
Related reading: Replay documentation, Proxy History documentation, the HTTP/3 extension source, and Intercepting QUIC and HTTP/3 when mitmproxy isn't enough.
You can reproduce every step here on your own test server with the 7-day trial. Only test servers you own or are allowed to test.
Updates and new write-ups: @InterceptSuite on X.

articles.title: US Banks report outages in latest tech hiccup
articles.body:
Big bank customers report outages; JPMorgan Chase blames software bug with potential ripple effects
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Customers at banks including Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo said they experienced outages coast to coast on Monday — days after technical snafus wreaked havoc for flight passengers and Microsoft customers.
There were nearly 5,000 reports of outages at Chase and about 1,400 between BofA and Wells Fargo, according to Downdetector.com.
JPMorgan Chase said a software bug in systems it runs in-house slowed service for some customers – and may have affected other banks.
“It is taking longer than usual to service some customers,” JPMorgan said in a statement. It added that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds.”
Advertisement
The nation’s largest bank said other lenders may have been affected when JPMorgan was a party to a transaction with them, but that “this is not a systemic issue.”
In other words, reported outages at other banks appeared to be due to customers trying to do business with Chase accounts.
JPMorgan said it was working to resolve the problem by the end of the day.
Advertisement
Customers reported issues at Capital One, PNC, US Bank and the Zelle money transfer app.
Zelle indicated any problems customers faced sending payments were due to problems at partner banks.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should. Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds,” a Zelle spokesperson told The Post.
Advertisement
Capital One made a similar statement, suggesting it was indirectly affected by banking woes at Chase.
“Capital One has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time,” a Capital One spokesperson said.
Some customers said online they couldn’t use their banking apps.
“My Chase App has a warning that I’ve never seen before: Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later,” one user wrote on Reddit.
Advertisement
Earlier in the day, Chase said it was sorry to an X user complaining of banking woes.
“I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking. Please try again at a later time. We’re sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience,” a Chase support account wrote on X.
The technical difficulties were the latest in a series of incidents to cause major inconvenience for Americans.
Advertisement
Air travel slammed to a halt on Friday, with authorities blaming a botched contractor job or a faulty router. After thousands of flights were cancelled through the weekend, some stranded travelers were still trying to make their way home on Monday.
Also last week, Microsoft had a widespread outage that prevented online communications for governments and companies for over 24 hours.
The software giant said Saturday services was fully operational for Teams, Outlook and other products.
Advertisement
Independent cybersecurity expert Katie Moussouris told the Post the extent of the bank problems suggested they were interconnected.
“It could be a really wild coincidence, but it seems like they share a component on the backend,” she said.
A former top Treasury Department official urged calm.
Advertisement
Ex-Assistant Treasury Secretary Graham Steele said things can get out of hand if people start to lose trust in the banking system.
“What really becomes a problem is when people don’t trust the banking system because they think it has become corrupted or compromised in some way,” he told The Post, adding that the Federal Reserve does worst-case-scenario drills to prepare for extended problems.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title: Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — without new hardware
articles.body:
Apple is working on a face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo that uses the front-facing camera for authentication, and it’s already testing it with the new iOS 27.3 beta released today, as reported by MacRumors. Currently, the only way to unlock the iPhone Duo is by using Touch ID or entering a passcode, which might feel like a step back if you prefer face authentication using the Face ID feature available on other iPhones.
Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — without new hardware
Apple is testing a new iPhone Duo feature that would use the front-facing camera to look at your face for authentication.
The iPhone Duo’s face unlock feature seemingly has a few caveats, however: it’s only available for the lock screen, you can only use your face for an unlock if you have used Touch ID or input a passcode within 45 minutes, and you can’t use the face authentication for Apple Pay purchases.
iOS 27.3 is set to launch publicly in December, Apple said last month, so should the feature make it to the full release, you may not have to wait too long for it to be officially available.
Apple reportedly wants to add Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo, Bloomberg reports.

articles.title: Some OLED MacBook Pro Owners Report Eye Strain and Dizziness
articles.body:
Some owners of Apple's new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display say they experience eye strain, headaches, and dizziness when using the laptop, with affected users pointing to the screen's brightness-control system as a possible explanation.
A significant number of complaints have appeared on Reddit, X, and the MacRumors forums since the new models launched earlier this month. The discussions on MacRumors include a dedicated PWM thread, a separate owner poll, and comments in the reviews and display-details threads.
On X, one user said trying the PROLED MacBook Pro in an Apple Store for around 30 minutes left them with a severe headache. The user said they had previously struggled with OLED screens before finding newer implementations tolerable, and called for an option to change the Mac's dimming behavior.
A Reddit user described how reading text, especially against a black background, brought on dizziness and nausea. They said their OLED iPad Pro did not produce the same symptoms. In the main MacRumors forum thread, a 16-inch PROLED owner reported a headache and mild nausea that began to ease after switching back to a mini-LED MacBook Pro. Another member, posting in the separate poll thread, said they were returning their PROLED laptop for similar reasons after previously having no difficulty with OLED devices.
The suspected issue is pulse width modulation (PWM). An OLED screen produces light through its individual pixels. With PWM dimming, the display changes the time spent at brighter and darker levels during a rapidly repeating cycle. Spending less time at the brighter level reduces the average amount of light reaching the viewer, making the screen look dimmer.
Those fluctuations can occur too quickly to look like an obvious flashing screen, but some people report discomfort with displays that use them. PWM frequency describes how often the brightness cycle repeats. It is different from refresh rate, which is how often the displayed image updates, so a 120Hz ProMotion specification does not tell you the screen's PWM frequency.
Notebookcheck's testing of the 14-inch PROLED MacBook Pro recorded 240Hz flickering whenever brightness was set to 99% or lower, with a measured amplitude of 56%. In other words, the light output fluctuated 240 times per second, and the amplitude describes the size of those fluctuations. The publication warned that sensitive users could experience eye strain or headaches due to the specification.
Mini-LED MacBook Pro displays also use brightness modulation, but Notebookcheck measured a much higher frequency of 14,880Hz on the 14-inch M4 Pro model. Such rapid fluctuations are generally less likely to cause discomfort for PWM-sensitive users.
Apple already provides a Display Pulse Smoothing accessibility option on supported iPhones. The setting offers another way to dim the OLED screen at low brightness, although Apple cautions that it can affect display performance under some conditions. macOS does not offer an equivalent control, but Apple could add one in the future.
The OLED MacBook Pro models start at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch version. Apple continues to sell the mini-LED models alongside them.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he’s willing to return as Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week, would be willing to return as CEO if the company’s board of directors wanted it, he said in a statement reported on by The Wall Street Journal.
Jensen Huang says he’s willing to return as Nvidia CEO
‘I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,’ Huang said.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang resigned on Thursday following reports of two affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and a direct report. CFO Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang said. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”
More than 193,000 people, including CEOs like Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, have signed a letter to “bring Jensen back.” President Trump has also been supportive of Huang returning as CEO, saying yesterday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea.” (Trump had earlier tossed out former Apple CEO Tim Cook as a potential replacement.) On Monday, Nvidia’s board reportedly was “not considering” having Huang return, and today, CNN reported that the board is “not considering reinstating Huang.”
Nvidia didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
Here is Huang’s full statement:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Jensen
Update, November 17th: CNN reports that Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating Huang.

articles.title: Nvidia’s first big move after Jensen Huang’s exit targets national security
articles.body:
Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers.
Nvidia said Tuesday that the new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.
The Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.
The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the company to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Collette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week.
The committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members.
Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month.

articles.title: 15 hotel guests were injured by chlorine poisoning due to Microsoft’s global email outage
articles.body:
Microsoft’s worldwide 365 and Outlook outage had real-world consequences after it cut off email alerts for a German hotel’s pool safety system. The German outlet Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR) said several people were injured at a Phantasialand hotel on Friday after its email system failed to deliver a safety alert about elevated chlorine levels in the pool, as spotted earlier by NotebookCheck and TechRadar.
15 hotel guests were injured by chlorine poisoning due to Microsoft’s global email outage
A German hotel missed email alerts about elevated chlorine levels in its pool during the outage last week.
A machine-translated Facebook post from a German fire department said it responded to a Phantasialand hotel after a “technical malfunction” caused an excessive amount of chlorine to enter a swimming pool, resulting in chlorine gas leaking into the surrounding area. As reported by WDR, 15 people were affected by the incident, including four who were transported to the hospital.
Microsoft has since published a post-incident report about the outage, and EVP Charles Lamanna posted an abridged version last night on X. The company says three factors contributed significantly to the incident, including a bug introduced in a previous update in July. This, coupled with a surge in load following an earlier Teams outage and an “unrelated issue” from the previous day that knocked out nearly 14 percent of its server capacity, activated the conditions for the “latent” bug in the July update to rear its head, which “caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding” during the peak traffic window in the US on Thursday.
The outage lasted from Thursday afternoon and well into Friday morning for many businesses on the East Coast, before Microsoft said service was fully restored on Sunday. “Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again,” Microsoft says. “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state.” Microsoft adds that it couldn’t “quickly revert the change” because the defect was a latent bug from several months ago.

articles.title: The Fire TV Stick 4K Plus is on sale for less than Amazon’s entry-level streamer
articles.body:
Amazon no longer considers the midrange Fire TV Stick 4K Plus as part of its official lineup following the launch of it latest Fire TV Stick 4K, but that doesn’t mean the streaming device isn’t still good value. In fact, it’s an even more attractive option now that it’s dropped to $29.99 ($40 off) at Amazon and Best Buy in the run-up to Black Friday. That’s just $5 shy of its lowest price to date, rendering it cheaper than both the entry-level Fire TV Stick HD and its new midrange replacement, the Fire TV Stick 4K.
The Fire TV Stick 4K Plus is on sale for less than Amazon’s entry-level streamer
It may not be Amazon’s latest streaming dongle, but it offers more features for just $29.99.
The Fire TV Stick 4K Plus still offers a good balance of price and performance. Unlike its replacement, it supports both Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, delivering more vibrant colors, better contrast, and immersive audio with compatible TVs and speakers. It does require a separate power adapter, though, whereas the newer model can draw power directly from your TV’s USB port. You also don’t get as much storage here as with the high-end Fire TV Stick 4K Max, though 8GB should be plenty for streaming apps like Netflix and Disney Plus.
The Plus model also supports Amazon’s redesigned Fire TV interface, which my colleague John Higgins found to be an impressive update. It makes it easier to browse different content categories and pin your favorite apps for quick access. Thanks to Alexa Plus support, you can also press the voice button on the included Alexa Voice Remote to find something to watch, control compatible smart home devices like lights and thermostats, check sports scores, and more without getting off your couch. Just don’t expect a customizable shortcut button, as that’s exclusive to the latest Fire TV Remote.
One final note: the Plus ships with Amazon’s Fire OS, and unlike the company’s Vega OS that ships in newer streaming sticks, the former allow for sideloading of Android TV apps, if that’s of interest to you.

articles.title: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
articles.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.”
Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
Altman suggested we all ‘share this memory’ and said, ‘I think the home tinkering is great.’
The comments were made onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday.
Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month, saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.”
AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles. Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.”
Onstage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying:
“The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.”
Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

articles.title: Voyage Labs raises $12 million for a specialized AI travel assistant
articles.body:
Planning a trip is a favorite demo for personal AI assistants — you can try it with Muse, or with Gemini, or half a dozen other choices. But while most pitches use travel-planning as part of a general-purpose agent pitch, a new startup from a Google Maps alum is betting that a specialized travel-planning agent can beat the competition.
The company is called Voyage Labs, and on Tuesday it announced $12 million in seed funding led by Kleiner Perkins, with participation from SignalFire and SV Angel. The company plans to use the funding to expand supplier partnerships and grow its engineering team.
Voyage Labs’ flagship product, called Atlas, is meant to work as a personal assistant for your trip-planning, available today in private beta.
“People can use it to plan and book and manage their entire journey, from the time they have an inspiration to the time they come back home,” says co-founder and CEO Manik Gupta.
Atlas is designed to serve as an always-on assistant throughout the planning process, fielding ideas and doing research on every idea that’s raised. The long time horizon means Atlas can tailor recommendations based on weeks of conversation, while also monitoring real-time price fluctuations and ultimately booking flights and hotels.
For the Voyage founders, it’s an ideal match between technology and use case. “Trip planning is a project that has its own lifecycle,” says Yogesh Jain, co-founder and CTO of the company. “You’re planning across days and weeks — so long-running agents as a technology matches that very well.”
Travel assistants are already a crowded field, but Voyage will be starting with a lot of experience in the space. Gupta was previously the director of Product Management for Google Maps, followed by four years as chief product officer at Uber. As he puts it, “I spent eight years where my only job was to wake up in the morning and go build the map. I’m just very obsessed with that problem.”
The biggest question is how Atlas will compete with the multi-purpose AI assistants built by frontier labs. But as Gupta notes, the space is still changing fast, and it’s hard for anyone to be sure what form factors will thrive in the coming years. Ultimately, Voyage is betting that travel is specialized enough to need a specialized product.
“We are making a bet that this vertical around travel and outdoors is a large enough vertical that it needs a focused product solution,” Gupta told TechCrunch. “Ultimately, we believe we can actually stitch together an end-to-end experience that will help users.”
